<h2 id="create-a-test-your-way">Create a test your way</h2>
<p class="dh-sub">Every way ends in the same plain-text files, so you can mix them in one project.</p>
<div class="cards cols-2">
<a class="card" href="https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/write"><span class="card-title">Write it in a spreadsheet</span><span class="card-text">No code needed. List the steps in CSV or YAML. Anyone on the team can read and review them.</span></a>
<a class="card" href="https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/record"><span class="card-title">Record it on the device</span><span class="card-text">No code needed. Run one step at a time in <code class="ic">optics live</code>. Every step that works is saved.</span></a>
<a class="card" href="https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/describe"><span class="card-title">Describe it in plain English</span><span class="card-text">Uses an AI model. Tell Optics what to do. An AI model drives the device and keeps the steps that mattered.</span></a>
<a class="card" href="https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/agent"><span class="card-title">Hand it to your AI agent</span><span class="card-text">Uses an AI model. Connect <code class="ic">optics mcp</code> to your agent. It explores the app and writes the suite.</span></a>

# Get started with Optics

> Learn what Optics does, what it tests, and the fastest way to see it run.

Optics is open-source test automation for apps on Android, iOS, the web and TV. You describe what a person does in your app, such as signing in or adding a product to the cart. Optics repeats it on a real device, an emulator or a browser, and tells you when the app stops behaving.

## How a test works

A test is a short list of steps in a file, one action per row. A step reads like a sentence: **Press Element** *Sign in*, **Enter Text** *email field* *ava@birch.shop*.

You don't write code to find things on screen. Optics looks for each element several ways, cheapest first: by its position in the app's UI tree, by its visible text, by reading a screenshot, and by matching a picture of it. When a redesign breaks one way, the next one takes over, so tests break less often.

When a run finishes, you get a pass or fail for every step, screenshots of what Optics saw, and a JUnit report that any CI system can read.

## What you can test

| Target | How Optics drives it |
|---|---|
| Android and iOS apps | Through [Appium](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/android), on emulators, simulators and real phones |
| Websites | Through [Playwright or Selenium](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/web), no device needed |
| Android TV, Samsung Tizen, LG webOS | Through Appium, with the remote's arrow keys. See [TV](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/tv) |
| Locked-down production devices | As a Bluetooth mouse and keyboard, with a camera watching the screen. See [Production devices](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/production) |

Optics runs on macOS, Linux and Windows with Python 3.12 or newer. There is no account, cloud service or API key. Everything runs on your machine or in your CI.

## When Optics is not the right tool

Optics tests what a person does through the interface. Reach for something else for unit tests, load testing, API-only contract tests, or pixel-by-pixel visual comparison.

## Start here

- [Quickstart](https://optics-framework.org/docs/get-started/quickstart): Install Optics and run a working test in about five minutes. (Recommended)
- [Install Optics](https://optics-framework.org/docs/get-started/install): Every install option, plus the drivers and engines each platform needs.
- [Write your first test](https://optics-framework.org/docs/get-started/first-test): Build a test from scratch against a real online store, step by step.
- [How Optics works](https://optics-framework.org/docs/get-started/concepts): The four ideas every test is built from.

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/get-started/quickstart

# Run your first test

> Install Optics and run a working test in a browser in about five minutes.

You'll install Optics, let it create a small project from a working sample, and run that project in a browser. You don't need a phone or an emulator for this.

### Install Optics

Run the installer for your system. It puts Optics in its own folder (`~/.optics`), so it doesn't touch the rest of your Python setup. You need Python 3.12 or newer.

**macOS and Linux**

```shell
$ curl -fsSL https://optics-framework.org/install | sh
```
**Windows**

```powershell
PS> irm https://optics-framework.org/install.ps1 | iex
```
**pip**

```shell
$ pip install optics-framework
```

Open a new terminal window, then check that the `optics` command works:

```shell
$ optics --version
Optics Framework 1.10.5
```

### Create a project

Run the guided setup:

```shell
$ optics quickstart
```

It asks a few questions. Every question has a default, shown in brackets. For this quickstart, answer like this:

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| What do you want to automate? | `web` |
| Install Playwright, Selenium now? | Yes |
| Start from the 'playwright' example? | Yes |
| Project name | Press Enter to keep `my-optics-project` |
| Where should the project live? | Press Enter for the current folder |
| Overwrite the template's config.yaml with your own answers? | No |

Optics installs the browser engine, copies the sample into `my-optics-project`, and checks your setup. Rows marked ⚠️ in that check are optional extras you can add later.

### Run the test

When Optics asks **Run your first test now?**, answer yes. You can also run it yourself at any time:

```shell
$ optics execute my-optics-project
```

A browser window opens, visits example.com, looks for some text and closes. On Optics 1.10.5 this first run fails, and that's worth seeing: it shows you how Optics reports a failure.

```terminal
Test Suite
├── Playwright Suite Setup                               |      1.54s |    PASS
│   └── Open Example Page                                |      1.54s |    PASS
│       └── Launch App (https://example.com)             |      1.54s |    PASS
├── TC1 Verify Landing                                   |      7.38s |    FAIL
│   └── Verify Example Page                              |      7.38s |    FAIL
│       └── Validate Element (text=Example Domain)       |      7.17s |    FAIL
└── Playwright Suite Teardown                            |      0.14s |    PASS
    └── Close Browser                                    |      0.13s |    PASS
        └── Close And Terminate App                      |      0.13s |    PASS
╭──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ Total Test Cases: 3 | Passed: 2 | Failed: 1                                  │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
╭────────────────────────────── Failure details ───────────────────────────────╮
│ TC1 Verify Landing → step 'Validate Element (text=Example Domain)' — Keyword │
│ 'Validate Element' failed after fallback attempts                            │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
```

The tree shows where the run broke: the test case `TC1 Verify Landing`, its module `Verify Example Page`, and the step `Validate Element`. **Failure details** names the step and the value it looked for, `text=Example Domain`. Optics tried every way it knows to find that text, and the page doesn't show it: example.com dropped its "Example Domain" heading after 1.10.5 shipped.

### Fix the element and run again

Steps refer to things on screen by name, and the names live in one file, so the fix is one line. Open `my-optics-project/test_data/elements.csv` and change the `Heading` row to text the page does show:

`test_data/elements.csv`:

```csv
Element_Name,Element_ID
Heading,text=This domain is for use in documentation examples
```

Run it again:

```shell
$ optics execute my-optics-project
```

Every step passes:

```terminal
Test Suite
├── Playwright Suite Setup                               |      1.39s |    PASS
│   └── Open Example Page                                |      1.39s |    PASS
│       └── Launch App (https://example.com)             |      1.39s |    PASS
├── TC1 Verify Landing                                   |      0.12s |    PASS
│   └── Verify Example Page                              |      0.12s |    PASS
│       └── Validate Element (text=This domain is for... |      0.12s |    PASS
└── Playwright Suite Teardown                            |      0.10s |    PASS
    └── Close Browser                                    |      0.10s |    PASS
        └── Close And Terminate App                      |      0.10s |    PASS
╭──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ Total Test Cases: 3 | Passed: 3 | Failed: 0                                  │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
```

The next release ships the corrected sample. On a newer version the first run passes, and you can skip this step.

## What just happened

The project is three small spreadsheets and a settings file:

```tree
my-optics-project/
├── config.yaml                  # which browser or device to use
├── test_cases/test_cases.csv    # which flows to run
├── modules/modules.csv          # the steps in each flow
├── test_data/elements.csv       # names for things on screen
└── execution_output/            # results, written by each run
```

Open `modules/modules.csv` in any editor or spreadsheet app. Each row is one step: a **module** name, a **keyword** such as `Launch App`, and the values that keyword needs.

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2
Open Example Page,Launch App,https://example.com
Verify Example Page,Validate Element,${Heading}
Close Browser,Close And Terminate App
```

`${Heading}` is a name defined in `elements.csv`. Steps refer to things on screen by name, so when the page changes you update one line in `elements.csv` instead of every test.

## Testing a phone app instead

Choose `mobile` when `optics quickstart` asks what you want to automate. Optics then starts from a sample for the Android Contacts app. Before the run, you need an Android emulator or phone connected, and an Appium server running. [Set up Android testing](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/android) walks through both.

## Next steps

- [Write your first test](https://optics-framework.org/docs/get-started/first-test): Build a sign-in and add-to-cart test against a real online store. (Next)
- [How Optics works](https://optics-framework.org/docs/get-started/concepts): Test cases, modules, elements and keywords, explained.
- [Install Optics](https://optics-framework.org/docs/get-started/install): Every install option, and the engines for each platform.
- [Choose how to create tests](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/): Write, record, describe in plain English, or hand it to an AI agent.

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/get-started/install

# Install Optics

> Install the optics command, then add only the drivers and engines your platform needs.

Optics has two parts. The **core** is the `optics` command, which reads your tests and runs them. **Engines** are optional add-ons: a driver for each kind of target (browser, phone, TV) and extra ways to find things on screen. You install the core once and add engines as you need them.

## Before you begin

You need **Python 3.12 or newer**. Check with:

```shell
$ python3 --version
Python 3.12.13
```

If you have an older version, install a current one from [python.org](https://www.python.org/downloads/) or your system's package manager.

## Install the core

We recommend the installer. It creates a private Python environment under `~/.optics`, adds `optics` to your PATH, and leaves your system Python alone.

**macOS and Linux**

```shell
$ curl -fsSL https://optics-framework.org/install | sh
```
**Windows**

```powershell
PS> irm https://optics-framework.org/install.ps1 | iex
```
**pip**

Use pip when you manage your own virtual environment, for example inside a CI job or an existing test repository.

```shell
$ python3 -m venv .venv
$ source .venv/bin/activate
$ pip install optics-framework
```

Open a new terminal so it picks up the updated PATH, then check the install:

```shell
$ optics --version
Optics Framework 1.10.5
```

**Installer options**
Pass options after `sh -s --`. On Windows, set the matching environment variable before running the installer.

| Option | Windows variable | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--version 1.10.5` | `OPTICS_VERSION` | Install a specific release. |
| `--extra appium,easyocr` | `OPTICS_EXTRA` | Install engines at the same time. |
| `--dir PATH` | `OPTICS_INSTALL_DIR` | Install somewhere other than `~/.optics`. |
| `--no-modify-path` | `OPTICS_NO_MODIFY_PATH` | Don't edit your shell profile. |
| `--dry-run` | | Print what would happen and change nothing. |
| `--uninstall` | | Remove Optics and the PATH entry it added. |

```shell
$ curl -fsSL https://optics-framework.org/install | sh -s -- --extra playwright,easyocr
```

## Add engines for your platform

The core install ships without drivers, so it stays small. Add the ones for what you test. `optics setup` installs engines that match your Optics version:

**Web**

```shell
$ optics setup --install playwright
```
Playwright needs no server. Optics downloads its Chromium browser for you. To use Selenium instead, see [Web](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/web).
**Android**

```shell
$ optics setup --install appium
```
You also need the Appium server, the Android SDK (for `adb`) and a device or emulator. [Set up Android testing](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/android) covers each one.
**iOS**

```shell
$ optics setup --install appium
```
You also need the Appium server with the XCUITest driver, Xcode, and a simulator or device. See [iOS](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/ios).

Run `optics setup` with no options to pick engines from a list instead, or `optics setup --list` to see every name.

### Optional engines

Add these when a page tells you to. You don't need them for your first test.

| Engine | Install name | Adds |
|---|---|---|
| EasyOCR | `easyocr` | Finds elements by reading text on a screenshot. Runs locally. |
| Tesseract | `pytesseract` | A lighter OCR engine. Needs the Tesseract program installed too. |
| Google Vision | `google-vision` | Cloud OCR. Needs Google Cloud credentials. |
| AI model | `gemini`, `openai` or `anthropic` | Plain-English test creation and AI self-heal. Pick the one for your account; see [Describe it](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/describe#before-you-begin). |
| MCP server | `mcp` | Lets AI agents drive Optics. The installer always includes it; with pip: `pip install "optics-framework[mcp]"`. |

Bundles install several at once: `mobile` (Appium), `web` (Playwright and Selenium), `vision` (all OCR engines), `llm` (all three AI engines) and `all` (everything except the MCP server). The [engines reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/engines) lists every engine.

## Check your setup

`optics doctor` checks Python, each engine, and the tools around them:

```shell
$ optics doctor
```

```terminal
🩺 optics doctor

Core
  ✅ python                            3.12.13
  ✅ optics-framework                  installed, version 1.10.5

Engines
  ⚠️ Appium                            appium-python-client not installed
      → optics setup --install appium
  ✅ Playwright                        playwright 1.63.0

Web
  ✅ playwright browser                Chromium download found
```

✅ rows are ready. ⚠️ rows are optional or not needed for your platform. Pass a project folder (`optics doctor my_project`) to also check its `config.yaml`.

## If the install doesn't work

- **`optics: command not found`.** Open a new terminal. If it still fails, add `~/.optics/bin` to your PATH, as the installer printed.
- **`optics setup` refuses to install.** Conda, pipx and tool-managed environments (uv tool, Poetry, PDM) manage their own packages, so `optics setup` prints the right command for that tool instead. Run that command, or use a plain virtual environment.
- **EasyOCR fails under Conda.** EasyOCR and Optics need different NumPy versions under Conda. Use the installer or a standard `venv`.

[Troubleshooting](https://optics-framework.org/docs/help/troubleshooting) covers more cases.

## Next steps

- [Quickstart](https://optics-framework.org/docs/get-started/quickstart): Run a working sample in a browser.
- [Write your first test](https://optics-framework.org/docs/get-started/first-test): Build a test of your own, step by step.

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/get-started/first-test

# Write your first test

> Build a test from scratch that signs in to an online store and adds a product to the cart.

You'll write a complete test by hand: open a store, sign in, add a backpack to the cart, and check that it worked. Along the way you'll meet the four files every Optics project uses, and see what happens when a test fails.

The test runs in a browser against [Sauce Labs' demo store](https://www.saucedemo.com), a public site built for practising test automation. You don't need a phone, an emulator or an account.

**Before you begin:**
Install Optics and the Playwright engine. If you ran the [quickstart](https://optics-framework.org/docs/get-started/quickstart), you already have both.

```shell
$ optics setup --install playwright
```

### Create an empty project

```shell
$ optics init first-test
```

Optics asks which template to start from. Type `1` for **(Blank project)** and press Enter. You get a folder with empty files and headers already in place:

```tree
first-test/
├── config.yaml
├── test_cases/test_cases.csv
├── modules/modules.csv
└── test_data/elements.csv
```

The folder names are only a convention. Optics recognises each file by the column names in its first row, so you can move files around later.

### Tell Optics to use a browser

`config.yaml` says what Optics drives. Replace its contents with this:

`config.yaml`:

```yaml
driver_sources:
  - playwright:
      enabled: true

elements_sources:
  - playwright_find_element:
      enabled: true
  - playwright_page_source:
      enabled: true
  - playwright_screenshot:
      enabled: true

log_level: WARNING
```

`driver_sources` picks the browser driver. `elements_sources` lists the ways Optics may look at the page: asking the browser directly, reading the page's HTML, and taking screenshots. `log_level: WARNING` keeps the terminal quiet so you can read the results.

### Name the things you'll touch

Before writing steps, give each field and button a name. Open `test_data/elements.csv` and add four rows under the header:

`test_data/elements.csv`:

```csv
Element_Name,Element_ID
username_field,//input[@id='user-name']
password_field,//input[@id='password']
login_button,//input[@id='login-button']
backpack_add_button,//button[@id='add-to-cart-sauce-labs-backpack']
```

The left column is the name you'll use in steps. The right column tells Optics how to find it. These are **XPaths**: paths into the page's structure. `//input[@id='user-name']` means "the input whose id is `user-name`".

**Finding an element's id:**
Open the store in Chrome, right-click a field and choose **Inspect**. The highlighted HTML shows the element's `id`. You don't always need XPaths: [Define elements](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/define) shows how to use visible text and pictures instead.

### Write the steps

Steps live in **modules**: small, reusable groups of actions. Open `modules/modules.csv` and add three modules:

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2
Open the store,Launch App,https://www.saucedemo.com
Sign in,Enter Text,${username_field},standard_user
Sign in,Enter Text,${password_field},secret_sauce
Sign in,Press Element,${login_button}
Sign in,Assert Presence,Products
Add the backpack to the cart,Press Element,${backpack_add_button}
Add the backpack to the cart,Assert Presence,Remove
```

Read each row left to right: the module it belongs to, a **keyword** (the action), then the values the keyword needs. `${username_field}` refers to the name you defined in the previous step. `Products` and `Remove` are plain text that should appear on screen: the products page title, and the label the backpack's button changes to once it's in the cart.

**Enter Text fails in browsers on Optics 1.10.5:**
On 1.10.5, every Enter Text in a browser fails with `Object of type Locator is not JSON serializable`. A fix is on its way in the next release. Until you upgrade, click the field and type into it in two steps. Replace the two `Enter Text` rows with these four:

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
Sign in,Press Element,${username_field}
Sign in,Enter Text Direct,standard_user
Sign in,Press Element,${password_field}
Sign in,Enter Text Direct,secret_sauce
```

### Turn the modules into a test case

A **test case** is a named flow made of modules, run in order. Open `test_cases/test_cases.csv`:

`test_cases/test_cases.csv`:

```csv
test_case,test_step
Shopper can add a backpack,Open the store
Shopper can add a backpack,Sign in
Shopper can add a backpack,Add the backpack to the cart
```

### Check the test without running it

`optics dry_run` reads every file and checks that each keyword exists and each `${name}` is defined. It doesn't click anything, so it's a quick way to catch typos:

```shell
$ optics dry_run first-test
```

```terminal
Test Suite
└── Shopper can add a backpack                                  |  0.00s |    PASS
    ├── Open the store                                          |  0.00s |    PASS
    ├── Sign in                                                 |  0.00s |    PASS
    └── Add the backpack to the cart                            |  0.00s |    PASS
╭──────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ Total Test Cases: 1 | Passed: 1 | Failed: 0          │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
```

### Run it

```shell
$ optics execute first-test
```

A browser window opens, signs in and adds the backpack. The terminal prints every step with its time:

```terminal
Test Suite
└── Shopper can add a backpack                                     |  1.88s |    PASS
    ├── Open the store                                             |  0.85s |    PASS
    │   └── Launch App (https://www.saucedemo.com)                 |  0.85s |    PASS
    ├── Sign in                                                    |  0.82s |    PASS
    │   ├── Enter Text (//input[@id='user-name'], standard_user)   |  0.17s |    PASS
    │   ├── Enter Text (//input[@id='password'], secret_sauce)     |  0.09s |    PASS
    │   ├── Press Element (//input[@id='login-button'])            |  0.11s |    PASS
    │   └── Assert Presence (Products)                             |  0.45s |    PASS
    └── Add the backpack to the cart                               |  0.21s |    PASS
        ├── Press Element (//button[@id='add-to-cart-sauce-labs... |  0.11s |    PASS
        └── Assert Presence (Remove)                               |  0.09s |    PASS
╭──────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ Total Test Cases: 1 | Passed: 1 | Failed: 0          │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
```

You've written and run a test. Everything Optics produced is in `first-test/execution_output/`: a screenshot taken before each step, and `junit_output.xml`, a standard report your CI can read.

## Watch a test fail

A test is only useful if it fails when the app is broken. Pretend the store renamed its button: change the last row of `modules.csv` to look for `Removed` instead of `Remove`, then run the test again.

```terminal
    └── Add the backpack to the cart                               | 20.74s |    FAIL
        ├── Press Element (//button[@id='add-to-cart-sauce-labs... |  0.12s |    PASS
        └── Assert Presence (Removed)                              | 20.51s |    FAIL
╭──────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ Total Test Cases: 1 | Passed: 0 | Failed: 1          │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
╭─────────────────── Failure details ──────────────────╮
│ Shopper can add a backpack → step 'Assert Presence   │
│ (Removed)' — Keyword 'Assert Presence' failed after  │
│ fallback attempts                                    │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
```

The run is slower this time because Assert Presence keeps looking for the text, in case the page is still loading, before it gives up. The tree shows exactly which step failed, and the **Failure details** box names it. The command also exits with code `1`, which is how CI knows to mark the build red. Change `Removed` back to `Remove` before you continue.

## Make the test survive a redesign

Locators break when developers rename things. Optics lets an element have more than one value and tries them in order until one works. Add a second row for `login_button` that uses the button's visible text, and break the first one on purpose:

`test_data/elements.csv`:

```csv
Element_Name,Element_ID
username_field,//input[@id='user-name']
password_field,//input[@id='password']
login_button,//input[@id='sign-in-button']
login_button,Login
backpack_add_button,//button[@id='add-to-cart-sauce-labs-backpack']
```

Run the test again. It still passes: the XPath finds nothing, so Optics tries the text `Login` and clicks the button. Put the correct id back afterwards, but keep the text row as a safety net. [How Optics finds elements](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/) explains every fallback.

## What you learned

- A project is a **config** (what to drive), **elements** (names for things on screen), **modules** (steps) and **test cases** (flows).
- Steps are keywords with values. `${name}` refers to an element.
- `optics dry_run` checks your files. `optics execute` runs them and writes results to `execution_output/`.
- An element can have several values, so one broken locator doesn't break the test.

## Next steps

- [How Optics works](https://optics-framework.org/docs/get-started/concepts): The ideas behind what you just built, in more depth.
- [Record a test](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/record): Build the same test by doing it, one step at a time.
- [Read the results](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/results): Screenshots, logs and the JUnit report.
- [Set up Android testing](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/android): Run tests on a phone or emulator.

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/get-started/concepts

# How Optics works

> Learn the five ideas every Optics test is built from, and what happens when a test runs.

An Optics test is data, not code. You write down **what** a person does in plain rows. Optics works out **how** to do each step on the screen in front of it.

## Keywords

A **keyword** is one action or check, such as `Press Element`, `Enter Text` or `Assert Presence`. Every step in a test is one keyword plus the values it needs. Keywords fall into four groups:

| Group | Use it to | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| App management | Open and close the app or website | `Launch App`, `Close And Terminate App` |
| Actions | Tap, type, swipe and press keys | `Press Element`, `Enter Text`, `Scroll` |
| Verification | Check what's on screen | `Assert Presence`, `Validate Element` |
| Flow control | Repeat steps, branch, read data, call APIs | `Run Loop`, `Condition`, `Read Data` |

The same keywords work on every platform. `Press Element` taps on a phone and clicks in a browser. The [keyword reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/) lists all of them, and `optics list` prints them in your terminal.

## Elements

An **element** is a name for something on screen, like `sign_in` or `search_bar`. Steps use the name inside `${…}`, and `elements.csv` says how to find it:

`test_data/elements.csv`:

```csv
Element_Name,Element_ID
sign_in,//*[@resource-id='login']
sign_in,Sign in
search_bar,//*[@resource-id='search']
```

Keeping locators in one file means a redesign is a one-line change, not an edit to every test. An element can have several values. `sign_in` above can be found by its id or by its text, and Optics tries them in order until one works.

A value can be an XPath (a path through the app's UI tree), visible text, or the file name of a picture of the element. Elements can also hold plain data, such as a username, so one file holds everything a test might change.

## Modules

A **module** is a named, reusable sequence of steps, like *Sign In* or *Add To Cart*. Write a flow once as a module and reuse it in as many test cases as you like. When the sign-in screen changes, you fix one module.

## Test cases

A **test case** is a flow you want to check, made of modules in order. *Checkout* might run *Sign In*, *Add To Cart* and *Pay*. Each test case passes or fails on its own.

Two names are special. A test case called **Suite Setup** runs before all the others, and **Suite Teardown** runs after them. Use them to launch the app once and close it at the end.

## Configuration

`config.yaml` says what Optics drives and how it may look at the screen. It holds lists of **engines**:

- A **driver** controls the target: Appium for phones and TVs, Playwright or Selenium for browsers, or a Bluetooth keyboard and mouse for locked-down devices.
- **Element sources** are ways to look at the screen: ask the app directly, read its UI tree, or take a screenshot.
- **Text detection** (OCR) and **image detection** are optional. They let Optics find elements on a screenshot when the UI tree can't help.

The tests themselves never mention engines. That's why the same test runs on a phone today and against a different device tomorrow.

## What happens during a run

When you run `optics execute`, Optics:

1. Reads every file in the project folder and decides what each one is from its column names.
2. Runs **Suite Setup**, then each test case in order, then **Suite Teardown**.
3. For each step, takes a screenshot, finds the element, and performs the action.
4. If a step fails, skips the rest of that test case and moves on to the next one. One broken flow doesn't stop the run.
5. At the end, checks the last screen for known error messages, if you've [defined any](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/error-detection).
6. Writes the results to `execution_output/`, and exits with `0` if every test case passed or `1` if any failed.

### How Optics finds an element

For each value of an element, Optics tries the cheapest ways first. An XPath is looked up in the UI tree. Text is looked up in the UI tree, and if it isn't there, Optics reads a screenshot with OCR. A picture is matched against a screenshot. If everything fails and you've switched on [AI self-heal](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/self-heal), an AI model looks at the screen and tries to recover.

[How Optics finds elements](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/) covers the full order and how to tune it.

## See also

- [Write your first test](https://optics-framework.org/docs/get-started/first-test)
- [Choose how to create tests](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/)
- [Project files reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/files)
- [Glossary](https://optics-framework.org/docs/help/glossary)

# What to learn next

> Pick your next page based on what you want Optics to do for you.

You've run a test and know the basic pieces. Optics has a lot more in it, and you don't need most of it on day one. Start from the goal closest to yours.

## I want to test my own app

- [Android](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/android): Emulators and phones through Appium.
- [iOS](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/ios): Simulators and iPhones through Appium.
- [Web](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/web): Any website through Playwright or Selenium.

## I want to create tests faster

- [Record a test](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/record): Run steps one at a time against the live app and save the ones that worked. (No code)
- [Describe a test in plain English](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/describe): Let an AI model drive the app from a sentence, then keep its steps. (AI)
- [Let your AI agent build tests](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/agent): Connect Optics to Claude, Cursor or any MCP client. (AI)
- [Use Optics from Python](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/python): Call keywords from pytest or your own scripts. (Code)

## I want tests that break less

- [Define elements](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/define): Give elements fallback values that survive redesigns.
- [Find elements by text and image](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/text-and-images): Use OCR and pictures when the UI tree can't help.

## I want to run tests every day

- [Run tests in CI](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/ci): Run the suite on every pull request.
- [Catch error screens](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/error-detection): Fail the run when the app shows a crash or "Session expired".

## A suggested order

If you're learning Optics from scratch, this order adds one idea at a time:

1. [Write a test suite](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/write): the file formats in full.
2. [Define elements](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/define): locators that last.
3. [Run a suite](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/) and [read the results](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/results).
4. [Organise a suite](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/organise): setup, teardown and reuse.
5. [Variables](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/variables) and [data-driven tests](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/data-driven): one flow, many inputs.
6. [Run tests in CI](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/ci), then work through the [readiness checklist](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/checklist).

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/

# Choose how to create tests

> Learn which way of creating tests fits your team. Every way produces the same files.

Optics gives you several ways to turn a user flow into a test. They all end in the same plain-text suite: CSV or YAML files that live in your repository and run with `optics execute`. You can mix them in one project, so a test someone recorded can sit next to one an AI agent wrote.

## Choose your approach

- [Write it](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/write): List the steps in a spreadsheet or text editor. Anyone can read and review them. (No code)
- [Record it](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/record): Run steps one at a time against the live app in `optics live`. What works is saved. (No code)
- [Describe it](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/describe): Type what you want in plain English. An AI model drives the app and keeps the steps. (AI)
- [Delegate it](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/agent): Connect your AI agent with `optics mcp`. It explores the app and writes the suite. (AI)
- [Code it in Python](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/python): Call keywords from pytest or any Python script. (Code)
- [Code it in Robot Framework](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/robot): Use Optics keywords in `.robot` files. (Code)

### Which one should I use?

We recommend **recording** for most people starting out. You see each step work on the real app before it's saved, and you end up with readable CSV files you can edit by hand later. Teams then usually **write** small changes directly in the files.

Choose **describe** or **delegate** when you have an AI model key (Gemini, OpenAI, Claude) or an AI agent, and want a first draft of a long flow quickly. Review what the AI saved, the same way you'd review a colleague's change.

Choose **Python or Robot Framework** only if your tests need logic that the files can't express, or your team already runs everything through pytest or Robot. Code-based tests lose the main benefit of Optics files: that anyone on the team can read them.

| | Write | Record | Describe | Delegate | Python / Robot |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Best for** | Small edits, reviews | Building a flow on the real app | Long flows, quick drafts | Agent-driven teams | Custom logic |
| **You need** | An editor | A running app | An AI model key | An MCP client | Python skills |
| **Output** | CSV or YAML | CSV | CSV | CSV | Python or `.robot` |
| **Runs with** | `optics execute` | `optics execute` | `optics execute` | `optics execute` | pytest or `robot` |
| **Effort** | No code | No code | No code | No code | Code |

## Every way ends in plain text

Tests are files in your repository, not records in someone else's cloud. That has two practical benefits:

- **Changing a test is a pull request.** When a redesign moves the sign-in button, the diff shows the one element that changed.
- **CI runs exactly what was merged.** There's no separate test-management system to keep in sync.

`test_data/elements.csv`:

```diff
 Element_Name,Element_ID
 email_field,//*[@resource-id='email']
-sign_in,//*[@text='Sign in']
+sign_in,//*[@resource-id='login']
+sign_in,Sign in
 search_bar,//*[@resource-id='search']
```

## See also

- [How Optics works](https://optics-framework.org/docs/get-started/concepts)
- [Organise a suite](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/organise)
- [Project files reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/files)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/write

# Write a test suite

> Write test cases, modules and elements by hand, in CSV or YAML.

Writing a suite by hand is the most direct way to create tests, and it's how most edits happen once a suite exists. You need a text editor or a spreadsheet app. This page covers the three files a suite is made of, in the order we recommend writing them.

## Set up a project

Create a project with `optics init`, then fill in its files:

```shell
$ optics init birch-tests
```

Pick **(Blank project)** when asked for a template. You get this layout:

```tree
birch-tests/
├── config.yaml                  # what to drive
├── test_cases/test_cases.csv    # which flows run
├── modules/modules.csv          # the steps
└── test_data/elements.csv       # names for things on screen
```

Optics finds each file by what's inside it, not by its name or folder. A CSV whose first row is `test_case,test_step` is a test-cases file wherever it sits. You can split a big suite across several files of each kind. If you haven't set up `config.yaml` yet, [Install Optics](https://optics-framework.org/docs/get-started/install) and the [platform guides](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/) show what to put in it.

## Choose CSV or YAML

Both formats load into the same suite, and one project can hold both. Pick the one your team reads best:

- **CSV** opens in any spreadsheet. Each step is one row, so a diff shows exactly which step changed.
- **YAML** keeps a whole flow in one indented file, which reads well in a code editor.

The examples on this page show both. Choose a tab and the rest of the page follows. [Write tests in YAML](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/yaml) covers the YAML rules in detail.

## Name the things on screen

Start with **elements**: a name for each field, button or label your test touches, and how to find it.

**CSV**

`test_data/elements.csv`:

```csv
Element_Name,Element_ID
email_field,//*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/email']
password_field,//*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/password']
sign_in,//*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/login']
sign_in,Sign in
search_bar,Search Birch
password,correct-horse
```
**YAML**

`birch.yaml`:

```yaml
Elements:
  email_field: "//*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/email']"
  password_field: "//*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/password']"
  sign_in: ["//*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/login']", "Sign in"]
  search_bar: Search Birch
  password: correct-horse
```

The header must be exactly `Element_Name,Element_ID`. Repeat a name, or give a list in YAML, to add **fallbacks**: Optics tries the values in order until one works. Here `sign_in` is found by its id, or by its text if the id changes.

A value can be an XPath, visible text, or the file name of a picture of the element. [Define elements](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/define) explains each kind and when to use it.

**Tip:**
Elements can hold test data too, such as `email,ava@birch.shop`. Keeping data next to locators means one file holds everything that changes between environments.

## Write the steps as modules

A **module** is a named list of steps. Each step is one [keyword](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/) and its values.

**CSV**

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2
Launch Birch,Launch App
Sign In,Enter Text,${email_field},ava@birch.shop
Sign In,Enter Text,${password_field},${password}
Sign In,Press Element,${sign_in}
Sign In,Assert Presence,Picked for you
Add To Cart,Press Element,${search_bar}
Add To Cart,Enter Text Direct,trail runner
Add To Cart,Press Element,Trail Runner 2
Add To Cart,Press Element,Add to cart
Add To Cart,Assert Presence,Added to cart
```
**YAML**

`birch.yaml`:

```yaml
Modules:
  - Launch Birch:
      - Launch App
  - Sign In:
      - Enter Text ${email_field} ava@birch.shop
      - Enter Text ${password_field} ${password}
      - Press Element ${sign_in}
      - Assert Presence "Picked for you"
  - Add To Cart:
      - Press Element ${search_bar}
      - Enter Text Direct "trail runner"
      - Press Element "Trail Runner 2"
      - Press Element "Add to cart"
      - Assert Presence "Added to cart"
```

How a step is read:

- **Keyword names** are case-insensitive. `Press Element`, `press element` and `press_element` all work.
- **Values** fill the keyword's parameters in order. Add more `param_3`, `param_4` columns when a keyword needs them. Empty cells are skipped.
- **`${name}`** is replaced by the element called `name`. It only works when it's the whole value: `${email_field}` works, `Hello ${name}` is typed exactly as written.
- **Named values** like `index=1` or `timeout_str=20` set one parameter by name, so you can skip the ones in between. They only work with the keyword's real parameter names, which the [keyword reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/) lists.
- **Plain text** such as `Add to cart` is used as-is. For `Press Element`, plain text means "the element showing this text".

**Values with commas in CSV:**
A comma ends a CSV cell. Wrap a value that contains commas in double quotes, and double any quotes inside it: `"{""script"": ""mobile: pressKey""}"`. Spreadsheet apps do this for you when they save as CSV.

### Wait for the screen before you act

Action keywords like `Press Element` and `Enter Text` act on the screen as it is at that moment. They don't wait for a page to finish loading. After a step that changes screens, add a check that waits, such as `Assert Presence` (waits up to 30 seconds by default). The `Sign In` module above does this with `Assert Presence,Picked for you`.

## Combine modules into test cases

A **test case** is a flow made of modules, run in order. List one row per module:

**CSV**

`test_cases/test_cases.csv`:

```csv
test_case,test_step
Suite Setup,Launch Birch
Shopper can buy running shoes,Sign In
Shopper can buy running shoes,Add To Cart
```
**YAML**

`birch.yaml`:

```yaml
Test Cases:
  - Suite Setup:
      - Launch Birch
  - Shopper can buy running shoes:
      - Sign In
      - Add To Cart
```

A test case named **Suite Setup** runs once before the others, and **Suite Teardown** runs once after them. [Organise a suite](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/organise) covers setup, teardown and sharing modules.

## Check the suite, then run it

Check that every keyword exists and every `${name}` is defined, without touching the device:

```shell
$ optics dry_run birch-tests
```

When the dry run passes, run the suite for real:

```shell
$ optics execute birch-tests
```

## See also

- [Keyword reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/)
- [Define elements](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/define)
- [Project files reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/files)
- [Record a test](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/record) to build modules by doing the flow

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/record

# Record a test

> Build a test by running steps one at a time against the live app, then save the ones that worked.

`optics live` opens an interactive session next to your device or browser. You type a step, Optics runs it straight away, and you see whether it worked. Every step that succeeds is recorded. When the flow is done, `/save` writes it into your suite as a module, ready for `optics execute`.

## Before you begin

You need a project with a working `config.yaml` that has **exactly one** driver enabled. Any project from `optics quickstart` or the [first test tutorial](https://optics-framework.org/docs/get-started/first-test) works. For a phone, start the Appium server and your emulator first. See [Android](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/android) or [iOS](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/ios).

## Start a session

```shell
$ optics live birch-tests
```

Leave out the folder to use the current one. Optics opens the app straight away (it runs `launch_app` for you), so the first line of the session is already a recorded step.

The screen has three parts:

```terminal
  ✓ launch_app
     1.21s
  ✓ enter_text ${email_field} ava@birch.shop
     0.48s  [XPath]
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
› press_element "Sign in"
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
appium:emulator-5554  ·  rec ●  ·  /help · /quit · Tab complete · Ctrl-K keywords · Ctrl-N AI mode
```

- **History**, at the top: each step with ✓ or ✗, how long it took, and how the element was found (`[XPath]`, `[Text]`, `[OCR]` or `[Image]`).
- **Input**, in the middle: where you type.
- **Status bar**, at the bottom: the device or browser you're connected to, and `rec ●` to show recording is on.

## Run steps

Type a keyword and its values, separated by spaces, and press Enter:

```terminal
› enter_text ${email_field} ava@birch.shop
› enter_text ${password_field} "correct horse"
› press_element "Sign in"
› assert_presence "Picked for you"
```

- Write keyword names in `snake_case` or in words: `press_element`, `Press Element` and `press element` all work.
- Put quotes around a value that contains spaces.
- Type `${` to pick from the elements already defined in your project.
- Press Tab to complete a keyword name. The rest of its parameters appear in grey as a hint.
- Press Ctrl+K to browse every keyword.

If a step fails, it's shown with ✗ and the reason, and it isn't recorded. Try a different value and run it again. Only steps that work end up in your test.

## Save the recording

When the flow works, save it with a test case name and a module name:

```terminal
› /save Checkout Sign_In
  • Saved 4 step(s) → module 'Sign_In' in modules/modules.csv, test case 'Checkout' in test_cases/test_cases.csv
```

Optics then:

- appends the steps to `modules/modules.csv` as the module `Sign_In`,
- adds a `Checkout,Sign_In` row to `test_cases/test_cases.csv`,
- copies the session's screenshots to `execution_output/Sign_In/`,
- clears the recording, so the next steps you run become the next module.

Run more steps, then `/save Checkout Add_To_Cart` to add a second module to the same test case.

**Note:**
Names in `/save` can't contain spaces. Use underscores, or rename the module in `modules.csv` afterwards. If the module or test case already exists, Optics asks you to run the same `/save` again to confirm that you want to append to it.

`/save` writes the steps exactly as you typed them. If you typed `press_element "Sign in"`, the module uses the text `Sign in`. To use a named element instead, type `${sign_in}`, or edit `modules.csv` afterwards and add the element to `elements.csv`. `/save` always writes CSV, even in a project that uses YAML.

## Commands and keys

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `/save <test_case> <module>` | Save the recorded steps as a module in a test case. |
| `/elements` | Show every element defined in the project. |
| `/screenshot` | Save a screenshot to `screenshots/`. |
| `/device` | Pick a different connected phone or emulator (Appium only). `/device <id>` switches directly. |
| `/help` | Show help. |
| `/quit` | Leave. If you have unsaved steps, Optics warns you once; `/quit` again discards them. |

| Key | What it does |
|---|---|
| Enter | Run the step. |
| Tab / Shift+Tab | Complete a keyword or element name. |
| ↑ / ↓ | Recall earlier input. |
| Ctrl+K | Browse keywords. |
| Ctrl+N | Switch to plain-English mode. See [Describe a test](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/describe). |
| Ctrl+X | Stop a plain-English run. |
| Esc | Close a popup. |
| Ctrl+C or Ctrl+D | Quit. |

On Android, plugging in a new phone during a session switches to it automatically and opens the app.

## Where files go

| Path | What's in it |
|---|---|
| `modules/modules.csv`, `test_cases/test_cases.csv` | Saved modules and test cases |
| `screenshots/session_<time>/` | Screenshots from every step in the session |
| `logs/optics_live_<time>.log` | A full log of the session, useful when a step fails for unclear reasons |

## If it isn't working

- **"optics live needs a config.yaml…"**: run it from a project folder, or pass the folder: `optics live my_project`.
- **"optics live supports exactly one enabled driver"**: set `enabled: false` on every driver in `config.yaml` except one.
- **Every step fails with "run `launch_app` first"**: the app didn't open. Check that the Appium server is running and the device is connected (`optics doctor my_project`), then type `launch_app`.

## See also

- [Describe a test in plain English](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/describe)
- [Write a test suite](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/write)
- [Keyword reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/describe

# Describe a test in plain English

> Tell Optics what to do in a sentence, let an AI model drive the app, and keep the steps it took.

In plain-English mode, you type a goal like *add trail runners to the cart*. An AI model looks at the screen, picks one keyword at a time, and runs it on the real device until the goal is done. The steps it took are recorded like any other `optics live` steps, and `/save` writes them into your suite.

It works with Gemini, Claude, OpenAI, or a model you run yourself. It's the fastest way to draft a long flow, and the result is ordinary keywords you can read and edit.

## Before you begin

You need:

- A project that works in [`optics live`](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/record).
- An API key for an AI model, or a local model server such as Ollama.

### Install the AI engine

Pick the engine for the account you have:

| You have | Install |
|---|---|
| A Gemini API key, or Google Cloud Vertex AI | `gemini` |
| An OpenAI or OpenRouter key, Azure OpenAI, or a local model in Ollama, vLLM or LM Studio | `openai` |
| A Claude API key, or Claude on Amazon Bedrock or Vertex AI | `anthropic` |

Install that name, for example:

```shell
$ optics setup --install gemini
```

### Turn it on in config.yaml

Add an `llm_models` section to your project's `config.yaml`, using the same name:

`config.yaml`:

```yaml
llm_models:
  - gemini:
      enabled: true
```

For a server such as OpenRouter or Ollama, add its `url`. Gemini uses `gemini-2.5-flash` unless you set a `model`; the other engines need one. Pick a model that accepts screenshots. See [llm_models](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/config#llm-models) for every setting.

### Give Optics your key

Set the engine's key in the terminal you run `optics live` from:

**macOS and Linux**

```shell
$ export GEMINI_API_KEY="your-key"
```
**Windows**

```powershell
PS> $env:GEMINI_API_KEY = "your-key"
```

Use `GEMINI_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, or the variable you named in `api_key_env`. A local server needs no key.

**Warning:**
Don't put API keys in `config.yaml`. The file is meant to be committed with your tests, and a key in it would be shared with everyone who can read the repository.

## Describe a flow

Start `optics live`, then press Ctrl+N. The prompt changes from `›` to `ai ›`. Type what you want in plain English:

```terminal
ai › add trail runners to the cart
  ⋯ [ai] add trail runners to the cart
     thinking: open search and look for the shoes
    ✓ press_element "Search Birch"
       0.42s  [Text]
    ✓ enter_text "Search Birch" "trail runner"
       0.51s  [Text]
     thinking: Trail Runner 2 is the first result
    ✓ press_element "Trail Runner 2"
       0.88s  [OCR]
    ✓ press_element "Add to cart"
       0.37s  [Text]
  ✓ [ai] add trail runners to the cart
     done · 4 step(s) · 9.4s · recorded 4 (/save to keep)
```

Each turn, the model sees a screenshot, the list of elements on screen, your project's element names and the steps so far. Its reasoning appears as `thinking:` lines. Every action is a normal keyword, so it uses the same ways of finding elements as a test you wrote yourself.

Press Ctrl+X to stop a run, or Ctrl+N again to go back to typing keywords. You can mix both modes in one session.

## Keep the steps

When the goal is reached, Optics asks the model to drop dead ends and detours, so the recording keeps only the steps that mattered. If it pruned anything, the summary says so, for example `(kept 4 of 6 steps)`.

Save the steps the same way as a manual recording:

```terminal
ai › /save Checkout Add_To_Cart
```

Only runs that finish successfully are recorded. If the model gives up, hits its step limit, or you stop it, nothing from that run is saved.

### Review what you saved

Open `modules/modules.csv` and read the new rows before you commit them. The model names elements by their visible text, such as `"Add to cart"`. For steps that matter, replace the text with a named element from `elements.csv` and add a fallback, as described in [Define elements](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/define).

## Write goals the model can finish

- **Describe one outcome per instruction.** *Sign in as ava@birch.shop* works better than a whole checkout in one sentence. Run several instructions in a row instead.
- **Use the words on screen.** *Tap Add to cart* is clearer than *buy it*.
- **Give values explicitly.** *Search for "trail runner"*, not *search for shoes*.

Each run stops after 15 steps, after 3 failed steps in a row, or when the model repeats gestures without getting closer. Break long flows into smaller goals.

## Limits

- Each step is a call to the model, so a run costs API usage and takes several seconds per step.
- Screenshots go to your model provider while the mode is on, unless you run the model locally. Don't use a hosted model on screens that show data you can't send to a third party.

## See also

- [Record a test](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/record)
- [AI self-heal](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/self-heal), which uses the same model to recover a failing step during a run
- [Let your AI agent build tests](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/agent)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/agent

# Let your AI agent build tests

> Connect Optics to Claude, Cursor or any MCP client so your agent can drive a device and write the suite.

`optics mcp` is a [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) server. It gives an AI agent eyes and hands on a phone, TV or browser: every Optics keyword becomes a tool the agent can call, and the screen becomes something it can read. The agent explores your app, then writes an ordinary Optics suite that you review and run with `optics execute`.

The agent is yours. Optics doesn't call any AI service in this mode, so it works with whichever model your client uses.

## Before you begin

- An MCP client, such as Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor or VS Code.
- A target to drive: a browser (Playwright needs nothing else), or a phone or emulator with an Appium server running. See [Platforms](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/).

### Install the MCP server

The installer includes the MCP server, so if you used it there is nothing to do. With pip, install the `mcp` extra in the same environment as Optics:

```shell
$ pip install "optics-framework[mcp]"
```

### Add Optics to your client

**Claude Code**

```shell
$ claude mcp add optics -- optics mcp
```
**Claude Desktop**

Add this to `claude_desktop_config.json` (**Settings → Developer → Edit config**), then restart Claude Desktop:

`claude_desktop_config.json`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "optics": { "command": "optics", "args": ["mcp"] }
  }
}
```
**Cursor**

Add this to `.cursor/mcp.json` in your project, or `~/.cursor/mcp.json` for every project:

`.cursor/mcp.json`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "optics": { "command": "optics", "args": ["mcp"] }
  }
}
```
**VS Code**

Add this to `.vscode/mcp.json`:

`.vscode/mcp.json`:

```json
{
  "servers": {
    "optics": { "type": "stdio", "command": "optics", "args": ["mcp"] }
  }
}
```

If your client can't find `optics`, use its full path, for example `~/.optics/bin/optics`.

### Ask for a test

Describe the flow and where the app runs. The agent starts a session, explores, and writes files:

```text
Use the optics tools to open https://www.saucedemo.com in Playwright.
Sign in as standard_user / secret_sauce, add the backpack to the cart,
and check that the cart badge shows 1. Then write it as an Optics suite
in ./checkout, run optics dry_run on it, and tell me how to run it.
```

For a phone app, include the Appium details: *start an appium session at http://127.0.0.1:4723 with platformName Android, deviceName emulator-5554, appPackage com.birch.shop*.

### Review and run the suite

The agent writes the same files you would: test cases, modules and elements, in CSV. Read them like a colleague's pull request, then run them:

```shell
$ optics execute checkout
```

## What the agent can do

The server gives the agent:

- **Session tools**: `start_session` (picks the driver, URL and device settings, and opens the app), `screenshot` and `terminate_session`.
- **A tool for each keyword**, such as `press_element`, `enter_text`, `assert_presence` and `launch_app`. Each takes the session id plus the keyword's values.
- **Resources to read**: the current screen as an image, the list of elements on screen, the raw UI tree, the keyword catalogue, and `optics://project-format`, which teaches the agent how to write suite files.

A typical session goes: start a session, look at the screen, act with keywords, read the project format, write the files, run `optics dry_run`, and end the session. The [MCP reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/mcp) lists every tool and resource.

## Keep the agent on track

- **Agents tap by name, not by position.** Tapping raw screen coordinates is hidden by default, because those tests break on any other screen size. Set `OPTICS_MCP_ALLOW_COORDINATE_TAPS=1` before starting the server if you really need it.
- **Saving is the agent's job.** There's no record button in MCP. The agent writes the files using `optics://project-format`. Ask it to run `optics dry_run` before it finishes.
- **Loops and conditions** (`Run Loop`, `Condition`, `Read Data` and the rest) aren't tools, because they only make sense inside suite files. The agent can still write them into modules.
- **Sessions are private to the server.** A session started over MCP isn't visible to `optics serve` or `optics live`, and it ends when the server stops.

**Run the server over HTTP**
By default the server talks to one client over standard input and output. To share it on a network, or run it in a container, start it in HTTP mode:

```shell
$ optics mcp --transport http --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8090
```

Then point your client at `http://127.0.0.1:8090/mcp`:

```json
{ "mcpServers": { "optics": { "url": "http://127.0.0.1:8090/mcp" } } }
```

The server has no authentication. Keep it on `127.0.0.1` or a trusted network.

**Let the agent recover failing steps with AI self-heal**
Self-heal uses an AI model to recover a step when every locator fails (see [AI self-heal](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/self-heal)). Over MCP it's controlled by environment variables on the server, or by `ai_self_heal: true` in `start_session`:

```shell
$ export OPTICS_AI_SELF_HEAL=1
$ export GEMINI_API_KEY="your-key"
$ optics mcp
```

For OpenAI, Claude or a local model, also set `OPTICS_LLM_PROVIDER`, `OPTICS_LLM_MODEL` and the engine's key. See [Environment variables](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/mcp#environment-variables).

When a step is healed, the tool result includes `"healed": true` and the steps that worked, so the agent can update the suite.

## See also

- [MCP server reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/mcp)
- [Describe a test in plain English](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/describe), the built-in AI mode
- [Run keywords over HTTP](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/http-api)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/python

# Use Optics from Python

> Call Optics keywords from pytest or any Python script when a test needs real code.

Every keyword is also a method on the `Optics` class. Use it when a test needs logic the suite files can't express, or when your team already runs everything through pytest. You keep the same fallbacks, OCR and image matching as a CSV suite.

**Note:**
If CSV or YAML files can express your test, prefer them. Anyone on the team can read and review a suite file, and the runner gives you the step tree, screenshots and error detection for free. See [Choose how to create tests](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/).

## Write a test with pytest

This test signs in to the Sauce Labs demo store, adds a backpack to the cart, and reads the cart badge. It runs as written with `pip install "optics-framework[playwright]" pytest`.

`test_checkout.py`:

```python
import pytest
from optics_framework import Optics

CONFIG = {
    "driver_sources": [{"playwright": {"enabled": True}}],
    "elements_sources": [
        {"playwright_find_element": {"enabled": True}},
        {"playwright_page_source": {"enabled": True}},
        {"playwright_screenshot": {"enabled": True}},
    ],
}

@pytest.fixture
def optics():
    with Optics(CONFIG) as session:  # quits the browser when the test ends
        yield session

def test_shopper_can_add_a_backpack(optics):
    optics.launch_app("https://www.saucedemo.com")
    optics.enter_text("//input[@id='user-name']", "standard_user")
    optics.enter_text("//input[@id='password']", "secret_sauce")
    optics.press_element(["//input[@id='login-button']", "Login"])  # fallbacks
    optics.assert_presence("Products", timeout="10")
    optics.press_element("//button[@id='add-to-cart-sauce-labs-backpack']")
    badge = optics.get_text("//span[@data-test='shopping-cart-badge']")
    assert badge == "1"
```

```shell
$ pytest test_checkout.py
```

**Typing and reading text in browsers on Optics 1.10.5:**
On 1.10.5, `enter_text` and `get_text` fail with Playwright (`Object of type Locator is not JSON serializable`). The next release fixes it. Until then, click the field with `press_element` and type with `enter_text_direct`.

## Configure the session

Pass the same lists you'd put in `config.yaml`, as a Python dict. `driver_sources` and `elements_sources` are required. The SDK reads these keys:

| Key | What it's for |
|---|---|
| `driver_sources`, `elements_sources` | What to drive and how to look at the screen. See the [config reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/config). |
| `text_detection`, `image_detection` | OCR and image matching engines, if you use them. |
| `project_path` | A folder to search for image files and to resolve relative paths in `read_data`. Required for image elements. |
| `execution_output_path` | Where screenshots and results go. |

To reuse a project's `config.yaml`, load it yourself and pass the dict:

```python
import yaml
from optics_framework import Optics

with open("birch-tests/config.yaml") as f:
    config = yaml.safe_load(f)
config["project_path"] = "birch-tests"

with Optics(config) as optics:
    optics.launch_app()
```

Settings such as `ai_self_heal`, `llm_models` and `log_level` aren't read by the SDK.

## How calls differ from suite files

- **Method names are snake_case.** `Press Element` is `press_element`. Your editor's autocomplete lists them all.
- **Pass every value as a string.** `optics.press_by_coordinates("540", "1600")` works; numbers raise `TypeError`.
- **A list means "try these in order".** `press_element(["//button[@id='login']", "Login"])` tries the XPath, then the text. To check several elements at once, separate them with a pipe in one string: `assert_presence("Products|Your Cart")`.
- **`${name}` isn't looked up** in action methods. Pass the locator itself, or keep your own dict of locators.
- **Methods return values.** `get_text` returns the text, `capture_screenshot` returns a base64 PNG, and `assert_presence` returns `True`. A failed check raises an exception, which fails the pytest test.
- **Some defaults differ.** `assert_presence` and `assert_visibility` wait 60 seconds by default, and `detect_and_press` waits 10.

## Python-only methods

These have no CSV equivalent:

| Method | What it does |
|---|---|
| `add_element(name, value)` | Add a value to a named element, for use in flow-control methods. |
| `get_element_value(name)` | Return the list of values for a named element. |
| `add_module(name, steps)` | Define a module as a list of `(keyword, [values])` pairs, for `run_loop` and `condition`. |
| `add_api(path_or_dict)` | Load API definitions for `invoke_api`. See [Call APIs in a test](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/api-calls). |
| `add_error_definitions(dict)` | Load on-screen error definitions. |
| `capture_and_detect()` | Check the current screen against those definitions and return the matches. |
| `quit()` | End the session. The `with` block calls it for you. |

```python
optics.add_element("term", "trail runner")
optics.add_module("Search", [("Enter Text", ["//input[@type='search']", "${term}"])])
optics.run_loop("Search", "${term}", "trail runner|pace knit")
```

## See also

- [Use Optics in Robot Framework](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/robot)
- [Generate pytest code from a suite](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/generate)
- [Keyword reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/)
