Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/robot

# Use Optics in Robot Framework

> Import Optics as a Robot Framework library and use its keywords in .robot files.

Optics is also a [Robot Framework](https://robotframework.org) library. If your team already writes `.robot` suites, you can add Optics keywords to them and get its fallbacks, OCR and image matching without changing tools.

## Before you begin

Robot Framework isn't installed with Optics. Add it to the same environment:

```shell
$ pip install robotframework "optics-framework[appium]"
```

Swap `appium` for the engine you use. You also need a `config.yaml` with `driver_sources` and `elements_sources`. Any Optics project's config works.

## Write a suite

`checkout.robot`:

```robot
*** Settings ***
Library           OperatingSystem
Library           optics_framework.optics.Optics
Suite Setup       Open Optics
Suite Teardown    Quit

*** Variables ***
${EMAIL_FIELD}    //*[@resource-id="com.birch.shop:id/email"]

*** Keywords ***
Open Optics
    ${config}=    Get File    ${CURDIR}/config.yaml
    Setup    config=${config}

*** Test Cases ***
Shopper Can Sign In
    Launch App
    Detect And Press    Allow    timeout=5
    Enter Text    ${EMAIL_FIELD}    ava@birch.shop
    ${sign_in}=    Create List    //*[@resource-id="com.birch.shop:id/login"]    Sign in
    Press Element    ${sign_in}
    Assert Presence    Picked for you|Search Birch    timeout=20    rule=any
```

Run it like any Robot suite:

```shell
$ robot checkout.robot
```

## How Optics keywords behave in Robot

- **Setup takes the config's contents, not its path.** Read the file with `Get File` as shown above, then pass the text to `Setup`. If you use image elements, add `project_path: .` to the config so Optics can find the pictures.
- **Pass fallbacks as a list.** `Create List` builds the values to try in order. Writing several plain arguments fills the keyword's next parameters instead.
- **Separate several elements with a pipe** inside one argument: `Picked for you|Search Birch`.
- **Named arguments use the Python names**: `timeout=20`, `rule=any`, `index=1`.
- **Robot replaces `${…}` itself.** To pass an Optics variable to `Evaluate` or `Condition`, escape it: `\${total}`.
- **`Sleep` and `Evaluate` exist in Robot's BuiltIn library too.** Robot warns and uses the Optics version, which only accepts whole seconds. Write `BuiltIn.Sleep    2s` or `Optics.Sleep    2` to be explicit.

The [keyword reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/) lists every keyword. The Python-only keywords in [Use Optics from Python](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/python#python-only-methods), such as `Add Element` and `Add Module`, work in Robot too.

## Generate Robot code from a suite

If you already have a CSV or YAML suite, `optics generate` can write a starting `.robot` file from it. See [Generate pytest or Robot code](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/generate).

## See also

- [Use Optics from Python](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/python)
- [config.yaml reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/config)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/organise

# Organise a suite

> Structure a growing suite with setup and teardown, shared modules, several files and run selection.

A handful of tests fits in three files. A suite that covers a whole app needs a little structure so changes stay small. This page covers the tools Optics gives you for that.

## Open and close the app once

Name a test case **Suite Setup** and it runs once, before every other test case. **Suite Teardown** runs once at the end. Use them to launch and close the app, so each test case can focus on its own flow:

`test_cases/test_cases.csv`:

```csv
test_case,test_step
Suite Setup,Launch Birch
Shopper can sign in,Sign In
Shopper can search,Sign In
Shopper can search,Search For Shoes
Suite Teardown,Close Birch
```

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1
Launch Birch,Launch App
Close Birch,Close And Terminate App
```

Optics matches these names loosely: any test case name containing both "suite" and "setup" counts, so `Birch Suite Setup` works too. Setup and teardown always run, even when you [select which tests run](#run-only-some-test-cases).

**Per-test Setup and Teardown:**
Test cases named just **Setup** or **Teardown** are meant to run around every test case. In Optics 1.10.5 they only wrap the first test case, so don't rely on them yet. Put shared steps in a module and list it at the start of each test case instead, as `Sign In` is above.

Avoid "setup" and "teardown" in ordinary test names for the same reason: a test called *Setup wizard works* is treated as the per-test setup.

## Reuse modules

A module can appear in as many test cases as you like. Keep each module small and focused on one screen or one task, such as *Sign In*, *Search For Shoes* or *Open Cart*. When that screen changes, you fix one module and every test that uses it follows.

To call one module from inside another, use `Execute Module`:

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1
Buy Trail Runners,Execute Module,Search For Shoes
Buy Trail Runners,Press Element,Trail Runner 2
Buy Trail Runners,Press Element,Add to cart
```

Listing a module's name as a step on its own doesn't work; you need `Execute Module`. Steps inside a module called this way use only the first value of each element, so give important elements a value that's reliable on its own. [Conditions and loops](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/conditions) explains the details.

## Split a suite across files

Optics reads every CSV and YAML file in the project folder and its subfolders, and recognises each by its first row (or top-level key in YAML). So you can split a large suite however suits your team:

```tree
birch-tests/
├── config.yaml
├── checkout/
│   ├── test_cases.csv
│   └── modules.csv
├── search/
│   ├── test_cases.csv
│   └── modules.csv
└── elements/
    ├── shared.csv
    └── checkout.csv
```

When two files define the same thing:

- **Elements** with the same name are merged, and every value becomes a fallback.
- **Modules** and **test cases** with the same name: the one read last wins, and Optics logs a warning. Keep names unique.

**Tip:**
Optics also reads files inside `execution_output/`. Keep stray CSV or YAML files, and copies of old suites, out of the project folder so they don't get picked up.

## Run only some test cases

There's no command-line flag for this. List the test cases to run, or to skip, in `config.yaml`:

`config.yaml`:

```yaml
include:
  - Shopper can sign in
  - Shopper can search
```

`config.yaml`:

```yaml
exclude:
  - Shopper can pay with a gift card
```

Names match exactly, ignoring case. Use `include` or `exclude`, not both. Suite Setup and Suite Teardown always run.

## Run the same suite on different devices

Keep one config file in a project. Optics uses the config it finds in the project folder, so two of them would compete. To run the same suite on several targets, keep one config per target outside the project and copy the one you need into place before the run:

```tree
birch/
├── configs/
│   ├── pixel-8.yaml
│   └── chrome.yaml
└── birch-tests/
    ├── config.yaml        # copied from configs/ before each run
    └── …
```

```shell
$ cp configs/pixel-8.yaml birch-tests/config.yaml
$ optics execute birch-tests
```

## Name things so failures explain themselves

The run's tree and the JUnit report use your names, so a good name saves a trip into the files:

- **Test cases** describe an outcome: *Shopper can add a backpack*, not *Test 3*.
- **Modules** describe a task: *Sign In*, *Apply Discount Code*.
- **Elements** describe what's on screen: `sign_in`, `cart_badge`, `promo_code_field`.

## See also

- [Write a test suite](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/write)
- [Write tests in YAML](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/yaml)
- [Project files reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/files)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/yaml

# Write tests in YAML

> Keep a whole flow in one indented file, and learn the quoting rules that make YAML steps work.

YAML suites hold the same test cases, modules and elements as CSV, in one file you can read top to bottom. Optics loads both formats into the same suite, so a project can mix them.

## A complete suite in one file

`checkout.yaml`:

```yaml
Test Cases:
  - Suite Setup:
      - Launch Birch
  - Shopper can add trail runners:
      - Sign In
      - Add To Cart

Modules:
  - Launch Birch:
      - Launch App
  - Sign In:
      - Enter Text ${email_field} ava@birch.shop
      - Enter Text ${password_field} ${password}
      - Press Element ${sign_in}
      - Assert Presence "Picked for you"
  - Add To Cart:
      - Press Element "Trail Runner 2"
      - Press Element "Add to cart"
      - Assert Presence "Added to cart" timeout_str=10

Elements:
  email_field: "//*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/email']"
  password_field: "//*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/password']"
  sign_in:
    - "//*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/login']"
    - Sign in
  password: correct-horse
```

Keep `config.yaml` as its own file. You can split the suite into several YAML files, or keep elements in CSV and steps in YAML.

## The rules

### Section names are exact

Write the three top-level keys exactly as `Test Cases`, `Modules` and `Elements`, with that capitalization. Other spellings, such as `test_cases:`, are recognised as a suite file but load nothing, and the run then reports that there are no test cases.

### Each step is one line

A step is a single string: the keyword name, then its values separated by spaces. Optics matches the longest keyword name it knows at the start of the line, so `Press Element Sign in` is read as the keyword `Press Element` with the value `Sign`, then `in` as a second value. Quote any value that contains spaces:

```yaml
- Press Element "Sign in"
- Enter Text ${email_field} "Ava Birch"
```

A step that is exactly a module name runs that module.

### Named values

`name=value` sets one parameter by name, like `timeout_str=10` above. Quote the value if it contains spaces: `event_name="tap sign in"`.

### Expressions with = in them

Optics splits a quoted value on its first `=` to support named values. That breaks quoted expressions that contain `==`. Write such expressions without spaces, and without quotes:

```yaml
# Works
- Condition ${status}=='ready' "Go Home" "Sign In"
# Doesn't work: the quotes around the expression are kept
- Condition "${status} == 'ready'" "Go Home" "Sign In"
```

Quoted values without `=` are fine, such as `"Go Home"`.

### Module names as values

When a keyword takes a module name, such as `Run Loop` or `Execute Module`, quote names that contain spaces: `Run Loop "Search One" term "trail runner|pace knit"`.

### Elements

An element is a single value or a list. A list gives fallbacks, tried in order:

```yaml
Elements:
  sign_in: ["//*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/login']", "Sign in", sign_in.png]
```

Quote XPaths. They contain characters YAML treats specially, such as `[`, `@` and `:`.

## What stays in CSV

- **Error definitions** are CSV only. See [Catch error screens](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/error-detection).
- **`/save` in `optics live`** always writes CSV, even in a YAML project. Move the steps into your YAML file afterwards, or keep the CSV next to it.

## See also

- [Write a test suite](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/write), with CSV and YAML side by side
- [Project files reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/files)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/

# How Optics finds elements

> Learn how Optics tries several ways to find each element, so one changed locator doesn't fail a test.

Most test tools give an element one locator, and the test fails the moment that locator changes. Optics assumes an element has several identities (its place in the UI tree, its text, what it looks like) and tries them in order before giving up. A redesign that breaks one identity falls through to the next.

## The order Optics tries things

When a step needs an element, Optics works through three layers of fallback.

### 1. Each value of the element, in order

An element can have several values in `elements.csv`. Optics tries them top to bottom and stops at the first that works:

`test_data/elements.csv`:

```csv
Element_Name,Element_ID
sign_in,//*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/login']
sign_in,Sign in
sign_in,sign_in.png
```

### 2. Each way to find that kind of value

Optics looks at a value and decides what kind it is, then tries the ways that fit, cheapest first:

| Value looks like | Optics tries | Needs |
|---|---|---|
| An XPath, such as `//*[@resource-id='login']` | The UI tree | A driver that exposes a UI tree |
| Text, such as `Sign in` | 1. The UI tree<br>2. OCR on a screenshot | OCR needs a [text detection engine](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/text-and-images) |
| An image file, such as `sign_in.png` | Image matching on a screenshot | An [image detection engine](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/text-and-images) |
| `text_only:Sign in` | OCR only, skipping the UI tree | A text detection engine |

Looking something up in the UI tree takes milliseconds. OCR and image matching read a screenshot, which takes longer, so Optics only uses them when the tree can't help. [Define elements](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/define) shows every kind of value.

### 3. Each element source, in config order

`config.yaml` lists **element sources**: the ways Optics may look at the screen, such as asking the app directly, reading its UI tree, or taking a screenshot. Optics tries them in the order they're listed. If you enable more than one driver, each is tried in turn as well.

### Last resort: AI self-heal

If everything above fails and you've switched it on, an AI model looks at the screen and tries to finish the step, for example by spotting that *Sign in* is now *Log in*. It's off by default. See [AI self-heal](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/self-heal).

## See which way worked

Optics records how it found each element, so you can tell when a test is passing on a fallback:

- `optics live` shows it after each step: `0.31s  [Text]`.
- Screenshots in `execution_output/` show a box around the element Optics found, for drivers that report element positions. See [Read the results](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/results).

If a test keeps passing on its second or third value, the first one is probably out of date. Update it while you still know why.

## Make elements last

- **Put the most stable value first.** An id that developers don't change is better than text that marketing rewrites.
- **Add a text fallback** to important buttons. Text survives most layout changes.
- **Use images last.** Image matching is the slowest, and a restyled button stops matching. It's still the only option for icons with no text or id.
- **Narrow the search** when the same text appears twice on a screen. Use `index` to pick a match, or an [area of interest](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/area-of-interest) to look in one part of the screen.

## See also

- [Define elements](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/define)
- [Find elements by text and image](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/text-and-images)
- [Search part of the screen](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/area-of-interest)
- [AI self-heal](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/self-heal)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/define

# Define elements

> Name the things your tests touch, choose good values for them, and add fallbacks that survive redesigns.

An element is a name for something on screen, plus one or more values that tell Optics how to find it. Steps refer to elements by name (`${sign_in}`), so when the app changes, you update the element once and every test follows.

## Write elements

Elements live in any CSV whose header starts with `Element_Name,Element_ID`. The project template puts them in `test_data/elements.csv`.

`test_data/elements.csv`:

```csv
Element_Name,Element_ID
sign_in,//*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/login']
sign_in,Sign in
cart_icon,cart_icon.png
search_bar,Search Birch
email,ava@birch.shop
```

To give an element several values, repeat its name on more rows. Optics tries them top to bottom. You can also add more columns whose names start with `Element_ID`, such as `Element_ID_text` or `Element_ID_image`, and fill them in on the same row:

`test_data/elements.csv`:

```csv
Element_Name,Element_ID,Element_ID_text,Element_ID_image
sign_in,//*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/login'],Sign in,sign_in.png
```

Both layouts mean the same thing. Use whichever is easier to read for your team. Empty cells are ignored.

**The header is exact:**
The first column must be named exactly `Element_Name`, with that capitalization. A file headed `element_name,element_id` is recognised as an elements file but loads no elements, and every `${name}` then fails with "Element not found".

## Choose the kind of value

Optics decides what a value is from how it looks:

| Write | Optics treats it as | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Starts with `/`, `//` or `(` | XPath, looked up in the UI tree | `//*[@resource-id='login']` |
| Plain words | Text: UI tree first, then OCR on a screenshot | `Sign in` |
| `text_only:` then words | Text, OCR only | `text_only:Sign in` |
| Ends in `.png`, `.jpg`, `.jpeg` or `.bmp` | An image to match on a screenshot | `cart_icon.png` |
| `css=`, `#id`, `.class` or `tag[attr]` | A CSS selector. Works with Playwright, not Selenium | `#login-button` |
| Starts with `android.` or `XCUI` | A class name | `android.widget.Switch` |

### XPath

An XPath is a path through the app's UI tree. It's the fastest and most precise kind of value, and the best first choice when the app has stable ids:

- Android: `//*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/login']`
- iOS: `//XCUIElementTypeButton[@name='Sign in']`
- Web: `//button[@id='login']`

To pick the second of several matches, wrap the XPath in parentheses and add an index: `(//android.widget.Button)[2]`.

### Text

Plain text matches an element showing that text, or with that accessibility label. It's the most readable kind of value, and it survives layout changes. If the text isn't in the UI tree, for example because it's drawn inside an image or a game canvas, Optics reads the screenshot with OCR, as long as a [text detection engine](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/text-and-images) is enabled.

Text matching in the UI tree tolerates small differences. To require exact matches, set `strict_element_match: true` in `config.yaml`.

**Text that looks like something else:**
A value is checked against the rules in the table above, top to bottom. Text that happens to start with `(` or `/`, or contains `[` and `]`, is read as an XPath or CSS selector: `(optional)`, `Price [USD]`, `.com`. On Appium and Playwright, put `text=` in front to force text: `text=(optional)`.

### Images

An image value is the file name of a cropped picture of the element. Put the picture anywhere in the project folder (the templates use `test_data/input_templates/`) and refer to it by file name only. Image matching is the slowest kind and needs an image detection engine. Use it for icons with no text or id. [Find elements by text and image](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/text-and-images) shows how to capture a good picture.

### Values to avoid

`id:` values, such as `id:login`, aren't supported by any element source and always fail. Use an XPath on the id instead.

## Find the right locator

- **In `optics live`**, try a value with `press_element` or `assert_presence` before you write it down. The history line shows whether it worked and how it was found.
- **Android and iOS**: [Appium Inspector](https://github.com/appium/appium-inspector) shows each element's id, text and XPath.
- **Web**: right-click an element in Chrome and choose **Inspect**.
- **Any platform**: the `Get Interactive Elements` keyword lists the buttons, fields and text on the current screen. In `optics live`, run `get_interactive_elements` and open the JSON file it writes to the output folder.

## Pick one of several matches

When the same text appears more than once, `index` picks a match, counting from 0:

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2
Add Second Product,Press Element,Add to cart,index=1
```

To look in one part of the screen instead, use an [area of interest](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/area-of-interest).

## Keep data in elements too

Elements can hold any value a step needs, not only locators: an email address, a search term, a URL. Keeping them together means one file holds everything that changes between environments.

To keep a password out of log files, start its value with `@:`, for example `password,@:correct-horse`. Optics masks it as `****` in logs and types it without the prefix.

To put a line break or tab inside a value, write `\n` or `\t`. Write `\\` for a literal backslash.

## See also

- [How Optics finds elements](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/)
- [Variables](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/variables)
- [Project files reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/files)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/text-and-images

# Find elements by text and image

> Use OCR and image matching to find elements the UI tree can't see, such as text inside images, canvases and video.

Some things on screen never appear in the app's UI tree: text drawn inside an image, a game or map canvas, a video player's controls, or anything on a device you can only watch through a camera. Optics can find these by looking at a screenshot, the way a person would. It reads text with **OCR** (optical character recognition) and finds icons with **image matching**.

Both are slower than the UI tree, so Optics only uses them after the faster ways fail. You turn them on in `config.yaml`.

## Turn on OCR

### Install an OCR engine

We recommend EasyOCR. It runs on your machine and needs no account.

```shell
$ optics setup --install easyocr
```

The first run downloads EasyOCR's models, which takes a minute.

### Enable it, and a screenshot source

OCR reads screenshots, so `elements_sources` must include a screenshot source for your driver (`appium_screenshot`, `playwright_screenshot`, `selenium_screenshot`, or `camera_screenshot`):

`config.yaml`:

```yaml
elements_sources:
  - appium_find_element:
      enabled: true
  - appium_page_source:
      enabled: true
  - appium_screenshot:
      enabled: true

text_detection:
  - easyocr:
      enabled: true
```

### Use text values

Nothing changes in your tests. Any text value, such as `Press Element,Trail Runner 2`, is tried in the UI tree first and with OCR second. To skip the UI tree and use OCR straight away, write `text_only:Trail Runner 2`.

### OCR engines

| Engine | Name in config | Install | Good to know |
|---|---|---|---|
| EasyOCR | `easyocr` | `optics setup --install easyocr` | Local and accurate. Slower on the first call while models load. Reads English. |
| Tesseract | `pytesseract` | `optics setup --install pytesseract`, plus the [Tesseract program](https://tesseract-ocr.github.io/tessdoc/Installation.html) | Light and fast. Matches whole words exactly. |
| Google Cloud Vision | `google_vision` | `optics setup --install google-vision` | Cloud service. Set `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` to a service account key. Screenshots leave your machine. |
| Your own service | `remote_ocr` | Nothing | Sends screenshots to a URL you run. See the [engines reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/engines). |

List more than one engine and Optics tries them in order.

## Turn on image matching

Image matching finds a picture of an element, such as an icon, on the screen. It needs no extra install.

`config.yaml`:

```yaml
image_detection:
  - templatematch:
      enabled: true
```

Then use the picture's file name as an element value:

`test_data/elements.csv`:

```csv
Element_Name,Element_ID
cart_icon,//*[@content-desc='Cart']
cart_icon,cart_icon.png
```

### Capture a good template

The picture is called a **template**. How you crop it decides whether matching works:

1. Take a screenshot on the same kind of device you test on. Run the test once and use a `pre_…` screenshot from `execution_output/`, or run `/screenshot` in `optics live`.
2. Crop tightly around the element. Include its distinctive shape, and as little background as possible.
3. Don't resize the crop. Matching works best at the screen's own resolution, though it tolerates some scaling and rotation.
4. Save it as PNG anywhere in the project folder. The templates use `test_data/input_templates/`.
5. Refer to it by file name only: `cart_icon.png`, not a path. File names must be unique across the project.

Optics also picks up images inside `execution_output/`. Give templates distinctive names, so they never clash with a screenshot's name.

## When to use which

| Situation | Use |
|---|---|
| The element has a stable id or text in the UI tree | XPath or text, no vision needed |
| Text drawn inside an image, canvas or video | OCR |
| An icon with no text or id | Image matching |
| A device with no UI tree, watched through a camera | OCR and image matching. See [Production devices](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/production) |
| The same word appears in several places | OCR with an [area of interest](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/area-of-interest) or `index` |

## Speed things up

- **Keep the UI tree first.** List page source and element sources before screenshot sources, so vision only runs when it's needed.
- **Search part of the screen.** An [area of interest](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/area-of-interest) crops the screenshot before OCR or matching runs.
- **Turn off what you don't use.** An enabled OCR engine is loaded at the start of every run, even by `optics dry_run`.

## See also

- [How Optics finds elements](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/)
- [Search part of the screen](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/area-of-interest)
- [Engines and extras](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/engines)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/area-of-interest

# Search part of the screen

> Limit where Optics looks for an element, so repeated text can't be matched in the wrong place and vision runs faster.

An **area of interest** (AOI) is a rectangle on the screen. Give one to a step and Optics only accepts an element inside it. Use it when the same text appears in several places, such as an *Add to cart* button that also appears in a product description, or to make OCR faster by reading less of the screen.

## Set an area

Four values describe the rectangle, each as a **percentage** of the screen, from 0 to 100:

| Parameter | Meaning | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `aoi_x` | Left edge, from the left of the screen | `0` |
| `aoi_y` | Top edge, from the top of the screen | `0` |
| `aoi_width` | Width of the area | `100` |
| `aoi_height` | Height of the area | `100` |

The defaults cover the whole screen, which means "no area". Pass the values by name:

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2,param_3
Add To Cart,Press Element,Add to cart,aoi_y=75,aoi_height=25
```

This looks for *Add to cart* only in the bottom quarter: it starts 75% of the way down and covers the remaining 25%.

Some common areas:

| Area | Values |
|---|---|
| Top half | `aoi_height=50` |
| Bottom half | `aoi_y=50,aoi_height=50` |
| Right third | `aoi_x=67,aoi_width=33` |
| Centre | `aoi_x=25,aoi_y=25,aoi_width=50,aoi_height=50` |

The edges must stay on the screen: `aoi_x` plus `aoi_width`, and `aoi_y` plus `aoi_height`, can be at most 100.

## How it works

- **OCR and image matching** crop the screenshot to the area before they search. They read less, so they're faster too.
- **The UI tree** can't be cropped. Optics finds the element as usual, then keeps it only if its centre is inside the area.

Each step that uses an area saves a screenshot with the rectangle drawn on it (`…_with_aoi.jpg` in `execution_output/`), so you can check you chose the right part of the screen.

## Keywords that accept an area

`Press Element`, `Enter Text`, `Enter Number`, `Clear Element Text`, `Get Text`, `Swipe From Element` and `Scroll From Element`. Checks such as `Assert Presence` don't take an area.

In the Python library, only `press_element` accepts area parameters.

## Area or index?

Both pick one match out of several. Use `index` when you know which match you want by order (the second *Add to cart* button). Use an area when you know *where* it is, which keeps working when items are added or reordered. You can combine them.

## See also

- [Find elements by text and image](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/text-and-images)
- [Define elements](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/define#pick-one-of-several-matches)
- [Action keywords](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/actions)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/self-heal

# Recover failing steps with AI self-heal

> Let an AI model look at the screen and finish a step when every way of finding its element has failed.

AI self-heal is a last line of defence. When a step can't find its element by any value or any method, Optics sends a screenshot to an AI model and asks it to complete the step. If the button now says *Log in* instead of *Sign in*, the model can spot that and press it, and the test carries on. It's off by default.

## When to use it

Self-heal keeps long runs going through small, expected UI changes, such as monitoring a production app on a schedule, or a nightly regression where you'd rather get a full report than stop at the first renamed button.

It isn't a substitute for good elements. A healed step **passes**, so a real change in the app can go unnoticed unless you read the logs. Fix the element afterwards, as described in [Find out what healed](#find-out-what-healed).

## Turn it on

### Install the AI engine and set your key

Self-heal uses the same AI engine and key as [plain-English mode](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/describe#before-you-begin). Install it and set its key, for example:

```shell
$ optics setup --install gemini
$ export GEMINI_API_KEY="your-key"
```

### Enable it in config.yaml

`config.yaml`:

```yaml
ai_self_heal: true

llm_models:
  - gemini:
      enabled: true
```

For OpenAI, Claude or a local model, use that engine's entry instead. See [llm_models](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/config#llm-models).

### Enable a screenshot source

The model works from a screenshot, so `elements_sources` must include one, such as `appium_screenshot` or `playwright_screenshot`. Without it, self-heal does nothing.

If the AI engine isn't installed or the key is missing, Optics logs a warning and runs without self-heal. It never fails a run because self-heal is unavailable.

## What it does

When a step that finds an element fails, Optics gives the model:

- the step that failed and the element it was looking for,
- a screenshot of the screen, and the UI tree if there is one,
- the steps that ran just before.

The model can take up to five actions to finish the step, using only six keywords: Press Element, Enter Text, Scroll, Swipe By Percentage, Press Keycode and Press By Percentage. Each action goes through Optics' normal ways of finding elements. If the step is done within five actions, it passes. If not, it fails with the original error.

Self-heal covers steps that find an element and act on it: Press Element, Enter Text, Enter Number, Clear Element Text, Get Text, Swipe From Element, Scroll From Element, and the keywords built on them (Detect And Press, Select Dropdown Option). Checks such as Assert Presence don't self-heal, so a missing element still fails a check.

## Find out what healed

With `optics execute` and `optics live`, a healed step shows as passed. To see what happened, turn on file logs:

`config.yaml`:

```yaml
file_log: true
```

Then search `execution_output/internal_logs.log` for `AI self-heal`:

```text
AI self-heal: attempting recovery for 'press_element' on 'Sign in'
AI self-heal step 1/5 for 'press_element': action=keyword keyword=press_element params=['Log in'] reason=The button now reads 'Log in'
AI self-heal: recovered 'press_element' via keyword 'press_element'
```

Update the element with what the model used, here by adding `sign_in,Log in` to `elements.csv`.

Over the [HTTP API](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/http-api) and [MCP](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/agent), a healed step's result says so directly, with `"healed": true` and the steps that worked.

## Costs and limits

- Each healed step makes up to six calls to the model, and each call takes a few seconds and costs API usage.
- Screenshots go to your model provider while self-heal runs, unless you run the model locally. Don't use a hosted model on screens with data you can't share with a third party.
- The model's instructions are tuned for phones. It works in browsers, but key presses use Android key codes.

## See also

- [How Optics finds elements](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/)
- [Describe a test in plain English](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/describe)
- [config.yaml reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/config)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/

# Run a suite

> Check a suite without a device, run it for real, and choose which test cases run.

Two commands cover almost every run. `optics dry_run` checks your files without touching a device. `optics execute` runs the suite on the device or browser in your `config.yaml` and writes the results to `execution_output/`.

## Check the suite first

```shell
$ optics dry_run birch-tests
```

A dry run reads every file and checks that:

- every test step names a module or keyword that exists,
- every keyword in every module exists, with a suggestion when you mistype one,
- every `${name}` is defined in an elements file.

It doesn't tap, type or open anything, so it's quick and safe to run before every commit. It still starts the engines in your `config.yaml`, so they must be installed and a driver must be enabled.

## Run it

```shell
$ optics execute birch-tests
```

Before the run, Optics checks that the target is reachable: for Appium, that the server answers and (on Android) that a device is connected; for Selenium, that the server answers. If not, it stops with a message saying what to start. Playwright needs no check.

Then it runs **Suite Setup**, each test case in order, and **Suite Teardown**, and prints a live tree:

```terminal
Test Suite
├── Suite Setup                                       |  1.21s |    PASS
│   └── Launch Birch                                  |  1.21s |    PASS
├── Shopper can sign in                               |  1.38s |    PASS
│   └── Sign In                                       |  1.38s |    PASS
└── Shopper can add trail runners                     |  4.02s |    FAIL
    ├── Sign In                                       |  1.31s |    PASS
    └── Add To Cart                                   |  2.71s |    FAIL
╭──────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ Total Test Cases: 3 | Passed: 2 | Failed: 1          │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
```

### What happens when a step fails

- The rest of that test case is skipped, and its unrun steps show as `NOT_RUN`.
- The next test case runs as normal. One broken flow doesn't hide problems elsewhere.
- A **Failure details** box after the tree names each failed step and why it failed.

### Exit codes

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `0` | Every test case passed. |
| `1` | At least one test case failed, or the run couldn't start (no driver enabled, server unreachable, missing files). |

CI systems use this to mark a build as passed or failed.

## Choose which test cases run

List test cases to run, or to skip, in `config.yaml`. Names match exactly, ignoring case:

`config.yaml`:

```yaml
include:
  - Shopper can sign in
```

Use `include` or `exclude`, not both. Suite Setup and Suite Teardown always run. There's no command-line option for this, so a common pattern in CI is a small config per job. See [Organise a suite](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/organise#run-the-same-suite-on-different-devices).

## Options

| Option | What it does |
|---|---|
| `--no-use-printer` | Print plain log output instead of the live tree. Useful when a CI log viewer garbles the tree. |
| `--runner pytest` | Run the suite through pytest instead of Optics' own runner. Most projects don't need this. |

To skip the reachability check, for example when the server is behind a proxy the check can't see, set `OPTICS_SKIP_PREFLIGHT=1`.

## How long steps wait

Action keywords act on the screen as it is. They don't wait for it to change. Checks wait:

| Keyword | Waits up to |
|---|---|
| `Assert Presence`, `Assert Visibility` | 30 seconds |
| `Validate Element` | 10 seconds |
| `Detect And Press` | 30 seconds, then carries on without failing |

Pass a different time as the second value: `Assert Presence,Welcome,60`. Put a check after any step that loads a new screen, so the next action doesn't run too early.

## See also

- [Read the results](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/results)
- [Run tests in CI](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/ci)
- [CLI reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/cli)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/results

# Read the results

> Find out what happened in a run from the JUnit report, the screenshots and the logs.

Every run writes its results to `execution_output/` inside the project folder. The terminal tree tells you *what* failed. The files tell you *why*.

## What a run writes

```tree
birch-tests/execution_output/
├── junit_output.xml                              # pass/fail for every test, for CI
├── 2026-10-09T14-02-11-…-pre_press_element.jpg  # the screen before each step
├── 2026-10-09T14-02-11-…-press_element_element_detection_result.jpg
├── 2026-10-09T14-02-15-…-end_of_run.jpg         # the last screen
├── page_sources_log.xml                          # the UI tree, captured during the run
├── failed_steps_elements.json                    # the elements on screen when a step failed
├── internal_logs.log                             # with file_log: true
├── execution_logs.log                            # with file_log: true
└── logs.json                                     # with json_log: true
```

| File | When it's written | Use it to |
|---|---|---|
| `junit_output.xml` | Every run | Show results in CI. Standard JUnit XML that GitHub Actions, GitLab, Jenkins and others read. |
| `…pre_<keyword>.jpg` | Before each step that finds an element | See what was on screen when the step started. |
| `…_detection_result.jpg` | When Optics found an element by position | See exactly what Optics found, boxed in green. |
| `…_with_aoi.jpg` | When a step uses an [area of interest](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/area-of-interest) | Check the area covers the right part of the screen. It's drawn in blue. |
| `…end_of_run.jpg` | At the end of the run | See where the app was left. |
| `page_sources_log.xml` or `.html` | When the UI tree is read | Find the right XPath or text for an element. |
| `internal_logs.log`, `execution_logs.log` | With `file_log: true` | Read every attempt Optics made, including which ways of finding an element failed. |
| `logs.json` | With `json_log: true` | Feed results into your own dashboards. |
| `failed_steps_elements.json` | When a step fails | Pick a working locator. It lists each element on that screen with its label and, on the web, a `loc` locator. |
| `detected_errors_<id>.json` | When an [error screen](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/error-detection) was found | See which error definition matched. |

## Investigate a failure

1. **Read the Failure details box** in the terminal. It names the test case, the step and the reason.
2. **Open the last `pre_…` screenshot** before the failure. Is the screen what you expected? If it shows a loading spinner, the step ran too early: add an `Assert Presence` before it. If it shows a different screen, an earlier step went somewhere unexpected.
3. **Open `failed_steps_elements.json`** to see the elements that were on screen when the step failed. Use a `loc` or a label from it as the element's value.
4. **Search the logs** for the element's value. With `file_log: true`, `execution_logs.log` has a line for every attempt, such as `Trying … on 'Sign in' ... FAIL`.
5. **Reproduce it in `optics live`.** Run the steps before the failure, then try the failing step with different values until one works. See [Record a test](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/record).

## Turn on more logging

Add these to `config.yaml`:

`config.yaml`:

```yaml
file_log: true      # write internal_logs.log and execution_logs.log
json_log: true      # write logs.json, a list of every run event
log_level: DEBUG    # more detail in the terminal and log files
```

`log_level` takes `DEBUG`, `INFO` (the default), `WARNING` or `ERROR`. Use `WARNING` to keep the terminal quiet so the tree stands out.

## Read the JUnit report

`junit_output.xml` has one `<testcase>` per test case, with a `<failure>` when it failed. Inside each, Optics records every module and keyword with its status and timing, so CI tools that show nested steps display the same tree you saw in the terminal.

If error screens were detected, the report has an extra failing test case called `on-screen-error-detection`. See [Catch error screens](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/error-detection).

## Keep the folder tidy

Screenshots from every run accumulate in `execution_output/`. Clear the folder before runs where you need clean results, such as in CI:

```shell
$ rm -rf birch-tests/execution_output
$ optics execute birch-tests
```

To write results somewhere else, set `execution_output_path` in `config.yaml`. A relative path is relative to the folder you run `optics` from, and the folder must exist.

## See also

- [Catch error screens](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/error-detection)
- [Run tests in CI](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/ci)
- [Troubleshooting](https://optics-framework.org/docs/help/troubleshooting)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/error-detection

# Catch error screens

> Fail a run in CI when the app ends on a crash dialog, a "Session expired" message or any other error you define.

Some failures don't break a step. The app shows *Session expired*, or Android shows *Birch has stopped*, and the test still passes because no step looked for that message. Error detection catches these. You list the messages that mean something went wrong, and Optics checks the screen for them at the end of every run.

### List the error messages

Create a CSV anywhere in the project. The template uses `test_data/error_definitions.csv`:

`test_data/error_definitions.csv`:

```csv
error_code,match_string,description,severity
ERR_CRASH,has stopped,The app crashed with a system dialog,critical
ERR_NOT_RESPONDING,isn't responding,Android shows an ANR dialog,critical
ERR_SESSION,Session expired,The user was signed out,high
ERR_NETWORK,No internet connection,The app lost its connection,medium
ERR_SERVER,Something went wrong,The server returned an error page,high
```

| Column | Required | What it's for |
|---|---|---|
| `error_code` | Yes | A short name for the error. It appears in the report. |
| `match_string` | Yes | Text that means this error is on screen. |
| `description` | No | What the error means, for whoever reads the report. |
| `severity` | No | Any label you like, such as `critical` or `low`. |

### Run the suite as usual

```shell
$ optics execute birch-tests
```

There's nothing to switch on. If the project has an error definitions file, Optics uses it.

## What happens at the end of a run

After the last test case, Optics captures the screen one more time, reads all the text in the app's UI tree, and looks for each `match_string`. Matching ignores case and finds the text anywhere: `session expired` matches *Your session expired. Please sign in again.*

For each match, Optics:

- logs a warning, which you can read in `execution_logs.log` when `file_log: true` is set: `ON-SCREEN ERROR DETECTED — code: ERR_SESSION | matched_on: match_string | match_string: 'Session expired' | severity: high | The user was signed out`,
- adds a failing test case named `on-screen-error-detection` to `junit_output.xml`, with one failure per match,
- writes the details to `execution_output/detected_errors_<id>.json`.

CI tools that read the JUnit report then show the run as failed, even when every step passed. On 1.10.5 that last case has a bug:

**On Optics 1.10.5, an all-pass run can leave the entry out:**
When every test case passes, Optics 1.10.5 can finish the JUnit report before the error-detection entry is added, so the report shows no failure. The match is still written to `detected_errors_<id>.json`, and to `execution_logs.log` with `file_log: true`. Until a release fixes this, have CI check `detected_errors_<id>.json` as well as the JUnit report.

**The exit code doesn't change:**
A detected error appears in the JUnit report but doesn't change the exit code of `optics execute`. If your CI decides pass or fail from the exit code alone, have it read the JUnit report as well. See [Run tests in CI](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/ci).

## Write good match strings

- **Use a phrase only an error would show.** `has stopped` is good. `Error` matches too much, such as a help page about error messages.
- **Copy the exact words** from a screenshot of the error, and keep them short. Matching is plain text, not a pattern, so `*` or `.*` are matched literally.
- **Avoid text that appears in your own tests.** A match anywhere on the last screen counts.

## Limits

- The check runs once, on the last screen. If the app recovers before the run ends, the error isn't seen. Add an explicit check in your test for errors that can appear and disappear mid-flow, such as `Assert Presence` on the screen you expect next.
- It needs the app's UI tree. On [production devices](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/production) driven through a camera, there's no tree to read.
- It's skipped if the session is already closed, for example when Suite Teardown ran `Close And Terminate App`. To keep the check, don't close the app in Suite Teardown.
- Definitions are CSV only. `optics dry_run`, `optics live`, the HTTP API and MCP don't run the check.

## See also

- [Read the results](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/results)
- [Run tests in CI](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/ci)
- [Project files reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/files)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/ci

# Run tests in CI

> Run the same suite on every pull request and read the results in your CI system.

A suite earns its keep when it runs on every change. In CI, Optics needs the same three things as on your machine: Optics itself, the engines in your `config.yaml`, and something to drive. It reports through its exit code and a JUnit file, which every major CI system understands.

## Run a web suite

Web suites are the easiest to run in CI, because the browser runs on the CI machine itself.

**GitHub Actions**

`.github/workflows/optics.yml`:

```yaml
name: Optics

on: [push, pull_request]

permissions:
  contents: read
  checks: write   # lets the report step post a check

jobs:
  web:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      - uses: actions/setup-python@v7
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"

      - name: Install Optics and the browser
        run: |
          pip install "optics-framework[playwright]==1.10.5"
          python -m playwright install --with-deps chromium

      - name: Run the suite
        run: xvfb-run -a optics execute birch-tests --no-use-printer

      - name: Publish results
        if: always()
        uses: mikepenz/action-junit-report@v6
        with:
          report_paths: birch-tests/execution_output/junit_output.xml

      # Screenshot file names contain colons, which upload-artifact rejects,
      # so the output folder is uploaded as one archive.
      - name: Keep the run output
        if: failure()
        run: tar -czf optics-output.tgz birch-tests/execution_output

      - if: failure()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: optics-output
          path: optics-output.tgz
```
**GitLab CI**

`.gitlab-ci.yml`:

```yaml
optics-web:
  image: python:3.12-bookworm
  script:
    - apt-get update && apt-get install -y xvfb
    - pip install "optics-framework[playwright]==1.10.5"
    - python -m playwright install --with-deps chromium
    - xvfb-run -a optics execute birch-tests --no-use-printer
  artifacts:
    when: always
    paths:
      - birch-tests/execution_output/
    reports:
      junit: birch-tests/execution_output/junit_output.xml
```

`xvfb-run` gives the browser a virtual screen. Optics 1.10.5 always opens a visible browser window, even with `headless: true` in `config.yaml`, and CI machines have no display. Once the fix in [pull request #600](https://github.com/mozarkai/optics-framework/pull/600) is released, `headless: true` works and you can drop `xvfb-run`.

The `permissions` block lets the report step post its check. Without it, the step logs `Resource not accessible by integration` and no check appears. Pull requests from forks always get a read-only token, so on those the results are in the job log only.

## Run an Android suite

Android suites need an emulator and an Appium server on the CI machine. Linux runners with hardware acceleration, such as GitHub's `ubuntu-latest`, can run the Android emulator.

`.github/workflows/optics-android.yml`:

```yaml
name: Optics Android

on: [pull_request]

permissions:
  contents: read
  checks: write

jobs:
  android:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      - name: Enable KVM
        run: |
          echo 'KERNEL=="kvm", GROUP="kvm", MODE="0666", OPTIONS+="static_node=kvm"' | sudo tee /etc/udev/rules.d/99-kvm4all.rules
          sudo udevadm control --reload-rules
          sudo udevadm trigger --name-match=kvm

      - uses: actions/setup-python@v7
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: 22

      - name: Install Optics and Appium
        run: |
          pip install "optics-framework[appium]==1.10.5"
          npm install -g appium
          appium driver install uiautomator2

      - name: Run the suite on an emulator
        uses: reactivecircus/android-emulator-runner@v2
        with:
          api-level: 34
          arch: x86_64
          script: |
            adb install app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk
            appium > appium.log 2>&1 &
            sleep 5
            optics execute birch-tests --no-use-printer

      - name: Publish results
        if: always()
        uses: mikepenz/action-junit-report@v6
        with:
          report_paths: birch-tests/execution_output/junit_output.xml
```

Make sure `deviceName` in `config.yaml` matches the emulator (`emulator-5554` for the first one), and that `appPackage` and `appActivity` match the app you install.

## Decide pass or fail

`optics execute` exits with `1` when any test case fails, so the run step fails the job by itself.

There's one case the exit code misses: [error screens](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/error-detection) found at the end of a run. They're added to the JUnit report as a failing test case but don't change the exit code. To fail the build on them, have your JUnit reporter fail on any failure. For example, with `mikepenz/action-junit-report`, add `fail_on_failure: true`.

## Make CI runs reliable

- **Pin the Optics version** (`optics-framework==1.10.5`), so a new release doesn't change behavior in the middle of a sprint. Upgrade on purpose, in its own pull request.
- **Run `optics dry_run` first** in a fast job. It catches typos in seconds, before you pay for an emulator.
- **Start from a clean output folder.** CI checkouts usually are. On reused machines, delete `execution_output/` before the run.
- **Keep the artifacts.** Upload `execution_output/` when a run fails, as an archive (see the web example). Its logs and screenshots usually explain the failure faster than the CI log.
- **Keep secrets out of the suite.** Pass model API keys such as `GEMINI_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_API_KEY` or `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` as CI secrets, in environment variables.
- **Wait for screens to load.** Runners are often slower than your laptop. Put `Assert Presence` before actions that follow a screen change, rather than adding `Sleep` steps.

## See also

- [Readiness checklist](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/checklist)
- [Read the results](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/results)
- [Android](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/android) and [Web](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/web) setup
