Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/checklist

# Readiness checklist

> Use this checklist before you rely on a suite in CI or for production monitoring.

A suite that passes on your laptop can still be flaky, slow or hard to debug in CI. Work through these items before the team starts trusting its results. Your ticks are saved in this browser, so you can come back to the list.

## The suite

- [ ] **Every test case has a clear outcome in its name.** *Shopper can add a backpack* tells whoever reads a failure what broke. *Test 3* doesn't.
- [ ] **Every screen change is followed by a check.** Action keywords don't wait. Put `Assert Presence` or `Validate Element` after any step that loads a new screen, instead of `Sleep`. See [Run a suite](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/#how-long-steps-wait).
- [ ] **Important elements have a fallback.** Give key buttons and fields a second value, usually their visible text, so one renamed id doesn't fail the run. See [Define elements](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/define).
- [ ] **No test relies on another.** Each test case should be able to run on its own, with Suite Setup handling shared setup. Check with `include:` in `config.yaml`.
- [ ] **`optics dry_run` passes.** Run it before every commit, and as the first CI step.

## The configuration

- [ ] **The Optics version is pinned** in CI (`optics-framework==1.10.5`). Upgrade on purpose, in its own change.
- [ ] **Only the engines you use are enabled.** Every enabled OCR or image engine loads at the start of each run, even when no step needs it.
- [ ] **No secrets are in `config.yaml` or the suite files.** Keep API keys in environment variables, and passwords in CI secrets.
- [ ] **The project folder holds one config file** and no stray copies of old suites. Optics reads every CSV and YAML in the folder.

## The run

- [ ] **Error screens are defined.** Add the crash, timeout and "something went wrong" messages your app can show to an [error definitions file](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/error-detection).
- [ ] **CI fails on JUnit failures, not only the exit code.** Detected error screens only show up in the JUnit report. See [Run tests in CI](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/ci#decide-pass-or-fail).
- [ ] **Screenshots are kept when a run fails.** Upload `execution_output/` as a CI artifact.
- [ ] **File logs are on for CI runs.** `file_log: true` gives you every locator attempt when a failure is hard to explain.
- [ ] **Someone owns the failures.** Decide who looks at a red run, and how fast. A suite people learn to ignore is worse than no suite.

## If you use AI features

- [ ] **Healed steps are reviewed.** With [AI self-heal](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/self-heal) on, a healed step passes. Search the logs for `AI self-heal` after each run and update the elements.
- [ ] **Screens sent to the AI model are safe to share.** Plain-English mode and self-heal send screenshots to Google.

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/

# Supported platforms

> Learn which platforms Optics drives, what each one needs, and which keywords behave differently.

Optics runs the same tests on phones, TVs, browsers and locked production devices. A **driver** controls the device, and **element sources** are the ways Optics looks at the screen. You pick both in `config.yaml`.

## Support matrix

| Platform | Driver | Element sources | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Android | `appium` (UiAutomator2) | `appium_find_element`, `appium_page_source`, `appium_screenshot` | Needs the Appium server, adb, and a phone or emulator. |
| iOS | `appium` (XCUITest) | `appium_find_element`, `appium_page_source`, `appium_screenshot` | Needs a Mac with Xcode, and a simulator or a signed real device. |
| Android TV | `appium` (UiAutomator2) | `appium_find_element`, `appium_page_source`, `appium_screenshot` | Same setup as Android. Move around with D-pad key numbers. |
| Samsung Tizen | `appium` (`platformName: TizenTV`) | `appium_page_source`, `appium_screenshot` | Remote keys only. Touch and typing keywords fail with E0105. |
| LG webOS | `appium` (`platformName: LGTV`) | `appium_screenshot`, plus OCR | Remote keys only. Touch and typing keywords fail with E0105. |
| Web (Playwright) | `playwright` | `playwright_find_element`, `playwright_page_source`, `playwright_screenshot` | No server. Installs and opens its own Chromium. |
| Web (Selenium) | `selenium` | `selenium_find_element`, `selenium_page_source`, `selenium_screenshot` | Needs a WebDriver server or Grid. Chrome or Firefox. |
| Production devices (BLE + camera) | `ble` | `camera_screenshot`, plus OCR or image matching | Taps through a Bluetooth mouse and keyboard, and sees the screen through a camera. |

Enable one driver and the element sources whose names start with that driver's name. The [config.yaml reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/config) lists every key, and the [engines reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/engines) lists what each engine installs.

## Choose a driver for web

We recommend **Playwright** for most people. It needs no server, `optics setup` installs its browser for you, and it runs on your own machine.

Use **Selenium** when you already run a Selenium Grid, or need Firefox or a real Chrome on remote machines. It needs a WebDriver server running before each run. [Test websites](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/web) covers both.

## What changes between platforms

Between phones and browsers, only `config.yaml` changes. Your test cases, modules and keywords stay the same. To run a suite on another platform, copy the project and swap the driver and element sources.

TVs on Samsung Tizen and LG webOS are the exception. They have no touch screen, so Press Element and the typing keywords fail with E0105 there. Write those flows with Press Keycode steps that move the focus, such as `Press Keycode,RIGHT` and then `Press Keycode,ENTER`. [Test TV apps](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/tv) shows the key names.

Element values usually do change, because each platform names things differently. Give an element one row per platform, and Optics tries each value in turn:

`test_data/elements.csv`:

```csv
Element_Name,Element_ID
sign_in,//android.widget.Button[@text='Sign in']
sign_in,//XCUIElementTypeButton[@name='Sign in']
sign_in,Sign in
```

The last row is plain text, which works on any platform with a UI tree, and with OCR on any platform that takes screenshots. [Define elements](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/define) explains fallback values.

## What doesn't work everywhere

Most keywords work on every platform. These are the exceptions:

| Keyword | Where it differs |
|---|---|
| Press Element, Enter Text, Swipe, Scroll and other touch or typing keywords | Fail with E0105 on Samsung Tizen and LG webOS. Use Press Keycode with remote keys instead. |
| Press Keycode | Takes Android key numbers on Android and Android TV, remote key names on Tizen and webOS, and key names such as `Enter` on Playwright. Not supported on Selenium or iOS. |
| Swipe | Not supported on Selenium. On Playwright it turns the mouse wheel. |
| Scroll | Up and down only on Appium. Left and right are ignored. |
| Launch App | Opens a package or bundle id on Appium and a URL on Playwright. On Selenium it opens `browserURL`. Not supported on production devices. |
| Enter Text, Get Text | Fail in Playwright on Optics 1.10.5. See [Test websites](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/web) for the workaround. |
| XPath and UI-tree text | Not available on production devices, which only have camera pictures. Use OCR and images. |
| [Error detection](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/error-detection) | Needs the page source, so it doesn't run on production devices. |

The [keyword reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/) lists each keyword's behavior per driver.

## Platform guides

- [Android](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/android): Set up Appium and adb, then run on a phone or emulator.
- [iOS](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/ios): Run on a simulator or a signed device with XCUITest.
- [Web](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/web): Test websites with Playwright or Selenium. (Recommended)
- [TV](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/tv): Drive Android TV, Samsung Tizen and LG webOS with remote keys.
- [Production devices](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/production): Test locked devices through Bluetooth and a camera. (Advanced)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/android

# Test Android apps

> Set up Appium and adb, then run your tests on an Android phone or emulator.

Optics drives Android apps through **Appium**, an open-source server that taps, types and reads the screen on a device. You run the Appium server on your machine, Optics talks to it, and Appium talks to the phone or emulator over **adb** (Android Debug Bridge, the SDK's device tool).

This page uses Birch, a sample shoe store app with the package name `com.birch.shop`. Replace it with your own app.

## Before you begin

You need:

- Optics installed. See [Install Optics](https://optics-framework.org/docs/get-started/install).
- [Node.js](https://nodejs.org/) 20 or newer, to run the Appium server.
- The Android SDK. We recommend getting it with [Android Studio](https://developer.android.com/studio), which also creates emulators.
- An emulator, or an Android phone and a USB cable.

## Set up

### Install the Appium engine

```shell
$ optics setup --install appium
```

This adds the Python client that Optics uses to talk to Appium. It doesn't install the server.

### Install the Appium server and its Android driver

```shell
$ npm install -g appium
$ appium driver install uiautomator2
```

UiAutomator2 is the Appium driver for Android. It needs the `ANDROID_HOME` environment variable set to your SDK folder, and Java installed. Run `appium driver doctor uiautomator2` to check both.

### Make adb available

adb ships in the SDK's `platform-tools` folder. Add that folder to your PATH, then check it:

```shell
$ adb version
```

On macOS the SDK is usually in `~/Library/Android/sdk`, on Linux in `~/Android/Sdk`, and on Windows in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Android\Sdk`.

### Start an emulator or connect a phone

For an emulator, open Android Studio's **Device Manager** and start a virtual device.

For a phone, turn on **Developer options** (tap **Build number** seven times in **Settings > About phone**), then turn on **USB debugging**. Connect the cable and accept the "Allow USB debugging?" prompt on the phone.

Check that adb sees it:

```shell
$ adb devices
List of devices attached
emulator-5554	device
```

The first column is the device's serial. `device` in the second column means it's ready. `unauthorized` means you still need to accept the prompt on the phone.

### Find the app's package and activity

Optics needs the app's **package** (its id, such as `com.birch.shop`) and its **activity** (the screen it opens on). Open the app on the device, then ask adb what has focus:

```shell
$ adb shell dumpsys window | grep -E 'mCurrentFocus'
  mCurrentFocus=Window{4f2a1c u0 com.birch.shop/com.birch.shop.MainActivity}
```

The part before the `/` is the package, and the part after it is the activity. If you know the package, you can also ask Android for its launch activity:

```shell
$ adb shell cmd package resolve-activity --brief com.birch.shop
priority=0 preferredOrder=0 match=0x108000 specificIndex=-1 isDefault=true
com.birch.shop/.MainActivity
```

An activity that starts with a dot is short for the package plus that name: `.MainActivity` means `com.birch.shop.MainActivity`.

### Write config.yaml

Create a project with `optics init birch-android`, then replace its `config.yaml`:

`config.yaml`:

```yaml
driver_sources:
  - appium:
      enabled: true
      url: "http://127.0.0.1:4723"          # where the Appium server listens
      capabilities:                          # must not be empty
        platformName: Android                # required; picks the Android setup
        automationName: UiAutomator2
        deviceName: emulator-5554
        udid: emulator-5554                  # optional; pins one device
        appPackage: com.birch.shop           # app opened by "Launch App" with no value
        appActivity: com.birch.shop.MainActivity
        # appium:settings: {allowInvisibleElements: true}  # optional; include off-screen elements
elements_sources:
  - appium_find_element: {enabled: true}     # asks Appium for XPaths, ids and text
  - appium_page_source:  {enabled: true}     # searches the app's UI tree
  - appium_screenshot:   {enabled: true}     # screenshots for OCR and image matching
text_detection:
  - easyocr: {enabled: true}                 # needs: optics setup --install easyocr
image_detection:
  - templatematch: {enabled: true}           # finds .png templates anywhere in the project
log_level: INFO
file_log: true
json_log: true
```

Always set `url`. Optics can't connect if it's missing or empty. If you don't need OCR yet, delete the `text_detection` block, because an enabled OCR engine must be installed for every run.

### Check the setup

```shell
$ optics doctor birch-android
```

```terminal
Mobile
  ✅ adb                               found at /Users/you/Library/Android/sdk/platform-tools/adb
  ✅ adb devices                       1 connected: emulator-5554
  ⚠️ appium server                     not reachable at 127.0.0.1:4723
      → Start it in another terminal with the `appium` command.

Project
  ✅ config: driver                    appium enabled
  ✅ config: appium element source     enabled: appium_find_element, appium_page_source, appium_screenshot
  ✅ config: appium settings           required settings present
```

Fix every ❌ row. A ⚠️ on `adb devices` or `appium server` blocks the first run too, and the doctor lists them under "Before your first real run". A ⚠️ for `deviceName`, `appPackage` or `appActivity` means the key is missing from `capabilities`.

### Start Appium

Open a second terminal and leave this running:

```shell
$ appium
```

It listens on port 4723, which matches `url` in the config.

### Run the tests

```shell
$ optics execute birch-android
```

The app opens on the device and the terminal shows each step as it runs.

## Write steps for Android

Tests for Android look like any other Optics test. Elements can be XPaths into the Android UI tree, visible text, or images:

`test_data/elements.csv`:

```csv
Element_Name,Element_ID
email_field,//android.widget.EditText[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/email']
password_field,//android.widget.EditText[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/password']
sign_in,Sign in
password,@:trailrunner
```

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2
Open Birch,Launch App
Open Birch,Assert Presence,Sign in,20
Sign in,Enter Text,${email_field},ava@birch.shop
Sign in,Enter Text,${password_field},${password}
Sign in,Press Element,${sign_in}
Sign in,Assert Presence,Trail Runner 2,15
```

`Launch App` with no value opens `appPackage` from the config. Pass a package to open a different app: `Launch App,com.android.settings`. The `@:` prefix marks `password` as secret, so it's typed without the prefix and masked in log files. To find XPaths and ids, open the app in [`optics live`](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/record) or [Appium Inspector](https://github.com/appium/appium-inspector).

## What `optics execute` checks first

Before a run starts, `optics execute` runs a **preflight**. For Android it checks that:

1. The Appium server answers at `url`.
2. `adb` is on your PATH.
3. adb reports at least one device in the `device` state.

If a check fails, Optics stops and prints what to do:

```terminal
Cannot start

No Appium server reachable at http://127.0.0.1:4723.

Start one in another terminal:  appium
Then re-run:  optics execute birch-android
```

The adb checks only run when the plain `platformName` key is `Android`, in any capitalization. Optics doesn't read `appium:platformName` for this check. To skip the preflight, for example when Appium and the devices run on a remote device farm, set `OPTICS_SKIP_PREFLIGHT`:

```shell
$ OPTICS_SKIP_PREFLIGHT=1 optics execute birch-android
```

`optics dry_run` has no preflight, so it works without a device.

## Press keys

Press Keycode sends an Android key by its number:

| Key | Number |
|---|---|
| Back | `4` |
| Home | `3` |
| Enter | `66` |
| Backspace | `67` |
| Tab | `61` |
| Volume up / down | `24` / `25` |
| Recent apps | `187` |

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1
Go back,Press Keycode,4
```

Android's [KeyEvent list](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/view/KeyEvent) has every number. To press Enter after typing, you can also write `Enter Text Using Keyboard,<enter>`. See [Press Keycode](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/actions#press-keycode) for details.

## Tips

- **App data is kept between runs.** Optics starts each session with `noReset: true`, so Appium doesn't clear the app's data and a signed-in user stays signed in. Add `noReset: false` to `capabilities` to start every run from a fresh app.
- **Pick a device with `udid`.** When several devices are connected, set `udid` to the serial from `adb devices`. `deviceName` is only a label.
- **Include off-screen elements.** Android leaves elements that are scrolled out of view out of the UI tree. Add `appium:settings: {allowInvisibleElements: true}` under `capabilities` to include them.
- **Switch devices in `optics live`.** When you plug in another Android device during `optics live`, Optics notices and switches the session to it.
- **Android TV uses the same setup.** See [Test TV apps](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/tv) for remote-control keys.

## If it isn't working

- **"No Appium server reachable".** Start `appium` in another terminal. If it runs on another port or machine, make `url` match.
- **"No Android device/emulator attached".** Run `adb devices`. If the phone shows `unauthorized`, accept the prompt on it. If it shows `offline`, reconnect the cable or run `adb kill-server`, then `adb devices` again.
- **`E0104` "Appium capabilities not found in config".** `capabilities` is empty or missing. Add at least `platformName`.
- **`E0104` "Unsupported platform".** Check the spelling of `platformName`. Use `Android`.
- **Appium can't find the UiAutomator2 driver, or complains about `ANDROID_HOME`.** Run `appium driver install uiautomator2`, set `ANDROID_HOME`, and check with `appium driver doctor uiautomator2`.
- **The app opens on the wrong screen.** Check `appActivity`. If the app remembers an old state, set `noReset: false`.
- **A swipe or scroll passes but nothing moves.** Appium gesture errors are logged, not raised. Check the screenshots in `execution_output/`, and only use `up` and `down` with Scroll.
- **An element isn't found.** Actions don't wait, so put `Assert Presence` before them. [Troubleshooting](https://optics-framework.org/docs/help/troubleshooting) covers more cases.

## See also

- [Test TV apps](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/tv)
- [Define elements](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/define)
- [Run tests in CI](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/ci)
- [config.yaml reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/config)
- [CLI reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/cli)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/ios

# Test iOS apps

> Set up Appium with the XCUITest driver, then run your tests on an iOS simulator or device.

Optics drives iOS apps through **Appium** and its **XCUITest** driver, which uses Apple's own UI testing tools. You run the Appium server on a Mac, and Optics talks to it. iOS testing needs macOS, because Xcode only runs there.

This page uses Birch, a sample shoe store app with the bundle id `com.birch.shop`. Replace it with your own app.

## Before you begin

You need:

- A Mac with [Xcode](https://developer.apple.com/xcode/) installed from the App Store. Open it once to accept the license and install its components, then run `xcode-select --install` for the command-line tools.
- Optics installed. See [Install Optics](https://optics-framework.org/docs/get-started/install).
- [Node.js](https://nodejs.org/) 20 or newer, to run the Appium server.
- A build of your app: a `.app` for the simulator, or a signed build for a real device.

## Set up

### Install the Appium engine

```shell
$ optics setup --install appium
```

### Install the Appium server and the XCUITest driver

```shell
$ npm install -g appium
$ appium driver install xcuitest
```

### Start a simulator

List the simulators Xcode provides:

```shell
$ xcrun simctl list devices
== Devices ==
-- iOS 17.5 --
    iPhone 15 (5D1C2A60-8F0E-4B7A-9C41-2E6F0C3B9A17) (Shutdown)
    iPhone 15 Pro (A3E9F7B2-1C44-4D2B-8E0A-7B5D9C6E2F01) (Shutdown)
```

Boot one by name and open the Simulator app to watch it:

```shell
$ xcrun simctl boot "iPhone 15"
$ open -a Simulator
```

### Install the app and find its bundle id

Install your simulator build, then read its **bundle id**, the app's unique name:

```shell
$ xcrun simctl install booted Birch.app
$ plutil -extract CFBundleIdentifier raw Birch.app/Info.plist
com.birch.shop
```

### Write config.yaml

Create a project with `optics init birch-ios`, then replace its `config.yaml`:

`config.yaml`:

```yaml
driver_sources:
  - appium:
      enabled: true
      url: "http://127.0.0.1:4723"
      capabilities:
        platformName: iOS                    # picks the iOS setup
        automationName: XCUITest
        deviceName: "iPhone 15"              # the simulator's name
        bundleId: com.birch.shop             # required: the app Launch App opens
        # udid: <device udid>                # real devices
elements_sources:
  - appium_find_element: {enabled: true}
  - appium_page_source:  {enabled: true}
  - appium_screenshot:   {enabled: true}
```

If you have several iOS versions installed, add `platformVersion: "17.5"` so Appium picks the right simulator.

### Check the setup

```shell
$ optics doctor birch-ios
```

Without `bundleId`, the doctor shows a failure, because XCUITest has nothing to launch:

```terminal
Project
  ✅ config: driver                    appium enabled
  ✅ config: appium element source     enabled: appium_find_element, appium_page_source, appium_screenshot
  ❌ config: appium settings           bundleId missing in capabilities
      → Edit config.yaml in this project folder.
```

The `adb` rows in the Mobile section are for Android. Ignore them on iOS, even when the doctor lists the adb hint under "Before your first real run".

### Start Appium and run

Start the server in a second terminal and leave it running:

```shell
$ appium
```

Then run the tests:

```shell
$ optics execute birch-ios
```

Before the run, Optics checks that the Appium server answers at `url`. Set `OPTICS_SKIP_PREFLIGHT=1` to skip that check. The first session on a new simulator takes a few minutes, because Appium builds its helper app, WebDriverAgent, and installs it.

## Test on a real device

A real iPhone or iPad needs a few more steps:

1. Connect the device, trust the Mac, and turn on **Developer Mode** in **Settings > Privacy & Security**.
2. Find its id with `xcrun xctrace list devices` and set it as `udid` under `capabilities`.
3. Sign WebDriverAgent with your Apple developer team, so it can be installed on the device.

Signing is the step that most often goes wrong. Follow the [Appium XCUITest driver docs](https://appium.github.io/appium-xcuitest-driver/latest/) for real-device setup.

## Write steps for iOS

iOS elements have types such as `XCUIElementTypeButton` and attributes such as `name`, `label` and `value`. Use them in XPaths:

`test_data/elements.csv`:

```csv
Element_Name,Element_ID
email_field,//XCUIElementTypeTextField[@name='Email']
password_field,//XCUIElementTypeSecureTextField[@name='Password']
sign_in,//XCUIElementTypeButton[@name='Sign in']
sign_in,Sign in
back_button,//XCUIElementTypeButton[@name='Back']
```

Plain text such as `Sign in` is matched against the accessibility id and the `name`, `label` and `value` attributes. A value that starts with `XCUIElementType`, such as `XCUIElementTypeSwitch`, finds elements by type; add `index` to pick one of several.

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2
Open Birch,Launch App
Open Birch,Assert Presence,Sign in,20
Sign in,Enter Text,${email_field},ava@birch.shop
Sign in,Press Element,${sign_in}
Sign in,Assert Presence,Trail Runner 2,15
```

To see the real names in your app, open it in [`optics live`](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/record) or [Appium Inspector](https://github.com/appium/appium-inspector).

## Keys on iOS

iOS has no Back key and no Android key numbers, so Press Keycode doesn't work on iOS. Instead:

- **Go back.** Tap the app's own back button, such as `${back_button}` above.
- **Press Home.** Run XCUITest's `mobile: pressButton` command with Execute Script. Its buttons are `home`, `volumeup` and `volumedown`:

  `modules/modules.csv`:

  ```csv
  module_name,module_step,param_1
  Go home,Execute Script,"{""script"": ""mobile: pressButton"", ""args"": {""name"": ""home""}}"
  ```

- **Type and submit.** Type with Enter Text on a field, then tap the keyboard's own submit key by its label. Enter Text Direct, Enter Text Using Keyboard and `<enter>`-style keys are built on Android key commands.

## If it isn't working

- **The doctor shows ❌ for `bundleId`.** Add `bundleId` under `capabilities`. Only the plain key name counts for this check.
- **"No Appium server reachable".** Start `appium` in another terminal, and make `url` match its port.
- **Appium can't find the XCUITest driver.** Run `appium driver install xcuitest`, then restart `appium`.
- **Appium can't find the simulator.** Make `deviceName` match a name from `xcrun simctl list devices`, and add `platformVersion` if several iOS versions are installed.
- **WebDriverAgent fails to build or install on a device.** This is a signing problem. See the [XCUITest driver docs](https://appium.github.io/appium-xcuitest-driver/latest/).
- **`E0104` "Unsupported platform".** Check the spelling of `platformName`. Use `iOS`.
- **An element isn't found.** Actions don't wait, so put `Assert Presence` before them. [Troubleshooting](https://optics-framework.org/docs/help/troubleshooting) covers more cases.

## See also

- [Test Android apps](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/android)
- [Define elements](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/define)
- [Run tests in CI](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/ci)
- [config.yaml reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/config)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/web

# Test websites

> Set up Playwright or Selenium, then run your tests in a browser.

Optics tests websites with one of two drivers. **Playwright** starts a browser on your machine and needs no server. **Selenium** sends commands to a WebDriver server, such as a Selenium Grid, which runs the browser.

We recommend Playwright unless you already run a Selenium Grid, or need Firefox or a real Chrome on remote machines. The examples use the [Sauce Labs demo store](https://www.saucedemo.com), which you can sign in to with `standard_user` / `secret_sauce`.

## Set up

**Playwright**

Install the engine. Optics also downloads the Chromium browser that Playwright uses:

```shell
$ optics setup --install playwright
```

Then enable the driver and its three element sources:

`config.yaml`:

```yaml
driver_sources:
  - playwright:
      enabled: true                          # no url and no server needed
      capabilities:
        browser: chromium                    # ignored on 1.10.5: always Chromium
        headless: false                      # ignored on 1.10.5: always a visible window
        # viewport: {width: 1280, height: 800}  # ignored on 1.10.5: always 1280×800
elements_sources:
  - playwright_find_element: {enabled: true}
  - playwright_page_source:  {enabled: true}
  - playwright_screenshot:   {enabled: true}
```

**Note:**
On Optics 1.10.5, Playwright ignores `browser`, `headless` and `viewport` under `capabilities`. It always opens a visible Chromium window at 1280×800. You can leave the keys in place for when they take effect.

There's no server to start, so `optics execute` skips its preflight check for Playwright.

**Enter Text and Get Text fail in browsers on Optics 1.10.5:**
On 1.10.5, Enter Text and Get Text fail in Playwright with `Object of type Locator is not JSON serializable`. Both are fixed in the next release ([pull request #600](https://github.com/mozarkai/optics-framework/pull/600)). Until you upgrade, click the field, then type into it:

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2
Sign in,Press Element,${username_field}
Sign in,Enter Text Direct,standard_user
```

**Selenium**

Install the engine:

```shell
$ optics setup --install selenium
```

Selenium needs a WebDriver server. The quickest is Selenium's Docker image, which runs Chrome inside a container:

```shell
$ docker run -d -p 4444:4444 selenium/standalone-chrome
```

For Firefox, use `selenium/standalone-firefox`. If you already run a Selenium Grid, point `url` at it instead.

Then enable the driver and its element sources:

`config.yaml`:

```yaml
driver_sources:
  - selenium:
      enabled: true
      url: "http://localhost:4444/wd/hub"   # your Grid or standalone server
      capabilities:                          # must not be empty
        browserName: chrome                  # required: chrome or firefox
        browserURL: "https://www.saucedemo.com"  # page opened when the browser starts
elements_sources:
  - selenium_find_element: {enabled: true}
  - selenium_page_source:  {enabled: true}
  - selenium_screenshot:   {enabled: true}
```

`capabilities` must include `browserName`, and only `chrome` and `firefox` work. `optics configure` writes `capabilities: {}` for Selenium, which can't start, so add these keys by hand. Other keys under `capabilities` are passed to the browser as WebDriver capabilities.

Before each run, `optics execute` checks that the server answers at `url`. If it doesn't, Optics stops with a "Cannot start" panel. Set `OPTICS_SKIP_PREFLIGHT=1` to skip the check.

Then check the setup and run your tests:

```shell
$ optics doctor my-web-tests
$ optics execute my-web-tests
```

## Open the site

Launch App starts the browser. How it picks the page depends on the driver:

| Step | Playwright | Selenium |
|---|---|---|
| `Launch App,https://www.saucedemo.com` | Opens the browser at that URL. | Opens the browser at that URL the first time. |
| `Launch App` with no URL | Opens a blank page. | Opens `browserURL`, or a blank page if it isn't set. |
| `Launch Other App,https://www.saucedemo.com/cart.html` | Opens the URL in a new tab. | Goes to the URL in the current tab. |

We recommend putting the URL in the Launch App step. Then the same module works with both drivers.

## Write steps for the web

Here is a full sign-in test for the Sauce Labs demo store. It works with both drivers on Optics 1.10.5:

`test_data/elements.csv`:

```csv
Element_Name,Element_ID
username_field,//input[@id='user-name']
password_field,//input[@id='password']
login_button,//input[@id='login-button']
backpack_add_button,//button[@id='add-to-cart-sauce-labs-backpack']
```

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2
Open the store,Launch App,https://www.saucedemo.com
Open the store,Assert Presence,Swag Labs,15
Sign in,Press Element,${username_field}
Sign in,Enter Text Direct,standard_user
Sign in,Press Element,${password_field}
Sign in,Enter Text Direct,secret_sauce
Sign in,Press Element,${login_button}
Sign in,Assert Presence,Products,10
Add the backpack,Press Element,${backpack_add_button}
Add the backpack,Assert Presence,Remove,5
```

`test_cases/test_cases.csv`:

```csv
test_case,test_step
Shopper can add a backpack,Open the store
Shopper can add a backpack,Sign in
Shopper can add a backpack,Add the backpack
```

### Locators for web pages

| Kind | Example | Playwright | Selenium |
|---|---|---|---|
| XPath | `//input[@id='user-name']` | Yes, also with `xpath=` | Yes. Leave out `xpath=`. |
| Visible text | `Products`, `text=Add to cart` | Yes | Yes |
| Bare id or name | `user-name` | No | Yes. Tried as an id, name, class or link text when no text matches. |
| CSS selector | `#user-name`, `.inventory_item_name`, `css=button[data-test='login-button']` | Yes | No |
| Image | `cart_icon.png` | With image matching on | With image matching on |

We recommend XPath for web elements. It's the one kind of value that works the same way with both drivers, so you can switch drivers without editing elements.

To see an element's id or attributes, right-click it in Chrome and choose **Inspect**. [Define elements](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/define) explains each kind of value.

**Assertions skip CSS selectors:**
Assert Presence and Assert Visibility only check text, XPath and image values, even on Playwright. A CSS value such as `#user-name` is skipped without an error. Use visible text or an XPath in assertions.

## Press keys

| Driver | How to press Enter | Other keys |
|---|---|---|
| Playwright | `Press Keycode,Enter` | `Tab`, `Escape`, `Backspace`, `Delete`, `Space`, `ArrowUp`, `ArrowDown`, `ArrowLeft`, `ArrowRight`, and other [Playwright key names](https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-keyboard#keyboard-press) |
| Selenium | `Enter Text Using Keyboard,<enter>` | `<tab>`, `<backspace>`, `<space>`, `<escape>` |

Press Keycode isn't supported on Selenium. The keys go to whichever field has focus, so press the field first.

## Run in CI without a screen

On Optics 1.10.5, Playwright always opens a visible window, even when you set `headless: true`. On a Linux CI machine with no display, run Optics under a virtual display:

```shell
$ xvfb-run optics execute my-web-tests
```

With Selenium in Docker, the browser runs inside the container, so the CI machine needs no display. To run Chrome headless on a Grid, pass Chrome's own arguments. They replace the arguments Optics adds, so keep the ones you need:

`config.yaml`:

```yaml
driver_sources:
  - selenium:
      enabled: true
      url: "http://localhost:4444/wd/hub"
      capabilities:
        browserName: chrome
        goog:chromeOptions:
          args: ["--headless=new", "--no-sandbox", "--disable-dev-shm-usage"]
```

[Run tests in CI](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/ci) covers the rest of the CI setup.

## If it isn't working

- **"Object of type Locator is not JSON serializable".** Enter Text or Get Text ran in Playwright on 1.10.5. Use Press Element, then Enter Text Direct. See [Troubleshooting](https://optics-framework.org/docs/help/troubleshooting#locator-not-serializable).
- **The Playwright browser isn't installed.** Run `optics setup --install playwright` again. `optics doctor` shows a ✅ for `playwright browser` once Chromium is downloaded.
- **"Selenium capabilities not found in config".** Add `browserName: chrome` or `browserName: firefox` under `capabilities`.
- **"Cannot start" with "No Selenium/WebDriver server reachable".** Start the server, and check that `url` points to it.
- **Swipe fails on Selenium.** Selenium has no Swipe. Use Scroll, which moves one screen in any direction.
- **A step acts before the page loads.** Actions don't wait. Put `Assert Presence` on something from the new page before you act on it.

## See also

- [Write your first test](https://optics-framework.org/docs/get-started/first-test)
- [Define elements](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/define)
- [Run tests in CI](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/ci)
- [Actions reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/actions)
- [config.yaml reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/config)

# Test TV apps

> Drive Android TV, Samsung Tizen and LG webOS apps with remote-control keys.

Optics tests TV apps through **Appium**, the same server it uses for phones. Each TV platform has its own Appium driver, and you pick it with `platformName` in `config.yaml`. On a TV you move around with remote-control keys and check what's on screen with assertions.

| TV platform | `platformName` | Appium driver | How you move around |
|---|---|---|---|
| Android TV | `Android` | UiAutomator2 | Android key numbers, plus taps and typing |
| Samsung Tizen | `TizenTV` | [appium-tizen-tv-driver](https://github.com/headspinio/appium-tizen-tv-driver) | Remote key names only |
| LG webOS | `LGTV` | [appium-lg-webos-driver](https://github.com/headspinio/appium-lg-webos-driver) | Remote key names only |

The examples use a TV app for Birch, a sample shoe store, with rows of shoes such as "Trail Runner 2" and "Pace Knit".

## Before you begin

You need Optics with the Appium engine and the Appium server:

```shell
$ optics setup --install appium
$ npm install -g appium
```

Each TV also needs its own setup: developer mode on the TV, the vendor's tools, and the TV on the same network as your machine. Those steps belong to each Appium driver, and its project page covers them.

## Android TV

Android TV uses the same setup as an Android phone. Follow [Test Android apps](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/android), with `platformName: Android` and the TV's serial from `adb devices` as `udid`. Connect to the TV with `adb connect <tv-ip>` when it isn't on a cable.

Touch and typing keywords work on Android TV, but most TV apps expect the D-pad. Send it with Press Keycode and Android key numbers:

| Remote button | Number |
|---|---|
| Up / Down / Left / Right | `19` / `20` / `21` / `22` |
| Select (center) | `23` |
| Back | `4` |
| Home | `3` |
| Play/pause | `85` |

Remote key names such as `UP` don't work on Android TV. They only apply to Tizen and webOS.

## Samsung Tizen

Install the Tizen driver into Appium:

```shell
$ appium driver install --source=npm appium-tizen-tv-driver
```

Then configure Optics:

`config.yaml`:

```yaml
driver_sources:
  - appium:
      enabled: true
      url: "http://localhost:4723"
      capabilities:
        platformName: TizenTV
        appium:automationName: TizenTV
        appium:deviceAddress: 192.168.1.50
        appium:rcToken: "14184553"
        appium:appPackage: com.birch.tv
        appium:app: /path/to/birch.wgt
        appium:chromedriverExecutableDir: /path/to/chromedrivers
elements_sources:
  - appium_page_source: {enabled: true}
  - appium_screenshot:  {enabled: true}
```

Optics reads `platformName` and the app id (`appPackage`, with or without the `appium:` prefix). It passes every other capability to the Tizen driver unchanged. The [driver's README](https://github.com/headspinio/appium-tizen-tv-driver) explains each one, including how to get the `rcToken`.

## LG webOS

Install the webOS driver into Appium:

```shell
$ appium driver install --source=npm appium-lg-webos-driver
```

Then configure Optics:

`config.yaml`:

```yaml
driver_sources:
  - appium:
      enabled: true
      url: "http://localhost:4723"
      capabilities:
        platformName: LGTV
        appium:automationName: webOS
        appium:deviceHost: 192.168.1.50
        appium:appId: com.birch.tv
        appium:rcMode: rc
        appium:useSecureWebsocket: true
        appium:newCommandTimeout: 600
elements_sources:
  - appium_screenshot: {enabled: true}
text_detection:
  - easyocr: {enabled: true}               # reads text on the TV screenshot
```

This setup finds things on screen with screenshots only, so add an OCR engine (`optics setup --install easyocr`) to check text, or [image matching](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/text-and-images) for icons. The [driver's README](https://github.com/headspinio/appium-lg-webos-driver) explains the capabilities.

## Check the setup

Start `appium` in another terminal, then run the doctor:

```shell
$ optics doctor birch-tv
```

The doctor's checks are written for phones. On Tizen and webOS it warns that `deviceName`, `appPackage` or `appActivity` is missing. You can ignore those warnings, and the `adb` rows, as long as `config: driver` and `config: appium element source` show ✅.

Before each run, `optics execute` checks that the Appium server answers at `url`. It doesn't check the TV itself.

## Move around with remote keys

On Tizen and webOS, Press Keycode takes the name of a remote button:

| Key name | Button |
|---|---|
| `UP`, `DOWN`, `LEFT`, `RIGHT` | Arrow keys |
| `ENTER`, `OK`, `SELECT` | OK, the center button |
| `BACK` | Back |
| `HOME` | Home |
| `PLAY`, `PAUSE`, `STOP` | Playback |
| `REWIND`, `FF` | Rewind and fast-forward. `FAST_FORWARD` also works. |

Names aren't case-sensitive. On Tizen, any raw Samsung key name that starts with `KEY_`, such as `KEY_MENU`, is also sent as is. On webOS, unknown names are passed to the TV unchanged.

## What doesn't work on Tizen and webOS

TVs have no touch screen, so touch and typing keywords fail with **E0105** ("not supported") on Tizen and webOS:

- Press Element, Detect And Press, Press By Coordinates, Press By Percentage, Select Dropdown Option
- Swipe, Swipe By Percentage, Swipe From Element, Swipe Until Element Appears
- Scroll, Scroll From Element, Scroll Until Element Appears
- Enter Text, Enter Text Direct, Enter Text Using Keyboard, Enter Number, Clear Element Text, Get Text, Assert Text

These still work: Launch App, Press Keycode, Assert Presence, Assert Visibility, Validate Element, Validate Screen, Is Element, Capture Screenshot, Sleep, Execute Script, the flow keywords, and Close And Terminate App.

To type on a TV, move over the on-screen keyboard with arrow keys and press `ENTER` on each letter.

## Example: open a title from a grid

A TV app usually shows rows of tiles. This module moves down one row, right one tile, opens it and starts playback. It checks the screen after each move that changes the page:

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2
Open Birch TV,Launch App
Open Birch TV,Assert Presence,Featured,30
Open the second shoe in Running,Press Keycode,DOWN
Open the second shoe in Running,Press Keycode,RIGHT
Open the second shoe in Running,Press Keycode,ENTER
Open the second shoe in Running,Assert Presence,Trail Runner 2,10
Watch the video,Press Keycode,ENTER
Watch the video,Sleep,5
Watch the video,Press Keycode,PAUSE
Watch the video,Validate Screen,Paused,5
Go home,Press Keycode,BACK
Go home,Press Keycode,BACK
Go home,Assert Presence,Featured,10
```

`test_cases/test_cases.csv`:

```csv
test_case,test_step
Watch a shoe video,Open Birch TV
Watch a shoe video,Open the second shoe in Running
Watch a shoe video,Watch the video
Watch a shoe video,Go home
```

A few habits make TV tests reliable:

- **Assert after each page change.** Keys don't wait for the app. Assert Presence waits for the next page, so the following key lands in the right place.
- **Start from a known place.** Begin each test with Launch App and an assertion on the first screen. Don't rely on where an earlier test left the focus.
- **Remember that Validate Screen never fails a step.** Use it for checks that are nice to have, and Assert Presence for checks that must pass.
- **Use text you can see.** On webOS, Assert Presence reads the screen with OCR, so check words that are drawn large and clear.

## See also

- [Test Android apps](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/android)
- [Find elements by text and image](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/text-and-images)
- [Press Keycode](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/actions#press-keycode)
- [Verification keywords](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/verification)
- [Error codes](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/errors)

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/production

# Test production devices

> Test locked devices and live apps through a Bluetooth mouse and keyboard and a camera.

Optics can test a device with no automation software on it at all. A **BLE dongle** (a small USB Bluetooth adapter) pairs with the device as an ordinary Bluetooth mouse and keyboard. A **camera** pointed at the screen shows Optics what's there. Optics finds things in the camera picture with OCR and image matching, then moves the pointer and taps.

## When to use it

Use this setup when the usual drivers can't reach the device:

- **USB debugging or developer mode isn't allowed**, for example on locked company phones or retail devices.
- **The app blocks screenshots**, as banking and streaming apps often do. The camera sees the screen anyway.
- **You monitor the live app.** Synthetic monitoring runs the same journey on a real, unmodified device and app, the way a customer would.

If you can use Appium or a browser driver, do. They're faster, read the UI tree directly, and support every keyword.

## What you need

- **A USB serial BLE HID dongle.** It plugs into your machine as a serial port, and pairs with the device as a Bluetooth mouse and keyboard.
- **A way to see the screen.** Either a camera or capture card that your machine sees as a webcam, or a TCP frame server that sends a picture on request.
- **An OCR engine**, such as EasyOCR, to read text in the camera picture.
- **Image templates** (optional), cropped pictures of icons that have no text. See [Find elements by text and image](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/text-and-images).
- **A stand** that holds the camera square over the screen, so the picture doesn't shift between runs.

## Set up

### Install the engines

```shell
$ optics setup --install ble easyocr
```

The `ble` engine adds serial-port support. The camera source and image matching need no extra install.

### Pair the dongle with the device

Plug the dongle into your machine. On the device, open Bluetooth settings and pair with the dongle like any keyboard. A pointer appears on screen once it's connected.

### Find the dongle's serial port

| System | Command | Looks like |
|---|---|---|
| macOS | `ls /dev/cu.usbmodem*` | `/dev/cu.usbmodem1101` |
| Linux | `ls /dev/ttyACM*` | `/dev/ttyACM0` |
| Windows | Device Manager, under **Ports (COM & LPT)** | `COM3` |

Instead of a path, you can give the dongle's USB product description, such as `MZ-BLE-VMK-001-v1.2.1`. Optics finds the matching port for you, which helps when the port number changes between reboots.

### Point the camera at the screen

Mount the camera straight on, with the screen upright and filling the picture edge to edge. Optics turns positions in the camera picture straight into pointer moves, so anything around the screen throws the taps off.

### Write config.yaml

`config.yaml`:

```yaml
driver_sources:
  - ble:
      enabled: true
      capabilities:
        device_id: "Birch test phone"        # a label for the device
        port: /dev/ttyACM0                   # or the dongle's USB product description
        pixel_width: 1080                    # size of the screen in the camera picture
        pixel_height: 2336
        mickeys_width: 1080                  # pointer units to cross the screen
        mickeys_height: 2336
        x_invert: 1                          # -1 if the pointer moves the wrong way
        y_invert: 1
elements_sources:
  - camera_screenshot:
      enabled: true
      capabilities:
        camera_index: 0                      # or url: "192.168.1.20:9000" for a frame server
text_detection:
  - easyocr: {enabled: true}
image_detection:
  - templatematch: {enabled: true}
```

### Calibrate, then run

Follow [Calibrate the pointer](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/production#calibrate-the-pointer) below, then start the app on the device by hand and run:

```shell
$ optics execute birch-production
```

There's no preflight for this setup, so check the dongle and camera before you start a long run.

## Settings

### `ble` driver

| Name | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `device_id` | Required | A name for the device. |
| `port` | Required | The dongle's serial port (`/dev/ttyACM0`, `/dev/cu.usbmodem1101`, `COM3`), or its USB product description. |
| `pixel_width`, `pixel_height` | `0` | The size of the device screen in camera-picture pixels. Set both. Optics fails to start when they're `0`. |
| `mickeys_width`, `mickeys_height` | `0` | How many pointer units it takes to cross the screen. Set both. Optics fails to start when they're `0`. |
| `x_invert`, `y_invert` | `1` | Set to `-1` to flip the direction the pointer moves on that axis. |

### `camera_screenshot` source

| Name | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `camera_index` | None | The webcam or capture card to use. `0` is the first one your system finds. |
| `url` | None | A TCP frame server as `host:port`. Use instead of `camera_index`. |
| `header_size` | `8` | Frame server only. The length of the size header in bytes, `4` or `8`. |
| `byte_order` | `little` | Frame server only. The byte order of the size header, `little` or `big`. |

Set either `camera_index` or `url`. With neither, Optics stops with "No camera_index or valid URL provided".

A frame server receives the line `screenshot`, then replies with the picture's size in a `header_size`-byte unsigned number, followed by the picture as JPEG or PNG.

## Calibrate the pointer

Optics resets the pointer to a corner before each tap, then moves it by the distance it calculated from the camera picture. Calibration makes that distance land in the right place.

1. **Set the pixel size.** Set `pixel_width` and `pixel_height` to the size of the camera picture. Take one with `Capture Screenshot` and check its size.
2. **Start with equal units.** Set `mickeys_width` and `mickeys_height` to the same numbers as the pixels.
3. **Tap a far corner.** Run a one-step module, `Press By Percentage,90,90`, and watch where the pointer lands.
4. **Adjust.** If the pointer stops short of the spot, raise the mickeys for that axis. If it overshoots, lower them. Repeat until the tap lands.
5. **Fix the direction.** If the pointer moves left when it should move right, set `x_invert: -1`. Do the same with `y_invert` for up and down.

Calibrate again whenever you move the camera, change the device, or change its display size or orientation.

## What works and what doesn't

| Works | How |
|---|---|
| Press Element, Detect And Press | With text values (found by OCR) or image values. Optics moves the pointer there and taps. |
| Press By Coordinates, Press By Percentage | Taps a spot in the camera picture. |
| Enter Text | Finds the field by OCR or image, taps it, then types through the Bluetooth keyboard. |
| Enter Text Direct | Types into the field that has focus. |
| Assert Presence, Validate Screen | Read the camera picture with OCR or image matching. |
| Swipe, Swipe By Percentage, Swipe From Element | Press, drag and release with the pointer. |
| Scroll | Up and down only. |

| Doesn't work | Instead |
|---|---|
| Launch App, Launch Other App | Start the app by hand, or tap its icon on the home screen with Press Element. |
| XPath and UI-tree text | There's no UI tree. Use visible text, which OCR reads, or images. |
| Get Text, Assert Text, Get App Version, Execute Script | Not available over Bluetooth. Use Assert Presence with the text you expect. |
| Back, Volume, Power and other phone-only keys | A Bluetooth keyboard has no such keys. Tap the app's own back button. |
| Named keys such as `Enter` | On 1.10.5, `Press Keycode,Enter` and `<enter>` type the letters of the key's name. Tap the on-screen key instead. |
| [Error detection](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/error-detection) at the end of a run | It needs the page source, which a camera can't provide. Add Assert Presence checks for error messages you care about. |

`optics live`, `optics serve` and `optics mcp` run Launch App when they start, so that first step fails with this setup. Start the app by hand before you begin.

Here is a sign-in journey written for a production phone. Every value is text that OCR can read on screen:

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2
Open Birch,Press Element,Birch
Open Birch,Assert Presence,Sign in,20
Sign in,Enter Text,Email,ava@birch.shop
Sign in,Enter Text,Password,@:trailrunner
Sign in,Press Element,Sign in
Sign in,Assert Presence,Trail Runner 2,20
```

The first step taps the Birch icon on the home screen, so the run starts from there.

## Known gaps

- **Camera correction isn't applied.** `deskew_corners`, `rotation`, `out_width` and `out_height` under `camera_screenshot` have no effect in 1.10.5. Frame the camera straight on, with the screen upright, instead.
- **The doctor reports a failure.** `optics doctor` expects an element source whose name starts with `ble_`, and none exists. It shows ❌ for `config: ble element source`. Ignore that row, and don't use `optics doctor --check` on this project in CI.

## If it isn't working

- **"Could not resolve serial port for product description".** No connected port has that description. Check the dongle is plugged in, or use the port path instead.
- **Optics stops at start with a division error.** `pixel_width`, `pixel_height`, `mickeys_width` or `mickeys_height` is `0` or missing. Set all four.
- **"No camera_index or valid URL provided".** Add `camera_index` or `url` under the `camera_screenshot` capabilities.
- **Taps land in the wrong place.** Recalibrate. Check that the screen fills the camera picture and that nothing moved.
- **Text isn't found.** Improve the picture: even light, no glare, the camera in focus. Use an [area of interest](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/area-of-interest) to search a smaller part of the screen.
- **The pointer doesn't move.** Check the device is still paired with the dongle and that its pointer shows on screen.

## See also

- [Find elements by text and image](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/text-and-images)
- [Search part of the screen](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/area-of-interest)
- [Engines reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/engines)
- [config.yaml reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/config)
