Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/

# Advanced

> Add data, logic and integrations to your suites once the basics are in place.

Most suites never need the features in this section. A list of modules with good elements and a few checks covers most user flows. Reach for these when a flow depends on data, needs to branch, or when another system needs to drive Optics.

## Logic and data

- [Variables](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/variables): Store values, compute new ones, and use them in later steps.
- [Data-driven tests](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/data-driven): Run one flow once per row of a data file.
- [Conditions and loops](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/conditions): Branch on what's on screen, and repeat modules.
- [Call APIs in a test](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/api-calls): Fetch or create data over HTTP mid-test, and use the response in later steps.

## Integrate

- [Run keywords over HTTP](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/http-api): Drive a device from your own service with `optics serve`.
- [Generate pytest or Robot code](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/generate): Turn a suite into code you can extend.
- [Let your AI agent build tests](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/agent): Connect `optics mcp` to Claude, Cursor or any MCP client.
- [Use Optics from Python](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/python): Call keywords from your own scripts.

**How logic runs in a suite:**
Flow-control keywords run other modules. Steps inside those modules work slightly differently from top-level steps: they use only the first value of each element, and they don't accept `name=value` parameters. Keep modules that run inside loops and conditions simple, and give their elements a reliable first value.

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/variables

# Variables

> Store values, compute new ones during a run, and use them in later steps.

In Optics, a variable is an element that holds a value instead of a locator. You define some in your elements file, and some keywords create or change them while the test runs. Any step can then use the value with `${name}`.

## Define a variable

Add a row to an elements file, like any element:

`test_data/elements.csv`:

```csv
Element_Name,Element_ID
email,ava@birch.shop
search_term,trail runner
discount_code,WELCOME10
```

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2
Search,Enter Text,${search_bar},${search_term}
```

## Where ${name} works

**As a whole value.** `${search_term}` on its own in a cell is replaced by the variable's value. When a variable has several values, they're tried in order, the same as [element fallbacks](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/define).

**Inside other text.** `Hello ${name}` becomes `Hello Ava`. Inside a longer value, a variable gives its first value. Write `$${name}` to type the text `${name}` itself.

**Inside expressions.** A few keywords read `${name}` anywhere in their text: the expressions in `Evaluate` and `Condition`, the query in `Read Data`, and the URL, headers and body of an API call in `Invoke API`. These use the variable's first value.

## Create variables during a run

These keywords write a variable. Write the **name** of the variable on its own, without `${}`:

| Keyword | Writes | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `Evaluate` | The result of an expression | `Evaluate,total,${price} + 5` |
| `Date Evaluate` | A date some days away | `Date Evaluate,delivery_date,${order_date},+5 days` |
| `Read Data` | A value from a CSV or JSON file, or an environment variable | `Read Data,admin_email,test_data/users.csv,role == 'admin';select=email` |
| `Invoke API` | Values from an API response | See [Call APIs in a test](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/api-calls) |
| `Run Loop` | The current item, once per pass | See [Data-driven tests](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/data-driven) |
| Any keyword with `store_as=name` | What the keyword returns | `Get Text,${price_label},store_as=price` |

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2,param_3
Check Total,Evaluate,expected_total,${price} * 2
Check Total,Assert Presence,${expected_total}
```

**Writing ${total} as the name:**
`Evaluate,${total},${price} + 5` doesn't create `total`. Optics replaces `${total}` before the keyword runs, so the step fails with "Element not found: total", or writes to a variable named after its old value. Write `Evaluate,total,${price} + 5`.

### Keep what a keyword returns

Add `store_as=name` to a step whose keyword returns a value, such as Get Text or Execute Script. Later steps use it as `${name}`:

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2
Check Order,Get Text,${order_number_label},store_as=order_number
Check Order,Enter Text,${search_bar},${order_number}
Check Order,Assert Text,${first_result},Order ${order_number}
```

Get Text on a text field returns what the field holds, so you can copy a value from one field to another.

### Declare run-time variables for dry runs

`optics dry_run` checks that every `${name}` is defined, but it doesn't run the keywords that create variables. Add a placeholder row for each variable a keyword creates, so the dry run passes. The keyword replaces the placeholder during the real run:

`test_data/elements.csv`:

```csv
Element_Name,Element_ID
price,64
expected_total,placeholder
```

This works for `Evaluate`, `Read Data`, `Invoke API`, `Run Loop` and `store_as`. Don't add a placeholder for `Date Evaluate`: in Optics 1.10.5 it adds its result after the placeholder instead of replacing it, so `${delivery_date}` would give `placeholder`. The dry run reports the date variable as missing, which you can ignore.

## Values are text

Every value is text, even when it looks like a number. That matters in expressions:

- **Evaluate** puts the value into the expression as you wrote it. `${price} + 5` with `price` set to `64` becomes `64 + 5`, which is `69`. To join text, quote it: `'${first_name}' + ' ' + '${last_name}'`.
- **Condition** puts quotes around each value. `${count} == '3'` works. `${count} > 2` fails, because it compares text with a number. Compare against quoted text, or compute the comparison with Evaluate first. See [Conditions and loops](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/conditions).

Evaluate allows arithmetic (`+ - * / % **`), comparisons, `and`, `or`, `not` and `x if condition else y`. It doesn't allow function calls such as `int()`.

## Hide sensitive values

Start a value with `@:` to keep it out of log files: `password,@:correct-horse`. Optics logs `****` and types the value without the prefix.

Values that Read Data or `store_as` keep under a name such as `password`, `pin`, `otp`, `token`, `secret` or `api_key` are masked as `****` too.

For real secrets, don't commit them at all. Read them from the environment at run time:

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2
Sign In,Read Data,password,ENV:BIRCH_PASSWORD
Sign In,Enter Text,${password_field},${password}
```

Add `password,placeholder` to your elements file so `optics dry_run` accepts `${password}`, and set `BIRCH_PASSWORD` in your shell or CI secrets.

## See also

- [Data-driven tests](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/data-driven)
- [Conditions and loops](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/conditions)
- [Flow control keywords](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/flow)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/data-driven

# Run a flow with different data

> Repeat one module for every value in a list, such as each user, search term or product.

A data-driven test runs the same flow several times with different inputs. In Optics, you write the flow once as a module, keep the inputs in a list, and use `Run Loop` to run the module once per item.

## Loop over a list of values

This example signs in to the Sauce Labs demo store as three different users, signing out after each one. It runs as written with the Playwright setup from [Write your first test](https://optics-framework.org/docs/get-started/first-test).

`test_data/elements.csv`:

```csv
Element_Name,Element_ID
username_field,//input[@id='user-name']
password_field,//input[@id='password']
login_button,//input[@id='login-button']
menu_button,//button[@id='react-burger-menu-btn']
logout_link,//a[@id='logout_sidebar_link']
shoppers,standard_user|visual_user|problem_user
username,placeholder
```

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2,param_3
Open the store,Launch App,https://www.saucedemo.com
Sign In Each Shopper,Run Loop,Sign In And Out,username,${shoppers}
Sign In And Out,Enter Text,${username_field},${username}
Sign In And Out,Enter Text,${password_field},secret_sauce
Sign In And Out,Press Element,${login_button}
Sign In And Out,Assert Presence,Products
Sign In And Out,Press Element,${menu_button}
Sign In And Out,Sleep,1
Sign In And Out,Press Element,${logout_link}
Sign In And Out,Assert Presence,${login_button}
```

`test_cases/test_cases.csv`:

```csv
test_case,test_step
Suite Setup,Open the store
Every shopper can sign in,Sign In Each Shopper
```

`Run Loop,Sign In And Out,username,${shoppers}` reads: *run the module **Sign In And Out** once for each value in `shoppers`, and set `username` to that value each time.* Inside the module, `${username}` is the current shopper.

A few details make this work:

- **`username` is written without `${}`** in the Run Loop step, because the loop writes it. See [Variables](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/variables).
- **`username,placeholder`** in the elements file lets `optics dry_run` accept `${username}`. The loop replaces it.
- **The values are separated by `|`.** You can also write them straight into the step: `Run Loop,Sign In And Out,username,standard_user|visual_user`.
- **`Sleep,1`** waits for the menu to slide open. Prefer a check such as `Assert Presence` to wait for a new screen, but use a short sleep for an animation on an element that's already on the page.

The run shows the loop as one step. If any pass fails, the loop stops and the step fails with the reason:

```terminal
└── Every shopper can sign in                                     |  5.86s |    PASS
    └── Sign In Each Shopper                                      |  5.86s |    PASS
        └── Run Loop (Sign In And Out, username, standard_user… |  5.86s |    PASS
```

## Loop over several lists at once

Give more name and list pairs to set several variables per pass. The lists are read side by side, and the loop stops at the end of the shortest:

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2,param_3,param_4,param_5
Every Search,Run Loop,Search And Check,term,trail|pace|ridge,expected,Trail Runner 2|Pace Knit|Ridge GTX
Search And Check,Press Element,${search_bar}
Search And Check,Enter Text Direct,${term}
Search And Check,Assert Presence,${expected}
```

Each pass sets `term` and `expected` from the same position in their lists: first `trail` and `Trail Runner 2`, then `pace` and `Pace Knit`, and so on. Add `term,placeholder` and `expected,placeholder` to your elements file for dry runs.

## Repeat a module a number of times

Give a count instead of lists:

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2
Fill Cart,Run Loop,Add One Item,3
```

## Keep the data in a file

Lists can live in an elements file, as `shoppers` does above, or as a JSON list: `sizes,"[""8"",""9"",""10""]"`. For a single value from a larger data file, such as the email address of the admin user, use `Read Data`:

`test_data/users.csv`:

```csv
username,email,role
ava,ava@birch.shop,admin
ben,ben@birch.shop,shopper
```

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2,param_3
Sign In As Admin,Read Data,admin_email,test_data/users.csv,role == 'admin';select=email
Sign In As Admin,Enter Text,${email_field},${admin_email}
```

The query picks rows with a filter (`role == 'admin'`) and columns with `select=`. Compare values as quoted text, because every value in the file is read as text. `Read Data` is designed to fetch one row; with several matching rows, the variable gets a combined value that's hard to use.

## Rules inside a loop

Steps inside a looped module run a little differently from top-level steps:

- **Only the first value of each element is used.** Fallbacks don't apply, so give looped elements a reliable first value.
- **`name=value` parameters aren't available.** Pass values in order instead.
- **The module's steps don't appear separately** in the run tree or the JUnit report. A failure names the step that failed in its message.
- **After the loop, the variable keeps its last value.**

## See also

- [Variables](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/variables)
- [Conditions and loops](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/conditions)
- [Flow control keywords](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/flow)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/conditions

# Conditions and loops

> Run different modules depending on what's on screen or in a variable, and handle optional screens such as popups.

Most tests follow one path. Sometimes the app doesn't: a welcome popup appears only on first launch, a returning user skips sign-in, or a feature is behind a flag. Optics handles these with three keywords: `Detect And Press` for optional taps, `Condition` for branches, and `Execute Module` for running one module from another.

## Tap something only if it appears

For a popup that may or may not show, `Detect And Press` waits for the element and taps it if it appears. If it doesn't, the step still passes:

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2
Launch Birch,Launch App
Launch Birch,Detect And Press,Allow notifications,5
Launch Birch,Detect And Press,Not now,5
```

The second value is how many seconds to wait (30 by default). Keep it short: the step always waits the full time when the element never appears.

## Branch with Condition

`Condition` checks one or more conditions in order and runs the module paired with the first one that's true:

```text
Condition, <condition 1>, <module 1>, <condition 2>, <module 2>, …, <otherwise module>
```

The last module, with no condition in front of it, runs when nothing matched. It's optional.

### Branch on what's on screen

A condition can be a **module name**. Optics runs that module: if it passes, the condition is true. Write a small module that checks for something, and use it as the test:

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2,param_3
Is Signed In,Assert Presence,Picked for you,5
Start Shopping,Condition,Is Signed In,Go To Search,Sign In
```

If the home screen's *Picked for you* appears within 5 seconds, Optics runs `Go To Search`. Otherwise it runs `Sign In`. Put `!` in front to flip a condition: `Condition,!Is Signed In,Sign In`.

**Warning:**
The checking module really runs, so keep it to checks with short timeouts. A failed check waits its full timeout, and an action in it would change the app.

### Branch on a variable

A condition can also be an **expression** that compares variables:

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2,param_3,param_4,param_5
Choose Flow,Condition,${account_type} == 'business',Business Checkout,${account_type} == 'gift',Gift Checkout,Standard Checkout
```

Optics puts each variable's value in quotes before checking, so always compare with **quoted text**: `${account_type} == 'business'`, `${count} == '3'`.

### Compare numbers

Because values are compared as text, `${count} > 5` fails. Compute the comparison with `Evaluate` first, then check its result:

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2,param_3
Check Cart,Evaluate,cart_is_big,${count} > 5
Check Cart,Condition,${cart_is_big} == 'True',Offer Free Shipping
```

`Evaluate` puts values into the expression without quotes, so `${count} > 5` works there and stores `True` or `False`. Declare `cart_is_big,placeholder` in your elements file for dry runs.

## Run one module from another

`Execute Module` runs a module's steps as part of another module:

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1
Buy Trail Runners,Execute Module,Sign In
Buy Trail Runners,Execute Module,Search For Shoes
Buy Trail Runners,Press Element,Add to cart
```

A module name written on its own as a step doesn't run that module. Use `Execute Module`.

## Rules for modules run by these keywords

Modules run by `Condition`, `Execute Module` and [`Run Loop`](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/data-driven) follow simpler rules than top-level steps:

- Each element uses only its **first value**. Fallbacks don't apply.
- **`name=value` parameters aren't available.** Give values in order: `Assert Presence,Picked for you,5`, not `timeout_str=5`.
- Their steps don't appear separately in the run tree. A failure message names the step that failed.

If a branch needs fallbacks, give it its own test case instead and choose which test cases run with `include` and `exclude` in `config.yaml`.

## See also

- [Variables](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/variables)
- [Data-driven tests](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/data-driven)
- [Flow control keywords](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/flow)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/api-calls

# Call APIs in a test

> Call an HTTP API in the middle of a test, check the response, and use values from it in later steps.

Some steps are faster or more reliable through an API than through the screen: creating a test account, fetching today's offer code, or checking that an order reached the backend. `Invoke API` calls an endpoint you describe in a YAML file, checks the response, and saves values from it as variables for later steps.

The example on this page runs as written. It uses [DummyJSON](https://dummyjson.com), a free public API for testing.

### Describe the API

Create a YAML file anywhere in the project, with a top-level `api:` key. Group endpoints into **collections**, each with a base URL:

`test_data/api.yaml`:

```yaml
api:
  collections:
    dummyjson:
      name: "DummyJSON"
      base_url: "https://dummyjson.com"
      global_headers:
        content-type: "application/json"
      apis:
        login:
          name: "Sign in"
          endpoint: "/auth/login"
          request:
            method: POST
            body:
              username: "${api_username}"
              password: "${api_password}"
          expected_result:
            jsonpath_assertions:
              - path: $.accessToken
                condition: "len($) > 0"
            extract:
              access_token: $.accessToken
        me:
          name: "Who am I"
          endpoint: "/auth/me"
          request:
            method: GET
            headers:
              Authorization: "Bearer ${access_token}"
          expected_result:
            extract:
              email: $.email
```

- **`request`** sets the method, headers and a JSON body. `${name}` is replaced anywhere in the endpoint, headers and body.
- **`jsonpath_assertions`** checks the response. `path` picks a value, and `condition` is a small expression where `$` stands for that value. A false condition fails the step.
- **`extract`** saves values from the response as variables, using JSONPath: `$.accessToken`, `$.customer.id`, `$.items[0].name`.

### Add the inputs to your elements file

`test_data/elements.csv`:

```csv
Element_Name,Element_ID
api_username,emilys
api_password,emilyspass
access_token,placeholder
email,placeholder
```

The `placeholder` rows let `optics dry_run` accept variables that only get their value during the run.

### Call the endpoints in a module

Refer to an endpoint as `collection.name`:

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1
Sign In Over The API,Invoke API,dummyjson.login
Sign In Over The API,Invoke API,dummyjson.me
```

Add a test case that runs the module:

`test_cases/test_cases.csv`:

```csv
test_case,test_step
API sign in works,Sign In Over The API
```

The first call signs in and saves `access_token`. The second sends the token and saves the account's `email`. From here, any step can use `${email}`: type it into a field, check it on screen, or compare it in a [condition](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/conditions).

A project with only API steps still needs a `config.yaml` with a driver enabled, but the driver doesn't open anything unless a step asks it to.

### Run it

```shell
$ optics execute api-demo
```

```terminal
└── API sign in works                                       |  1.31s |    PASS
    └── Sign In Over The API                                |  1.31s |    PASS
        ├── Invoke API (dummyjson.login)                    |  0.66s |    PASS
        └── Invoke API (dummyjson.me)                       |  0.64s |    PASS
```

Every request and response is logged to `execution_output/api_details.log`, and to `api_details.har`, which you can open in a browser's developer tools.

## Combine API and UI steps

A common pattern is to set up data through the API, then check it in the app:

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2
Order Shows In App,Invoke API,birch.create_order
Order Shows In App,Press Element,Orders
Order Shows In App,Assert Presence,${order_number}
```

Creating the order through the API takes a second. Going through the checkout screens takes a minute and tests something you probably cover elsewhere.

## Good to know

- **Responses must be JSON** when an endpoint has `expected_result`. Other responses fail the step.
- **Check status codes with an assertion.** `expected_status` and `json_schema` are accepted in the file but not checked yet. Check a field in the body instead.
- **Every request times out after 30 seconds.** `request.timeout` isn't used yet.
- **Keep credentials out of the file.** Put them in variables and read them from the environment with `Read Data,api_password,ENV:BIRCH_API_PASSWORD`. See [Variables](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/variables#hide-sensitive-values).
- **The top-level key must be `api:`.** A file starting with `apis:` is recognised but loads nothing.

## See also

- [Invoke API reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/flow#invoke-api)
- [Variables](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/variables)
- [Conditions and loops](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/conditions)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/http-api

# Run keywords over HTTP

> Start a local Optics server and drive a device or browser from your own service, one keyword per request.

`optics serve` runs Optics as a small web server on your machine. Another program, such as an internal dashboard, a test orchestrator or a script in another language, can then open a session on a device and run keywords on it with plain HTTP requests. Each request runs one keyword and returns its result.

Use the server when something other than Optics decides what to do next. If you want to run a suite, `optics execute` is simpler. If an AI agent is the caller, use [MCP](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/agent) instead.

### Start the server

```shell
$ optics serve
```

It listens on `http://127.0.0.1:8000`. Check it's up:

```shell
$ curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/health
{"status":"Optics Framework API is running","version":"1.10.5"}
```

Use `--port` to change the port. Interactive API docs are at `http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs` while the server runs.

### Start a session

A session is one connection to a device or browser. Send the same settings you'd put in `config.yaml`:

```shell
$ curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/sessions/start \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d '{
      "driver_sources": ["playwright"],
      "elements_sources": ["playwright_find_element", "playwright_page_source", "playwright_screenshot"]
    }'
{"session_id":"23db1bdc-07d8-4cca-bfaa-1e9deaf4b794","driver_id":"PLAYWRIGHT_SESSION","status":"created"}
```

Keep the `session_id`. Starting a session also opens the app, as `Launch App` would. For a phone, pass an Appium entry with its URL and capabilities:

```json
{
  "driver_sources": [{"appium": {"url": "http://127.0.0.1:4723", "capabilities": {
    "platformName": "Android", "automationName": "UiAutomator2",
    "deviceName": "emulator-5554", "appPackage": "com.birch.shop", "appActivity": ".MainActivity"}}}],
  "elements_sources": ["appium_find_element", "appium_page_source", "appium_screenshot"]
}
```

### Run keywords

Send one keyword per request, with its values in order:

```shell
$ curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/sessions/$SESSION/action \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d '{"mode": "keyword", "keyword": "Launch Other App", "params": ["https://www.saucedemo.com"]}'
{"execution_id":"ebbdc919-…","status":"SUCCESS","data":{"result":null}}

$ curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/sessions/$SESSION/action \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d '{"mode": "keyword", "keyword": "Assert Presence", "params": ["Accepted usernames are"]}'
{"execution_id":"71f5ee34-…","status":"SUCCESS","data":{"result":true}}
```

Keyword names work in any case: `Assert Presence` or `assert_presence`. `params` can also be an object of named values, such as `{"element": "Login", "index": "1"}`. A list inside it gives fallbacks: `{"element": ["//input[@id='login-button']", "Login"]}`.

### Look at the screen

```shell
$ curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/sessions/$SESSION/screenshot \
    | python3 -c 'import sys,json,base64; open("screen.png","wb").write(base64.b64decode(json.load(sys.stdin)["data"]["result"]))'
```

`/elements` lists the elements on screen, and `/source` returns the UI tree.

### Stop the session

```shell
$ curl -X DELETE http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/sessions/$SESSION/stop
{"status":"terminated"}
```

This closes the app and ends the session.

## Follow a session live

Two endpoints stream updates as [server-sent events](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Server-sent_events):

- `/v1/sessions/{id}/events` sends a message when each keyword starts, passes or fails.
- `/v1/sessions/{id}/workspace/stream` sends a new screenshot and element list whenever the screen changes, which is handy for showing a live view of the device.

```shell
$ curl -N http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/sessions/$SESSION/events
```

## Keep the server safe

The server has **no authentication**, and it accepts requests from any web page your browser opens. Anyone who can reach it can control the connected device.

- Keep the default `--host 127.0.0.1`, so only your machine can reach it.
- If another machine must call it, put it behind a proxy that adds authentication, on a trusted network.
- Run one worker (the default). Sessions live in the server's memory, so several workers would lose track of each other's sessions.

## See also

- [HTTP API reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/http-api), with every endpoint and field
- The [OpenAPI document](https://optics-framework.org/openapi.json), for generating a client
- [Let your AI agent build tests](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/agent)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/generate

# Generate pytest or Robot code

> Turn a CSV or YAML suite into a pytest or Robot Framework file you can extend with code.

`optics generate` reads a suite and writes the same test as code: a pytest file or a Robot Framework file. Use it when a suite needs logic the files can't express, or when you're moving a suite into a codebase that already runs everything through pytest or Robot.

The generated file is a starting point. Once you edit it, it no longer follows the suite files, so keep the suite as the source of truth for as long as you can.

## Generate a file

```shell
$ optics generate birch-tests
Generated test file: birch-tests/generated/Tests/test_generated.py
Generated requirements file: birch-tests/generated/requirements.txt
```

For Robot Framework:

```shell
$ optics generate birch-tests --framework robot --output checkout.robot
```

| Option | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--framework` | `pytest` | `pytest` or `robot`. |
| `--output` | `test_generated.py` or `test_generated.robot` | The file name. It's always written to `<project>/generated/Tests/`. |

The project needs a file named exactly `config.yaml`, plus test cases, modules and an elements file.

## What you get

Each module becomes a function (or Robot keyword), each test case becomes a test, and elements become a dictionary:

`generated/Tests/test_generated.py`:

```python
ELEMENTS = {
    'username_field': "//input[@id='user-name']",
    'login_button': "//input[@id='login-button']",
}

def sign_in(optics: Optics) -> None:
    optics.enter_text(ELEMENTS['username_field'], 'standard_user')
    optics.press_element(ELEMENTS['login_button'])
    optics.assert_presence('Products')

def test_shopper_can_add_a_backpack(optics):
    open_the_store(optics)
    sign_in(optics)
```

Run it with pytest from the `generated/Tests` folder:

```shell
$ pip install -r birch-tests/generated/requirements.txt
$ cd birch-tests/generated/Tests
$ pytest test_generated.py
```

**Generated code fails to run on Optics 1.10.5:**
In 1.10.5, the generated file uses config names that `Optics.setup()` doesn't accept, and values containing single quotes break the Python syntax. A fix is on its way in the next release. Until then, in the generated file, rename `driver_config` to `driver_sources`, `element_source_config` to `elements_sources`, `text_config` to `text_detection` and `image_config` to `image_detection`, and write XPaths in your elements file with double quotes, such as `//input[@id="user-name"]`.

## What isn't converted

- **Only the first value of each element** is used. Fallbacks are dropped. Pass a list to keep them: `optics.press_element([ELEMENTS['login_button'], 'Login'])`.
- **Flow-control keywords** (Run Loop, Condition, Read Data, Evaluate, Invoke API and others) and a few more, such as Select Dropdown Option, aren't converted. Steps that use them are left out of the generated code silently. Check the output against your modules.
- **Suite Setup and Suite Teardown** become ordinary tests.
- **Image templates** are copied only if they're in an `input_templates/` folder at the project's top level.

## See also

- [Use Optics from Python](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/python)
- [Use Optics in Robot Framework](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/robot)
- [CLI reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/cli)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/guides/

# Test Android TV, Samsung Tizen and LG webOS apps with one framework

> Test Android TV, Samsung Tizen and LG webOS apps with one tool and remote-control keys.

You can test a TV app the way a viewer uses it: press arrow keys on the remote, open a tile, start playback and check what's on screen. Optics drives Android TV, Samsung Tizen and LG webOS through **Appium**, the same server it uses for phones. Your tests are rows in CSV files, so one suite style covers your phone, web and TV apps.

This page walks you through the job and links to the pages that hold the details. [Test TV apps](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/tv) is the full reference.

## Check what each TV supports

Each TV platform has its own Appium driver. You pick it with `platformName` in `config.yaml`.

| TV platform | `platformName` | How you move around | How Optics sees the screen |
|---|---|---|---|
| Android TV | `Android` | Android key numbers, plus taps and typing | UI tree and screenshots, like an Android phone |
| Samsung Tizen | `TizenTV` | Remote key names only | Page source and screenshots |
| LG webOS | `LGTV` | Remote key names only | Screenshots, plus OCR to read text |

Tizen and webOS TVs have no touch screen. Touch and typing keywords, such as Press Element, Swipe and Enter Text, fail with **E0105** there. You move the focus with Press Keycode instead. [What doesn't work on Tizen and webOS](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/tv#what-doesnt-work-on-tizen-and-webos) lists every keyword.

## Set up

### Install Optics and Appium

[Install Optics](https://optics-framework.org/docs/get-started/install), then add the Appium engine and the Appium server:

```shell
$ optics setup --install appium
$ npm install -g appium
```

### Prepare the TV

Turn on developer mode on the TV, install the vendor's tools, and put the TV on the same network as your machine. Each Appium driver's project page covers these steps.

### Add the driver for your TV

- **Android TV** uses the same setup as an Android phone. Follow [Test Android apps](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/android) and connect with `adb connect <tv-ip>`.
- **Samsung Tizen**: `appium driver install --source=npm appium-tizen-tv-driver`, then copy the [Tizen config](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/tv#samsung-tizen).
- **LG webOS**: `appium driver install --source=npm appium-lg-webos-driver`, then copy the [webOS config](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/tv#lg-webos) and add an OCR engine with `optics setup --install easyocr`.

### Check the setup

Start `appium` in another terminal, then run `optics doctor` on your project. On Tizen and webOS, the doctor warns about phone settings such as `appActivity`. You can ignore those warnings as long as `config: driver` and `config: appium element source` show ✅. See [Check the setup](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/tv#check-the-setup).

## Write the test with remote keys

A TV test is a list of key presses with a check after each page change. This module opens the second tile in a row and checks the title:

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2
Open Birch TV,Launch App
Open Birch TV,Assert Presence,Featured,30
Open the second shoe,Press Keycode,DOWN
Open the second shoe,Press Keycode,RIGHT
Open the second shoe,Press Keycode,ENTER
Open the second shoe,Assert Presence,Trail Runner 2,10
```

On Tizen and webOS, Press Keycode takes key names such as `UP`, `ENTER`, `BACK` and `PLAY`. On Android TV, it takes Android key numbers instead: `19` to `22` for the arrows and `23` for Select. [Move around with remote keys](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/tv#move-around-with-remote-keys) has both tables.

To type on a Tizen or webOS TV, move over the on-screen keyboard with arrow keys and press `ENTER` on each letter.

## Keep TV tests reliable

- **Assert after each page change.** Keys don't wait for the app. Assert Presence waits for the next page, so the next key lands in the right place.
- **Start from a known place.** Begin each test with Launch App and an assertion on the first screen.
- **Check text that's drawn large and clear.** On webOS, Assert Presence reads the screen with OCR.
- **Use images for icons.** Add [image matching](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/text-and-images) when a tile or button has no text.

## Run it on every build

Run the suite with `optics execute`, as you would a phone suite. Before each run, Optics checks that the Appium server answers. It doesn't check the TV itself, so make sure the TV is on and reachable. [Run tests in CI](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/ci) covers the JUnit report your CI system reads.

## See also

- [Test TV apps](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/tv), the full TV reference
- [Supported platforms](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/)
- [Press Keycode](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/actions#press-keycode)
- [Find elements by text and image](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/text-and-images)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/guides/protected-apps

# Test apps that block screenshots or USB debugging

> Automate a banking or streaming app on a locked phone, with a Bluetooth dongle for input and a camera for eyes.

Some apps can't be tested the usual way. Banking and streaming apps often block screenshots, so a driver sees a black screen. Locked company phones and retail devices don't allow USB debugging or developer mode, so Appium can't connect at all.

Optics can still test them. It needs no automation software on the device. A **BLE dongle** pairs with the phone as an ordinary Bluetooth mouse and keyboard, and a **camera** pointed at the screen shows Optics what's there. Optics reads text in the camera picture with OCR, finds icons with image matching, then moves the pointer and taps.

This page helps you decide whether you need this setup and points you to each step. [Test production devices](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/production) is the full reference.

## Decide if you need it

Use the Bluetooth and camera setup when:

- **The app blocks screenshots.** The camera sees the screen anyway.
- **USB debugging or developer mode isn't allowed** on the device.
- **You monitor the live app.** The same journey runs on a real, unmodified device and app, the way a customer uses it.

If Appium or a browser driver can reach the device, use them instead. They're faster, read the UI tree directly, and support every keyword. See [Supported platforms](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/).

## Get the hardware

- **A USB serial BLE HID dongle**, which plugs into your machine as a serial port.
- **A camera or capture card** that your machine sees as a webcam, or a TCP frame server that sends a picture on request.
- **A stand** that holds the camera square over the screen, so the picture doesn't shift between runs.

You also need an OCR engine, such as EasyOCR, to read text in the camera picture.

## Set up

### Install the engines

```shell
$ optics setup --install ble easyocr
```

### Pair the dongle and frame the screen

Pair the dongle with the device like any Bluetooth keyboard. Then mount the camera straight on, with the screen upright and filling the picture edge to edge. [Set up](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/production#set-up) shows how to find the dongle's serial port on macOS, Linux and Windows.

### Write config.yaml

Enable the `ble` driver with the dongle's port and the screen size, a `camera_screenshot` element source, and an OCR engine. Copy the [example config](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/production#write-configyaml) and change the port and sizes.

### Calibrate the pointer

Tap a far corner with `Press By Percentage,90,90` and adjust the pointer units until the tap lands. [Calibrate the pointer](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/production#calibrate-the-pointer) has the five steps. Calibrate again whenever you move the camera or change the device.

## Write the test with visible text

There's no UI tree on this setup, so XPath doesn't work. Every element is text that OCR can read on screen, or a cropped image of an icon. Start the app by tapping its icon on the home screen, because Launch App doesn't work over Bluetooth:

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2
Open Birch,Press Element,Birch
Open Birch,Assert Presence,Sign in,20
Sign in,Enter Text,Email,ava@birch.shop
Sign in,Enter Text,Password,@:trailrunner
Sign in,Press Element,Sign in
Sign in,Assert Presence,Trail Runner 2,20
```

Enter Text finds the field by OCR, taps it, then types through the Bluetooth keyboard. The `@:` prefix masks the password in logs. See [Keep data in elements too](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/define#keep-data-in-elements-too).

## Know the limits

- **No app launch.** Launch App and Launch Other App don't work. Start the app by hand, or tap its icon.
- **No phone-only keys.** A Bluetooth keyboard has no Back, Volume or Power key. Tap the app's own back button.
- **No end-of-run error detection.** It needs the page source. Add Assert Presence checks for the error messages you care about.
- **Scroll moves up and down only.**

[What works and what doesn't](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/production#what-works-and-what-doesnt) lists every keyword, and [Known gaps](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/production#known-gaps) covers version-specific issues.

## Make text easier to read

Most failures on this setup come from the camera picture. Light the screen evenly, avoid glare, and keep the camera in focus. When the same word appears twice, search one part of the screen with an [area of interest](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/area-of-interest).

## See also

- [Test production devices](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/production), the full reference
- [Find elements by text and image](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/text-and-images)
- [Engines reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/engines)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/guides/ai-agent-phone

# Let your AI agent drive a real phone over MCP

> Give Claude Code, Cursor or Codex eyes and hands on a real Android phone or iPhone over MCP.

Your coding agent can read code, but it can't see your app running. `optics mcp` changes that. It's a [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) server that turns every Optics keyword into a tool your agent can call, and the phone's screen into something it can read. The agent can open the app, tap through a flow, reproduce a bug, then write what it did as a test you run again later.

Optics doesn't call any AI service in this mode. The model is whichever one your agent already uses.

This page covers the phone case from start to finish. [Let your AI agent build tests](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/agent) covers browsers and every client, and the [MCP server reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/mcp) lists every tool.

## Before you begin

- **An MCP client**, such as Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Claude Desktop or VS Code.
- **A phone the agent can reach through Appium.** Optics drives phones through an Appium server on your machine.
  - **Android**: turn on USB debugging, connect the cable and accept the prompt. Check that `adb devices` lists the phone. See [Test Android apps](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/android).
  - **iPhone**: a Mac with Xcode, Developer Mode on the phone, and WebDriverAgent signed with your Apple developer team. See [Test on a real device](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/ios#test-on-a-real-device).
- **The Appium server running** in a terminal: `appium`.

An emulator or simulator works the same way, if you'd rather start there.

## Set up

### Install the MCP server

The MCP server is a separate extra. Install it with the Appium engine, in the same environment as Optics:

```shell
$ pip install "optics-framework[mcp,appium]"
```

If you used the installer, run `~/.optics/venv/bin/pip install "optics-framework[mcp,appium]"` instead.

### Add Optics to your agent

**Claude Code**

```shell
$ claude mcp add optics -- optics mcp
```
**Cursor**

Add this to `.cursor/mcp.json` in your project, or `~/.cursor/mcp.json` for every project:

`.cursor/mcp.json`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "optics": { "command": "optics", "args": ["mcp"] }
  }
}
```
**Codex**

```shell
$ codex mcp add optics -- optics mcp
```
**Other clients**

Most clients read a JSON file that lists MCP servers, in this shape:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "optics": { "command": "optics", "args": ["mcp"] }
  }
}
```

If your agent can't find `optics`, use its full path, for example `~/.optics/bin/optics`.

### Ask for a flow

Tell the agent which phone and app to use, and what to do. Give it the Appium URL and the capabilities, including the phone's serial from `adb devices` as `udid`:

```text
Use the optics tools to start an appium session at http://127.0.0.1:4723
with platformName Android, udid R58M12ABCDE and appPackage com.birch.shop.
Sign in as ava@birch.shop, add Trail Runner 2 to the cart, and check
that the cart shows 1 item. Tell me each step you took.
```

For an iPhone, use `platformName iOS`, the phone's `udid` and the app's `bundleId`.

## What the agent does

A typical session goes like this:

1. **Start a session.** `start_session` connects to Appium with your capabilities and opens the app. It returns a `session_id` for every later call.
2. **Look at the screen.** The agent calls `screenshot` and reads the list of elements on screen, each with a label and what it can do with it.
3. **Act.** It calls keyword tools such as `press_element`, `enter_text` and `assert_presence`, with a label or locator from that list. It looks again after each action.
4. **End the session.** `terminate_session` closes the app.

The agent taps by name, not by position. Coordinate taps are hidden by default, because tests that guess positions break on any other screen size. See [Hidden coordinate taps](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/mcp#hidden-coordinate-taps).

## Keep the run as a test

What the agent did on the phone can become a suite you run without it. Ask it to save the flow:

```text
Read optics://project-format and write the steps you ran as an
Optics suite in ./checkout, with a config.yaml for this phone.
Run optics dry_run on it and fix any errors.
```

The agent writes the same CSV files a person would: test cases, modules and elements. Review them like a colleague's pull request, then run them:

```shell
$ optics execute checkout
```

The run writes a JUnit report and screenshots to `execution_output/`. See [Read the results](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/results).

## Know the limits

- **No loops or conditions as tools.** `Run Loop`, `Condition` and the other flow-control keywords only work inside suite files. The agent can still write them there.
- **No record button.** The agent writes the suite files itself, using `optics://project-format`.
- **Sessions are private to the server.** `optics serve` and `optics live` can't see an MCP session, and it ends when the server stops.
- **Apps that block screenshots.** The agent sees what the driver sees. For an app that blocks screenshots, see [Test apps that block screenshots](https://optics-framework.org/docs/guides/protected-apps).

## See also

- [Let your AI agent build tests](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/agent)
- [MCP server reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/mcp)
- [Test Android apps](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/android)
- [Test iOS apps](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/ios)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/guides/optics-vs-maestro

# Optics vs Maestro

> Compare two open-source UI test frameworks on platforms, test format, finding elements, TVs, AI agents and where tests run.

Optics and Maestro both let you write end-to-end UI tests as plain files, run them on emulators, devices and browsers, and hand a device to an AI agent over MCP. Both are open source under Apache 2.0. They differ in what they can reach, how they find things on screen, and where tests run.

This page sets out the facts so you can pick the one that fits your apps. Maestro facts come from [Maestro's documentation](https://docs.maestro.dev) and its [GitHub repository](https://github.com/mobile-dev-inc/maestro), checked in October 2026. Maestro changes quickly, so check its docs for anything that matters to your decision.

## At a glance

| | Optics | Maestro |
|---|---|---|
| Licence | Apache 2.0. No paid edition. | Apache 2.0 for the open-source CLI. [Maestro Cloud](https://docs.maestro.dev/maestro-cloud) is a hosted service that needs an account. |
| Android | Emulators and real phones, through Appium | Emulators and physical devices |
| iOS | Simulators and signed real devices, through Appium | Simulators. Its README says physical iOS devices aren't supported yet. |
| Web | Playwright (Chromium) or Selenium (Chrome or Firefox) | Beta, Chromium only |
| TV | Android TV, Samsung Tizen and LG webOS | Android TV remote keys in `pressKey`. Tizen and webOS aren't listed as supported platforms. |
| Locked devices | Bluetooth mouse and keyboard plus a camera, no software on the device | Not covered in its docs |
| How it drives the app | Through a driver you run: Appium, Playwright, Selenium or a BLE dongle | A single binary that drives the app through the accessibility layer, with no separate drivers. The CLI needs Java 17 or newer. |
| Test format | CSV or YAML rows of keywords, split into test cases, modules and elements. Also Python and Robot Framework. | YAML flows, with JavaScript for logic |
| Finding elements | Several values per element, then XPath, UI-tree text, OCR and image matching in turn | Selectors on the accessibility layer, such as text and id |
| AI agent support | `optics mcp`, a separate extra | `maestro mcp`, built into the CLI |
| Where tests run | Your machine or CI. No hosted service. | Your machine or CI, or Maestro Cloud |

## Platforms

Optics drives Android and iOS apps through [Appium](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/android), websites through [Playwright or Selenium](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/web), and TV apps through Appium's TV drivers. iOS tests run on simulators or on a signed real device. See [Supported platforms](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/).

Maestro's [supported platforms](https://docs.maestro.dev/get-started/supported-platform) page lists Android emulators and physical devices, iOS simulators, and web. Its [web support](https://docs.maestro.dev/get-started/supported-platform/web-browser) is in beta and runs on Chromium only. Maestro works with native, React Native and Flutter apps, and its docs cover moving between apps and into system settings.

**If you need to test on a physical iPhone, Optics supports it today.** Maestro's README says that physical iOS devices aren't supported yet.

## TV apps

Optics tests [Android TV, Samsung Tizen and LG webOS](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/tv) through Appium, with remote-control keys. On Tizen and webOS, you move the focus with key names such as `UP` and `ENTER`, and touch keywords fail with E0105.

Maestro's [`pressKey`](https://docs.maestro.dev/reference/commands-available/presskey) command includes Android TV remote keys, such as `Remote Dpad Up` and `Remote Media Play Pause`. Its supported platforms page doesn't list Tizen or webOS.

## Locked devices and apps that block screenshots

Optics can test a device that has no automation software on it. A [BLE dongle](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/production) pairs with it as a Bluetooth mouse and keyboard, and a camera shows Optics the screen. This works when USB debugging is off or the app blocks screenshots. See [Test apps that block screenshots](https://optics-framework.org/docs/guides/protected-apps).

Maestro's docs don't cover this kind of setup.

## Test format

An Optics test is rows in CSV or YAML files. Each row is a keyword and its values, such as `Press Element,${sign_in}`. Steps live in reusable modules, test cases list modules, and elements live in their own file, so a changed button means one edit. Anyone who can use a spreadsheet can read the suite. You can also call the same keywords from [Python](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/python) or [Robot Framework](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/robot). See [Write a test suite](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/write).

A Maestro test is a [flow](https://docs.maestro.dev/maestro-flows), a YAML file of commands such as `tapOn` and `assertVisible`. Logic and data go in [JavaScript](https://docs.maestro.dev/maestro-flows/javascript/javascript-overview), with `runScript` and `evalScript`.

## Finding elements

Optics gives each element several identities and tries them in order. You can list an XPath, visible text and an image for the same button. Text is looked up in the UI tree first, then read from a screenshot with OCR. Images are found by matching a cropped picture on the screen. When a redesign breaks one value, the next one takes over. See [How Optics finds elements](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/).

On top of that, optional [AI self-heal](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/self-heal) asks an AI model to finish a step when every value fails. It's off by default.

Maestro finds elements through the accessibility layer, with [selectors](https://docs.maestro.dev/reference/selectors/core-selectors) such as text and id. Its docs describe experimental AI commands: [`assertWithAI`](https://docs.maestro.dev/reference/commands-available/assertwithai) checks the screen against a sentence, and [`extractTextWithAI`](https://docs.maestro.dev/reference/commands-available/extracttextwithai) reads text from a screenshot into a variable. Its docs don't describe finding an element to tap by OCR or by a template image.

**If your app draws text in images, canvases or video players, Optics can find it.** Its OCR and image fallbacks work when the UI tree is empty.

## Waiting

Maestro [waits automatically](https://docs.maestro.dev/get-started/what-is-maestro) for content and animations, so you rarely add sleeps.

In Optics, assertions such as Assert Presence wait up to their timeout, but action keywords don't wait. Put an assertion before a step that needs a new screen. See [Action keywords don't wait](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/#action-keywords-dont-wait).

## Creating tests and AI agents

Optics has four ways to create a test, and each writes the same files:

- [Write it](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/write) in a spreadsheet or editor.
- [Record it](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/record) in `optics live`, a terminal session that runs each step on the device and saves the ones that work.
- [Describe it](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/describe) in plain English, and an AI model drives the app.
- [Delegate it](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/agent) to your AI agent through `optics mcp`.

The `optics mcp` server gives the agent a tool for each keyword and resources for the screenshot, the elements on screen and the project format. The agent then writes a suite for `optics execute`. See the [MCP server reference](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/mcp).

Maestro has [Maestro Studio](https://docs.maestro.dev/maestro-studio), a desktop app for building and debugging flows visually. Its [MCP server](https://docs.maestro.dev/get-started/maestro-mcp) ships inside the CLI. It lets the agent inspect the screen, take screenshots, run inline YAML and submit runs to Maestro Cloud, and it includes Maestro Viewer, a web view of the device.

## Running and reporting

Optics runs on your machine or in CI. A run writes a JUnit report and annotated screenshots to `execution_output/`, and [error detection](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/error-detection) can fail a run that ends on a crash dialog. One run uses one device. To test several devices at once, start one `optics execute` process per device. See [Run tests in CI](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/ci).

The Maestro CLI runs flows locally or in CI. It writes JUnit or HTML reports, and its [`--shards` options](https://docs.maestro.dev/maestro-cli/maestro-cli-commands-and-options) split a run across connected devices. Maestro Cloud runs flows in parallel on hosted devices, and needs a Maestro Cloud account.

## Which one fits

Choose **Optics** when you need:

- Smart TVs on Tizen or webOS, physical iPhones, or locked devices.
- Elements that the UI tree can't see, found with OCR or image matching.
- Suites that non-developers read and edit in a spreadsheet.
- Python or Robot Framework from the same keywords.

Choose **Maestro** when you want:

- A single binary with no Appium server to run.
- Automatic waiting with no extra assertions.
- A desktop app for building tests visually.
- A hosted service that runs suites in parallel for you.

## See also

- [What Optics adds to Appium](https://optics-framework.org/docs/guides/optics-and-appium)
- [Get started with Optics](https://optics-framework.org/docs/get-started/)
- [Frequently asked questions](https://optics-framework.org/docs/help/faq)

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/guides/optics-and-appium

# What Optics adds to Appium

> Optics runs on top of Appium. Keep your Appium server and devices, and add readable suites, fallback locators, OCR and AI agents.

Optics doesn't replace Appium. For Android, iOS and TV apps, Optics drives the device **through** an Appium server. Appium still talks to the device. Optics decides what to press, finds it on screen several ways, and turns the steps into a suite anyone on the team can read.

If you already run Appium, you keep your server, drivers, devices and capabilities. Optics adds a layer on top.

## What stays the same

- **The Appium server.** You run it as before, locally or remotely. Set its address as `url` in `config.yaml`. A device farm works too, as long as you can reach its Appium server.
- **The drivers.** UiAutomator2 for Android and Android TV, XCUITest for iOS, and the Tizen and webOS drivers for TVs.
- **Your capabilities.** Optics reads only `platformName` and the app id. It passes every other capability to Appium unchanged. See [Appium capabilities](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/config#appium-capabilities).
- **Your inspector.** [Appium Inspector](https://github.com/appium/appium-inspector) still shows each element's id, text and XPath.
- **Driver commands.** The Execute Script keyword runs Appium `mobile:` commands. See [Execute Script](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/actions#execute-script).

## What Optics adds

### Tests anyone can read

An Optics test is rows in CSV or YAML files, not code. Each row is a keyword and its values:

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2
Sign in,Enter Text,${email_field},ava@birch.shop
Sign in,Press Element,${sign_in}
Sign in,Assert Presence,Picked for you,20
```

Steps live in reusable modules, and test cases list the modules they run. Testers can write and review the suite in a spreadsheet. See [Write a test suite](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/write).

### Locators that fall back

An Appium locator either matches or fails. In Optics, an element can have several values, and Optics tries them in order:

`test_data/elements.csv`:

```csv
Element_Name,Element_ID
sign_in,//*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/login']
sign_in,Sign in
sign_in,sign_in.png
```

When a redesign changes the id, the text value takes over. Name the element once, and every step that uses `${sign_in}` follows. See [Define elements](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/define).

### OCR and image matching

Text drawn inside an image, a canvas or a video player isn't in the UI tree, so Appium can't find it. Optics can. It reads text from a screenshot with OCR, and finds icons by matching a cropped picture. It uses them only after the UI tree fails, because they're slower. See [Find elements by text and image](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/text-and-images).

Optional [AI self-heal](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/self-heal) goes one step further. When every value fails, an AI model looks at the screen and tries to finish the step. It's off by default.

### A live recorder

`optics live` opens a terminal session next to the device. You type a step, it runs straight away, and the steps that work are saved as a module. You can also switch to plain-English mode and let an AI model drive. See [Record a test](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/record) and [Describe a test](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/describe).

### Data-driven tests

`Run Loop` runs one module for each value in a list, such as each user or search term. See [Run a flow with different data](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/data-driven).

### An MCP server for AI agents

`optics mcp` lets an AI agent such as Claude Code or Cursor drive the device through Optics keywords, then write the suite. See [Let your AI agent drive a real phone over MCP](https://optics-framework.org/docs/guides/ai-agent-phone).

### Results and error screens

`optics execute` writes a JUnit report and a screenshot of each step. See [Read the results](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/results). [Error detection](https://optics-framework.org/docs/run/error-detection) fails a run that ends on a crash dialog or an error message you list.

### Targets beyond Appium

The same keywords run on websites through [Playwright or Selenium](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/web). Between phones and browsers, only `config.yaml` changes. On [locked devices](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/production), Optics skips Appium and taps through a Bluetooth mouse and keyboard, with a camera watching the screen.

## Keep your code if you want it

If your team writes tests in Python, you don't have to give that up. The `Optics` class exposes every keyword as a method, so you keep the fallbacks, OCR and image matching inside pytest. Robot Framework works the same way. See [Use Optics from Python](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/python) and [Use Optics in Robot Framework](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/robot).

`optics generate` goes the other way: it turns a CSV suite into a pytest or Robot Framework file. See [Generate pytest or Robot code](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/generate).

## Move existing Appium tests

Optics has no importer for Appium scripts. Rebuild each flow by [recording](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/record) it in `optics live`, or ask an AI agent to explore the app and write the suite through [MCP](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/agent). Your config can point at the Appium server and capabilities you already use.

## Get started

- [Test Android apps](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/android): Set up Appium and adb, then run on a phone or emulator.
- [Test iOS apps](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/ios): Run on a simulator or a signed device with XCUITest.
- [Test TV apps](https://optics-framework.org/docs/platforms/tv): Drive Android TV, Samsung Tizen and LG webOS.
- [Optics vs Maestro](https://optics-framework.org/docs/guides/optics-vs-maestro): Compare Optics with a framework that doesn't use Appium.

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/

# Reference

> Look up every command, setting, file format and keyword.

These pages describe Optics 1.10.5 exactly as it behaves. Use them when you know what you want to do and need the precise name, flag, column or code.

If you're new to Optics, start with the [quickstart](https://optics-framework.org/docs/get-started/quickstart) and come back here when you need a detail.

- [Keywords](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/): Every step you can write in a module, with its parameters and defaults.
- [CLI](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/cli): Every `optics` command, its flags, what it writes and its exit codes.
- [config.yaml](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/config): Every setting in a project's config.yaml, with examples for each platform.
- [Project files](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/files): The CSV and YAML formats for test cases, modules, elements, error definitions and API calls.
- [Engines and extras](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/engines): The drivers, element sources, OCR, image and LLM engines, and how to install them.
- [MCP server](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/mcp): The tools and resources `optics mcp` gives your AI agent.
- [HTTP API](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/http-api): The endpoints `optics serve` exposes, with request and response shapes.
- [Error codes](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/errors): What each Optics error code means and how to fix it.

---

Source: https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/

# Keywords

> Every keyword you can use in a step, grouped by what it does.

A keyword is one action or check, such as `Press Element` or `Assert Presence`. Each row of a module is one keyword followed by its parameters. This page covers the rules every keyword shares, then lists all of them.

`modules/modules.csv`:

```csv
module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2
Sign In,Enter Text,${email_field},ana@birch.example
Sign In,Press Element,${sign_in}
Sign In,Assert Presence,Welcome,20
```

## Keyword names

Write keyword names in Title Case in CSV and YAML files: `Press Element`, `Assert Presence`. In `optics live`, the MCP server and Python, the same keyword is written in snake_case: `press_element`, `assert_presence`.

The runner ignores capitalization and collapses spaces, so `Press Element`, `press element` and `press_element` all reach the same keyword. If you misspell a name, the error suggests the closest match. Run `optics list` to print every keyword name in snake_case.

## Parameters

Parameters are positional. They fill the keyword's parameters in the order shown in each parameter table on these pages.

To set a parameter by name, write `name=value`. This works only when `name` is a real parameter of that keyword. Use it to skip parameters you want to leave at their defaults:

```csv
Browse,Press Element,Trail Runner 2,index=1
```

Here `index=1` sets the fifth parameter of Press Element and leaves `repeat`, `offset_x` and `offset_y` at their defaults.

**Common mistake:**
Leaving a cell empty doesn't skip a parameter. Empty cells are dropped, so the next value slides into the empty slot. `Press By Percentage,50,90,,tap_cta` sets `repeat` to `tap_cta` and fails. Write `Press By Percentage,50,90,event_name=tap_cta` instead.

A value like `text=Sign in` or `css=#cart` stays positional, because `text` and `css` aren't parameter names. Values that start with `/`, `//` or `(` are never treated as named, and `==`, `!=`, `<=` and `>=` don't count as `=`.

**Note:**
Steps inside a module that runs through [Execute Module, Run Loop or Condition](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/flow) don't support `name=value`. Write every parameter positionally there.

### Every value is a string

Each keyword receives its parameters as text and converts them itself. Timeouts, counts, `index`, `repeat`, lengths and swipe percentages must be whole numbers. A decimal such as `2.5` fails the step. Timeouts are always in seconds.

## Element arguments

Many keywords take an `element`. Optics looks at the text you pass and decides what kind of locator it is. The checks run in this order, and the first match wins:

| If the value… | Optics reads it as |
|---|---|
| starts with `text=` | Text to find on screen |
| starts with `text_only:` | Text to find with OCR (reading the screenshot) only, skipping the app's UI tree |
| ends with `.png`, `.jpg`, `.jpeg` or `.bmp` | An image file name to find on screen |
| starts with `css=` | A CSS selector |
| starts with `xpath=`, `/`, `//` or `(` | An XPath, a path through the app's UI tree |
| starts with `android.` or `xcui` | A UI class name |
| contains `[` and `]`, starts with `.`, or starts with `#` followed by a letter | A CSS selector |
| anything else | Text to find on screen |

Text is matched against the app's UI tree first, then with OCR if you configured text detection. Image file names are matched by file name only, and Optics finds the file anywhere in your project folder. See [Text and images](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/text-and-images) for how matching works.

**Common mistake:**
Plain text that looks like another locator type is read as that type. `(optional)` starts with `(`, so it's read as an XPath. `Price [USD]` and `.com` are read as CSS selectors. Write `text=(optional)`, `text=Price [USD]` or `text=.com` to force text.

Other pitfalls:

- `id:` locators always fail. No element source supports them. Use an XPath such as `//*[@resource-id="com.birch.shop:id/cart"]`.
- The `text=` prefix is understood by the Appium and Playwright element sources. OCR and Selenium search for the whole value, including `text=`, so use it only where you need it.
- The `xpath=` prefix works only on Playwright. Use a bare `//…` XPath on Appium and Selenium.
- `.tif` and `.tiff` files aren't treated as images. Save templates as `.png`.

Most of the time you pass `${name}` instead and define the locator in your elements file. See [Define elements](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/define).

## Variables

A cell that is exactly `${name}` is replaced with the value of `name` from your elements file, or from a keyword that wrote it ([Read Data, Evaluate, Run Loop, Invoke API](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/flow)).

When an element has several values, Optics tries each one in order until the element is found. It moves on only when the element isn't found. Any other error fails the step at once. If `name` isn't defined anywhere, the step fails before the keyword runs.

**Common mistake:**
`${name}` is replaced only when it's the whole cell. `Hello ${name}` is typed literally, as `Hello ${name}`. The exceptions are expressions and queries in Evaluate, Condition, Read Data and Invoke API, which replace `${name}` anywhere inside them.

See [Variables](https://optics-framework.org/docs/advanced/variables) for how values are stored and passed between steps.

## Areas of interest

Keywords that find one element take four optional parameters: `aoi_x`, `aoi_y`, `aoi_width` and `aoi_height`. They limit the search to a rectangle of the screen, in percent from 0 to 100. The defaults `0`, `0`, `100`, `100` mean the whole screen.

```csv
Checkout,Press Element,Pay now,aoi_y=50,aoi_height=50
```

This searches the bottom half of the screen only. Assertion keywords don't take an area of interest. See [Area of interest](https://optics-framework.org/docs/elements/area-of-interest).

## Picking one of several matches

`index` picks which match to use when more than one element matches. It starts at `0`, the first match. `index=1` is the second match.

- Image matches are counted top to bottom, then left to right.
- On Appium, `index` doesn't apply to XPath. Write `(//android.widget.Button[@text="Add to cart"])[2]` to pick the second XPath match. XPath counts from 1.
- On Selenium, a non-zero `index` skips the native lookup, so only OCR and image matching can use it.

## Event names

Most action and app keywords take an optional `event_name`. When you set it, Optics records a timestamped event with that label right before the action. Events show in the live console and are sent to an events endpoint if you configured one. They never change whether a step passes.

## Action keywords don't wait

Press Element, Enter Text and the other action keywords look at the current screen once. If the element isn't there yet, the step fails at once. Put an assertion before an action when the screen may still be loading:

```csv
Search,Assert Presence,${search_bar},15
Search,Enter Text,${search_bar},Trail Runner 2
```

Use [Detect And Press](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/actions#detect-and-press) for pop-ups that may or may not appear. Assertion keywords are the only ones that wait. See [Verification keywords](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/verification).

## Keywords that never fail a step

These keywords pass even when you might expect a failure. Don't rely on them as checks.

- **Assert Equality** returns false on a mismatch but never fails. Use Assert Text to check text on screen.
- **Validate Screen** returns false when nothing is found but never fails.
- **Detect And Press** passes and skips the tap when the element doesn't appear.
- **Force Terminate App** on Appium logs any error and passes.
- **Swipe**, **Press By Coordinates** and **Scroll** on Appium log driver errors and pass. Scroll left or right on Appium does nothing and passes.
- **Assert Presence** and **Assert Visibility** pass without checking when every element you give is a CSS selector, an `id:` locator or a class name.
- **Initialise Setup** does nothing.

Keywords that return a value, such as Get Text, Execute Script and Capture Screenshot, can't store it in a variable from CSV or YAML. The value is returned to you over [`optics serve`](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/cli), MCP and [Python](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/python).

### Flow control

| Keyword | What it does | Page |
|---|---|---|
| Execute Module | Run another module | [Execute Module](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/flow#execute-module) |
| Run Loop | Repeat a module a number of times or once per value | [Run Loop](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/flow#run-loop) |

## Deprecated keywords

Press Checkbox and Press Radio Button still work but log a warning. Use [Press Element](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/actions#press-element) instead. Swipe Seekbar To Right Android fails on Appium. Use [Swipe From Element](https://optics-framework.org/docs/reference/keywords/actions#swipe-from-element) instead.

## Where each keyword works

- **CSV and YAML suites, `optics live` and `optics serve`** have every keyword on this page.
- **The MCP server** has every keyword except the flow-control ones. Press By Coordinates and Press By Percentage are hidden there unless you turn them on.
- **Python and Robot Framework** have every keyword except Execute Module, Initialise Setup and the three deprecated ones. Some parameters differ. See [Write tests in Python](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/python).
- **`optics generate`** skips flow-control keywords and a few others when it converts a suite to code.

## Python and Robot Framework only

These keywords exist only in the [Python library](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/python) and the [Robot Framework library](https://optics-framework.org/docs/create/robot). The CSV and YAML runner reports them as unknown keywords.

| Keyword | What it does |
|---|---|
| Setup | Create a session from a config dictionary or YAML text |
| Setup From File | Create a session from a config file |
| Quit | End the session |
| Add Element | Add a value to a variable, after any values it already has |
| Get Element Value | Return the list of values for a variable |
| Add API | Load API definitions for Invoke API |
| Add Module | Define a module for Run Loop and Condition |
| Add Testcase | Set the session's test cases |
| Add Error Definitions | Add on-screen error definitions |
| Capture And Detect Errors | Check the current screen for defined errors and return any matches |
| Press Element With Index | Press Element with an index |
